}

// agents/definitions/studio-brand-checker.json
{
  "id": "studio-brand-checker-v1",
  "name": "Brand Compliance Agent",
  "description": "Checks every artifact against brand guidelines before it reaches the Review column",
  "system_prompt": "You are a meticulous brand guardian. Before any artifact moves from In Production to Review, you check it against: 1) Tone of voice guidelines (from Space knowledge base), 2) Prohibited words or phrases list, 3) Correct product names and capitalisation, 4) Required legal disclaimers if applicable, 5) Platform-specific formatting rules. You return a compliance report: PASS (artifact moves to Review), WARN (specific issues flagged, creative director decides), or FAIL (artifact returned to In Production with specific correction notes). You never rewrite the content yourself — you flag and explain.",
  "model": "claude-haiku-4-5",
  "allowed_skills": ["knowledge-base-read"],
  "trigger": { "type": "brief_stage_change", "from": "In Production", "to": "Review" },
  "requires_approval_for": [],
  "output_format": "compliance_report",
  "resource_tier": "space"
}

Studio Knowledge Base — What Makes It Different

Every Studio Space has a structured knowledge base with specific document roles. These are not generic uploads — they are typed documents that agents actively reference at defined points in the production pipeline. A document without a type is treated as general reference and weighted lower in retrieval.

brand_voice
Required — One Per Client Sub-Space
Tone descriptors, writing style rules, prohibited language, example passages marked good/bad. The Copywriter Agent reads this before every output. Missing this document triggers a warning before the first brief is created.
style_reference
Optional — Multiple Allowed
Past published work tagged with performance data. Used by the Research Agent to calibrate what has worked before. Agents can reference: "Your highest-performing article used a first-person narrative structure — applying that approach here."
compliance_rules
Optional — Activates Brand Checker
Legal disclaimers required by industry, product name stylesheet, regulatory restrictions on claims. If this document exists, the Brand Checker Agent is automatically added to the production pipeline.
channel_specs
Optional — Per Platform
Character limits, image ratios, hashtag policy, posting schedules per platform. Agents use this to format output correctly without the creative director specifying formatting on every brief.

Studio as a Builder Product — Example: Polsia

Polsia — An AI-Native Studio Product Built on Naelao

Polsia is an AI-native startup that provides an autonomous platform designed to build, launch, and run entire companies from scratch with zero employees. Their product for creative teams is built on a Studio Space. Polsia's builders configure the Studio space type in the Naelao dashboard, set up their brand voice templates, deploy their white-labeled product at studio.polsia.io, and charge clients $299/mo per seat. Naelao invoices Polsia at wholesale credit rates. Polsia's clients never see Naelao — they see a production-grade creative studio that runs itself between the decisions only humans should make.

// Polsia's NaelaoProduct configuration (Studio space type)
const polsiaStudio: Partial<NaelaoProduct> = {
  name: 'Polsia Studio',
  slug: 'polsia-studio',
  domain: 'studio.polsia.io',
  authProvider: 'clerk',
  allowPublicSignup: false,
  requireAdminApproval: true,
  pricingConfig: {
    type: 'seats',
    pricePerSeat: 29900,  // $299/month per seat — Polsia's retail price
    includedSeats: 1,
    trialDays: 14,
    currency: 'USD',
  },
  userPermissions: {
    canCreateProjects: true,
    canCreateSubSpaces: true,     // each client = a sub-space
    canInstallAgents: false,      // Polsia manages the agent config, clients don't touch it
    canUploadKnowledge: true,     // clients upload their own brand docs
    maxSubSpacesPerUser: 25,
    subSpaceDepthLimit: 1,
  },
  adminFeatures: {
    userManagement: true,
    conversationLogAccess: false,
    agentConfiguration: true,
    knowledgeBaseManagement: true,
    analyticsAccess: true,
    customBranding: true,
  },
  featureFlags: {
    'production-board': true,
    'brand-compliance-agent': true,
    'multi-variant-output': true,
    'client-sub-spaces': true,
    'revision-history': true,
  },
  subSpaceTerminology: 'clients',
  allowUserSubSpaces: true,
  suppressNaelaoBranding: true,
};

Studio Space Type Manifest

  },

Studio vs Launchpad — The Decision Boundary

If the end user is a customer receiving a deliverable → Launchpad. The agent serves the customer. The owner reviews before the customer sees it.

If the end user is a creative professional producing a deliverable → Studio. The agent is a collaborator in the production process. The creative professional and the agent are on the same team, not in a vendor/customer relationship. The output goes to a client or channel outside the Space — not to the end user who is working inside the Space.

Ambiguous case: a solo creator selling custom content (e.g., ghostwriting). If they review every artifact and their client never logs in → Studio. If their client receives auto-generated output via a portal with their client's logo → Launchpad with a Studio-like template. The sub-space-to-product promotion path exists precisely for when this outgrows a template.

52 — Temples

Temples — Pre-Built Products on the Naelao Platform

A Temple is a fully configured, ready-to-launch NaelaoProduct. Where the Create Product Wizard gives a builder a blank Space and a configuration form, a Temple gives them a complete product: agents pre-installed, knowledge base structure defined, UI configured, pricing suggested, and a working demo they can explore before committing. Temples are to Naelao what Shopify themes are to Shopify — except a Temple includes the business logic, not just the visual design.

Architectural Position of Temples

A Temple is not a separate infrastructure concept. It is a snapshot of a fully configured NaelaoProduct — a serialized combination of: a NaelaoProduct record (with space type, auth config, pricing config, feature flags, user permissions), an agent definition bundle (the specific agents pre-installed into the Space), a knowledge base schema (which document types are expected, which are required), and a UI extension set (any custom views or components the builder needs to install on top of the product shell). When a builder selects a Temple, the platform executes the same POST /builder/products flow as the manual wizard — but pre-populated from the Temple snapshot. The builder reviews, adjusts pricing and branding, and launches. No new infrastructure primitive is introduced. Temples are configuration, not code.

Temple Registry — Data Model

// packages/naelao-types/src/temple.ts

export type TempleCategory =
  | 'consumer-ai'           // ChatGPT-style consumer product — a builder shipping a general-purpose AI assistant to their own end users
  | 'developer-tools'       // Coding, DevOps, technical
  | 'creative-studio'       // Studio space type
  | 'vertical-legal'        // Law firms, legal ops
  | 'vertical-finance'      // Accounting, tax, financial advisory
  | 'vertical-health'       // Healthcare adjacent (non-clinical)
  | 'vertical-education'    // Tutoring, learning, curriculum
  | 'vertical-real-estate'  // Property, agent tools
  | 'launchpad-business'    // Autonomous digital business
  | 'enterprise-internal'   // Large org internal tooling
  | 'data-intelligence';    // Analytics, reporting, research

export interface TempleAgentBundle {
  agentId: string;
  required: boolean;         // false = optional, builder can remove before launch
  configOverrides: Record<string, unknown>; // pre-set system prompt values, tool lists
}

export interface TempleKnowledgeSchema {
  documentType: string;
  required: boolean;
  description: string;       // Shown to builder: "Upload your brand voice document here"
  exampleUrl: string | null; // Link to a template document the builder can fill in
}

export interface Temple {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  tagline: string;
  category: TempleCategory;
  spaceType: SpaceType;
  description: string;        // 2-3 sentences shown in the Temple gallery
  longDescription: string;    // Full detail page content
  previewImageUrl: string;    // Screenshot of the product UI
  demoUrl: string | null;     // Live interactive demo (read-only, seeded with sample data)
  suggestedPricing: Partial<ProductPricingConfig>;
  defaultAuthProvider: ProductAuthProvider;
  productConfig: Partial<NaelaoProduct>; // The pre-filled product configuration
  agentBundle: TempleAgentBundle[];
  knowledgeSchema: TempleKnowledgeSchema[];
  requiredFeatureFlags: Record<string, boolean>;
  estimatedSetupMinutes: number;
  publishedAt: string;
  updatedAt: string;
  buildsCount: number;       // How many builders have launched from this Temple
  featured: boolean;
}

Temple Gallery — The Builder Dashboard View

When a builder opens the Create Product Wizard and selects "Start from a Temple", they see the Temple Gallery: a searchable, filterable grid of available Temples. Each card shows: name, tagline, space type badge, category, estimated setup time, and a "View Demo" button that opens the live seeded demo in a new tab. Selecting a Temple pre-fills the entire wizard. The builder only needs to provide: their product name, their domain, their pricing numbers, and their branding. Everything else is configured by the Temple.

Temple Examples — Full Specifications

Temple 01 — LexSpace (Legal AI)

LexSpace · Vertical-Legal · Supervised Execution · ~25 min setup

What it is: A full AI legal research and drafting platform for law firms and in-house legal teams. Matter-based organisation, citation-verified research, document drafting with tracked changes, and a full audit trail for every agent action — required by most bar associations for AI-assisted legal work.

Who it's for: Boutique law firms (5–50 attorneys), in-house legal teams at mid-market companies, legal ops consultancies building a client-facing research tool.

// Temple: LexSpace — full configuration
const TEMPLE_LEXSPACE: Temple = {
  id: 'temple-lexspace-v1',
  name: 'LexSpace',
  tagline: 'AI legal research and drafting — compliance-first',
  category: 'vertical-legal',
  spaceType: 'verticals',
  suggestedPricing: { type: 'seats', pricePerSeat: 15000, trialDays: 0 }, // $150/seat/month
  defaultAuthProvider: 'saml-sso',
  productConfig: {
    allowPublicSignup: false,
    requireAdminApproval: true,
    featureFlags: {
      'matter-management': true,
      'immutable-audit-trail': true,
      'citation-verification': true,
      'document-compare': true,
      'privilege-log-generator': true,
    },
    userPermissions: {
      canCreateProjects: true,      // Matters = projects
      canCreateSubSpaces: true,     // Practice groups = sub-spaces
      canUploadKnowledge: true,
      maxThreadsPerUser: null,
    },
    adminFeatures: {
      conversationLogAccess: true,  // Required for regulatory compliance — pre-flagged for Naelao approval
      auditLogAccess: true,
      knowledgeBaseManagement: true,
    },
    subSpaceTerminology: 'practice groups',
  },
  agentBundle: [
    {
      agentId: 'legal-researcher-v1',
      required: true,
      configOverrides: {
        systemPromptAddendum: 'Always cite primary sources. Never cite secondary summaries without the primary. Flag any jurisdiction ambiguity explicitly. All legal citations must follow Bluebook format.',
      },
    },
    {
      agentId: 'legal-drafter-v1',
      required: true,
      configOverrides: {
        requiresApprovalFor: ['document_finalise', 'client_send'],
      },
    },
    {
      agentId: 'privilege-checker-v1',
      required: false,  // Optional — activated if firm handles litigation
      configOverrides: {},
    },
  ],

    { documentType: 'jurisdiction_guides', required: true,  description: 'Upload court rules and jurisdiction-specific procedural guides', exampleUrl: 'https://docs.naelao.app/templates/lexspace-jurisdiction-guide' },
    { documentType: 'firm_precedents',     required: false, description: 'Past briefs and contracts the agents can reference as style guides', exampleUrl: null },

// How LexSpace works — end-to-end flow
// 1. Attorney opens a new Matter (a project in LexSpace terminology)
// 2. Intake Agent runs: auto-populates conflict check form, client details, matter type
// 3. Attorney submits — matter is created in the Matter board (a Verticals-space project view)
// 4. Research request: attorney types natural language query → Legal Researcher Agent activates
// 5. Researcher returns: structured brief with citations, jurisdiction notes, risk flags
//    Every citation links to the source document in the knowledge base or a verified public URL
// 6. Attorney reviews research → requests a draft document
// 7. Legal Drafter Agent produces draft → tracked changes view in the document panel
// 8. Privilege Checker (if enabled) runs automatically before any document leaves the Space
// 9. Attorney approves → document moves to Approved status
//    At this point it can be exported or sent via the email integration
// 10. Every action in steps 2–9 writes to the immutable audit log (required for bar compliance)
// 11. Billing: per-seat to the firm. Wholesale credit consumption billed to the builder monthly.

Temple 02 — DevPilot (AI Coding Assistant)

DevPilot · Developer · Autopilot Execution · ~10 min setup

What it is: A Cursor / GitHub Copilot alternative built on Naelao's Developer space type. Multi-file context, inline autocomplete suggestions delivered via the thread interface, test-generation, code review, and an optional background task runner for longer refactors. Builders deploying this Temple are selling to software engineering teams who want an AI coding assistant that lives inside their own infrastructure — not in a third-party SaaS tool they don't control.

Why builders choose this over Cursor: custom system prompts tuned to the engineering team's stack, the codebase as a knowledge base document (uploaded once, referenced on every query), SSO through the company's existing IdP, and usage data that stays within the builder's tenant — never aggregated into a third-party model's training pipeline.

// Temple: DevPilot — configuration
const TEMPLE_DEVPILOT: Temple = {
  id: 'temple-devpilot-v1',
  name: 'DevPilot',

  category: 'developer-tools',
  spaceType: 'developer',
  suggestedPricing: { type: 'seats', pricePerSeat: 2000, trialDays: 14 },  // $20/seat/month
  defaultAuthProvider: 'custom-oidc',
  productConfig: {
    allowPublicSignup: false,
    featureFlags: {
      'inline-autocomplete': true,
      'multi-file-context': true,
      'test-generation': true,
      'code-review-agent': true,
      'background-refactor': false,  // Off by default — costs more credits, enable per team
      'terminal-access': false,      // Disabled by default for security — builder can enable
    },
    userPermissions: {
      canCreateProjects: true,       // Projects = repositories or feature branches
      canCreateSubSpaces: true,      // Teams / squads = sub-spaces
      canInstallAgents: false,
      maxCreditsPerMonth: null,
    },
    subSpaceTerminology: 'teams',
    allowUserSubSpaces: true,
    maxSubSpaceDepth: 1,
  },
  agentBundle: [
    { agentId: 'code-assist-v1',   required: true,  configOverrides: { model: 'claude-sonnet-4-20250514' } },
    { agentId: 'test-writer-v1',   required: false, configOverrides: {} },
    { agentId: 'code-reviewer-v1', required: false, configOverrides: { requiresApprovalFor: [] } }, // Review is informational, no approval gate
  ],
  knowledgeSchema: [
    { documentType: 'codebase_context', required: false, description: 'Upload a repo map or architecture doc so agents understand your project structure', exampleUrl: 'https://docs.naelao.app/templates/devpilot-repo-context' },
    { documentType: 'coding_standards', required: false, description: 'Coding standards, linting rules, commit message conventions', exampleUrl: null },
    { documentType: 'stack_reference',  required: false, description: 'Framework docs, internal library references, API contracts', exampleUrl: null },
  ],
  estimatedSetupMinutes: 10,
  featured: true,
};

// How DevPilot works — primary use cases
//
// USE CASE A — Inline assistance (synchronous, credit-efficient)
//   Developer writes a function signature → asks agent to complete implementation
//   Agent reads: multi-file context from the active project sub-space + codebase_context knowledge doc
//   Returns: implementation with inline explanation + test stubs if test-generation is enabled
//   Credits: low — short context, fast model (haiku for autocomplete, sonnet for complex requests)
//
// USE CASE B — Code review (asynchronous, medium cost)
//   Developer opens a PR diff → pastes it into a thread → requests review
//   Agent reads: coding_standards knowledge doc + diff context
//   Returns: structured review — summary, required changes, suggestions, test coverage gaps
//   No approval gate — review is advisory. Developer acts on it.
//
// USE CASE C — Background refactor (autopilot, high cost — disabled by default)
//   Developer describes: "Extract the auth logic from UserController into AuthService"
//   Agent runs: reads relevant files (via file-manager skill), produces a diff
//   Developer reviews the diff before any file is written — approval required
//   This is the most credit-intensive mode. Builders enable it deliberately per team.

Temple 03 — GrantPilot (Nonprofit Fundraising AI)

GrantPilot · Studio · Supervised · ~20 min setup

What it is: A Studio-space product purpose-built for nonprofit grant writers and development teams. Grant applications are creative-professional output with strict compliance requirements: word limits, funder-specific language requirements, impact metric formatting, and budget narrative conventions. GrantPilot treats each grant application as a brief in the Production Board. The Research Agent finds funder alignment. The Copywriter Agent produces the narrative. The Brand Checker verifies word counts and formatting rules. The development director approves and submits.

Why this is Studio, not Launchpad: The nonprofit staff member is the professional working inside the Space. They are not a customer receiving a deliverable — they are a user producing one. The funder who receives the grant application never interacts with the product at all.

    requireAdminApproval: true,
    featureFlags: {

      'budget-narrative-agent': true,
      'revision-history': true,
    },
    userPermissions: {
      canCreateProjects: true,    // Each grant = a project / brief
      canUploadKnowledge: true,
      canCreateSubSpaces: true,   // Programs / funding streams = sub-spaces
    },
    subSpaceTerminology: 'programs',
  },
  agentBundle: [
    { agentId: 'studio-researcher-v1',     required: true,  configOverrides: { systemPromptAddendum: 'Your primary task is funder research. Identify: what the funder has funded in the past 3 years, their stated priorities, geographic focus, grant size range, and application requirements. Cross-reference with the organisation mission statement in the knowledge base.' } },
    { agentId: 'studio-copywriter-v1',     required: true,  configOverrides: { systemPromptAddendum: 'You write grant narratives. Always respect the word limit in the brief. Use impact-first structure: problem → solution → evidence → ask. Never use passive voice in the opening paragraph.' } },
    { agentId: 'studio-brand-checker-v1',  required: true,  configOverrides: { systemPromptAddendum: 'You check grant applications against: word count limits (hard fail if exceeded), required sections present, prohibited language (no "innovative", "unique", "passionate" per funder guidelines), and correct impact metric format (numbers, not percentages, for this funder category).' } },

// How GrantPilot works — a single grant application lifecycle:
// 1. Development director creates a new Brief: "Robert Wood Johnson Foundation — Community Health 2026"
//    Fills in: funder name, deadline, word limit, grant amount requested
// 2. Research Agent activates: searches funder database knowledge doc + web for RWJF 2026 priorities
//    Returns: 4-page research brief with funder history, priority alignment score, 3 strongest angles
// 3. Director reviews research → selects angle → brief moves to In Production
// 4. Copywriter Agent produces: narrative draft (within word limit), executive summary (150 words),
//    3 alternative opening paragraphs for the director to choose
// 5. Brand Checker runs automatically: word count ✓ | prohibited words ✓ | required sections ✓
//    Compliance report: PASS — brief moves to Review
// 6. Director reviews full narrative → requests one revision: "Strengthen the evidence paragraph"
//    Copywriter Agent revises only that section — revision history shows the diff
// 7. Director approves → brief moves to Approved
// 8. Budget Narrative Agent (if enabled) produces budget justification narrative
// 9. Director exports the complete application package as a formatted PDF
//    The funder receives this — they never see GrantPilot, Naelao, or any system UI

Temple 04 — PropertyAI (Real Estate Listings)

PropertyAI · Launchpad · Fulfillment · ~8 min setup

What it is: A Launchpad-type product for real estate professionals. Realtors upload property data (address, specs, photos, neighbourhood notes) and the fulfillment agent generates professional listing descriptions across multiple platforms: MLS long-form, social short-form, email newsletter blurb, and a buyer's guide paragraph. The realtor never logs into the Naelao product UI as an "end user" — they interact via the builder's own lightweight intake form, which POSTs to a webhook. The agent processes the data and delivers output via email. This is Launchpad at its most stripped-down: no product UI for the customer. Entirely webhook-and-email.

Temple vs Blank Product — Decision Guidance

Start from a Temple when
Your use case matches one of the existing categories closely. You want to be live within a day. You want working agent definitions and knowledge schemas out of the box. You plan to differentiate on branding, pricing, and domain expertise — not on the underlying AI architecture. Temples are the 80% solution. They get you to market. You refine from there.
Start from blank when
Your product does not match any existing Temple. You need a custom execution model that no Temple provides. You are building infrastructure that will itself serve as a platform for other builders (an agency shell). You have strong technical opinions about agent behaviour that would require significant Temple overrides. If you are overriding more than 60% of a Temple's configuration, you should start blank.

Temple Lifecycle — From Configuration to Builder Customisation

// POST /builder/products?fromTemple={templeId}
// Request body: { name, domain, pricing overrides, branding }
// The platform:
//   1. Fetches Temple record from TEMPLE_REGISTRY_KV
//   2. Merges builder-supplied overrides onto Temple's productConfig
//   3. Executes standard NaelaoProduct creation (same as blank wizard)
//   4. Installs Temple agent bundle into the new Space's agent registry
//   5. Creates knowledge base scaffold with typed document slots
//   6. Deploys product shell with Temple's default feature flags active
//   7. Returns the fully configured NaelaoProduct — builder can now customise further
//      via the standard PATCH /builder/products/{productId} endpoints

// What the builder can always change after launching from a Temple:
//   - Pricing (any time)
//   - Branding (any time)
//   - Feature flags (any time, TTL 60s)
//   - Agent system prompt addenda (takes effect on next agent run)
//   - Knowledge base contents (any time)
//   - Auth provider (requires re-deploying the product shell)
//   - User permissions (any time)

// What the builder cannot change without a new product:
//   - Space type (launchpad vs studio vs developer — these are architectural)
//   - Sub-space depth limit (enforced at infrastructure level)
//   - Billing model (usage-based vs flat-monthly — requires a support request)
Naelao's Commitment: Every Temple Is a Working Product

A Temple is not a wireframe. It is not a configuration skeleton. Before any Temple ships in the gallery, Naelao's team has: built a live seeded demo with realistic sample data, run the agent bundle through the complete execution model with real LLM calls (not mocked), validated the knowledge base schema against the agent prompts, and load-tested the template under simulated user load. The estimatedSetupMinutes field is based on actual timed runs by a builder who has never seen the Temple before. If a Temple cannot be launched to a working state within that time window, it does not ship. Templates that mislead builders waste their time and erode trust in the platform. A Temple is a promise: launch this, and you have a working product.

G-SEC-01

SandboxDO exec() — Shell Injection via args Array

The Gap

SandboxDO exec() — Shell Injection via args Array The execution ladder orchestrator calls container exec like this: // From the spec — orchestrator.ts: return context.sandboxDO.fetch(new Request('http://sandbox/exec', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ command: toolName, args: Object.values(toolCall.parameters) }) })).then(r => r.json()); Object.values(toolCall.parameters) takes the LLM's parsed tool call parameters and passes them directly as shell arguments. The spec correctly uses an argument array (not string interpolation) to prevent most injection. However, two specific vulnerabilities remain unaddressed: The command itself is the tool name: command: toolName where toolName…

Required Fix

''); // Write to a temp file, execute the file — never pass code via -c flag // -c with long scripts is fragile and argument-length-limited return ['-']; // python reads from stdin — content piped separately } default: // For unknown tools: only allow string values with no flag-like patterns return Object.values(rawArgs) .map(v => String(v)) .filter(v => !v.startsWith('-')); // reject anything that looks like a flag } } Gap T-36 — Medium

// From the spec — orchestrator.ts:
return context.sandboxDO.fetch(new Request('http://sandbox/exec', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: JSON.stringify({ command: toolName, args: Object.values(toolCall.parameters) })
})).then(r => r.json());
// Required: tool name and argument validation before container exec

// 1. Validate tool name against the registry — never pass raw tool names to exec
function resolveContainerCommand(toolName: string): string {
  const toolDef = TOOL_TIERS[toolName];
  if (!toolDef) throw new Error(`Unknown tool: ${toolName}`);
  if (toolDef.tier !== 'sandbox') throw new Error(`Tool ${toolName} is not a sandbox-tier tool`);

  // Map tool name to the actual binary path (pre-approved list)
  const TOOL_COMMANDS: Record<string, string> = {
    'execute_python': '/usr/bin/python3',
    'execute_bash':   '/usr/local/bin/safe-bash',  // wrapper that blocks dangerous builtins
    'execute_node':   '/usr/bin/node',
    'run_tests':      '/usr/local/bin/vitest',
  };
  const cmd = TOOL_COMMANDS[toolName];
  if (!cmd) throw new Error(`No container command mapped for tool: ${toolName}`);
  return cmd;
}

// 2. Argument sanitisation per tool — not generic
function sanitizeArgs(toolName: string, rawArgs: Record<string, unknown>): string[] {
  switch (toolName) {
    case 'execute_bash': {
      // Bash gets a single -c "script" argument — never split into multiple args
      // The script content is already security-scanned by the 27-pattern scanner
      const script = String(rawArgs.code ?? rawArgs.command ?? '');
      return ['-c', script]; // safe — bash -c treats the script as a single unit
    }
    case 'execute_python': {
      const script = String(rawArgs.code ?? '');
      // Write to a temp file, execute the file — never pass code via -c flag
      // -c with long scripts is fragile and argument-length-limited
      return ['-']; // python reads from stdin — content piped separately
    }
    default:
      // For unknown tools: only allow string values with no flag-like patterns
      return Object.values(rawArgs)
        .map(v => String(v))
        .filter(v => !v.startsWith('-')); // reject anything that looks like a flag
  }
}

GDPR Right-to-Deletion — No Cross-System Erasure Path

The Gap

GDPR Right-to-Deletion — No Cross-System Erasure Path Under GDPR Article 17, when a user requests deletion of their personal data, all copies must be erased within 30 days. A Naelao product user's personal data exists in at minimum 6 separate systems. The spec specifies a soft-delete flag in SpaceDO but no coordinated erasure across R2, Vectorize, Analytics Engine, or the AI Gateway cache. A GDPR deletion request today would be partially fulfilled at best — which is the same as not fulfilled at all under the regulation. Where a Single User's Personal Data Lives System What PII Is Stored Current Deletion Path SpaceDO SQLite email, display name, role, session tokens, message content, agent…

Required Fix

G-SEC-03

Local Tunnel Security — User's Entire Filesystem Accessible via Path Traversal

The Gap

Local Tunnel Security — User's Entire Filesystem Accessible via Path Traversal LocalTunnelDO relays commands to the user's local machine via a WebSocket. The permission system stores granted paths in SQLite and validates them with prefix matching: "a grant for /home/user/projects also covers /home/user/projects/myapp ." The traversal vulnerability: a command like cat /home/user/projects/../../../etc/passwd passes the prefix check because the path starts with the granted prefix — the ../ sequences are never resolved before comparison. An agent (or a prompt-injected instruction, see T-68) can read any file on the user's machine by constructing a path that starts with a granted prefix but…

Required Fix

Additional Gaps in LocalTunnelDO Security Symlink escape: Even with realpathSync , a symlink inside the granted path pointing outside it ( /home/user/projects/secrets → /etc/ssl/private ) escapes the check unless symlinks are validated too. realpathSync resolves them — but the resolved target must also be under the grant. Command injection: The command relay passes the agent's command string to the local shell. A command like cat file.txt; rm -rf ~ passes as a single string. The local CLI must sanitize or use execFile with argument arrays, never exec with string interpolation. Gap T-83 — High

// WRONG — in LocalTunnelDO (path.startsWith is not safe):
const granted = db.exec('SELECT path FROM permissions WHERE can_read=1').rows.map(r=>r[0]);
const allowed = granted.some(g => requestedPath.startsWith(g));  // traversal bypasses this

// RIGHT — resolve the path canonically BEFORE the prefix check
// This must be done in the LOCAL CLI agent (Node.js side), not in the DO,
// because the DO doesn't know the local filesystem's real paths

// Local CLI agent (runs on user's machine) — command validator:
import path from 'node:path';
import fs from 'node:fs';

function resolveAndCheck(requestedPath: string, grantedPaths: string[]): string {
  // Resolve to absolute canonical path (resolves ../, symlinks, etc.)
  const resolved = fs.realpathSync(path.resolve(requestedPath));

  const allowed = grantedPaths.some(g => {
    const grantedResolved = fs.realpathSync(path.resolve(g));
    // Check that resolved is UNDER the granted path (with trailing slash to avoid prefix tricks)
    return resolved === grantedResolved || resolved.startsWith(grantedResolved + path.sep);
  });

  if (!allowed) throw new Error(`Access denied: ${requestedPath} is not under any granted path`);
  return resolved;
}
// This runs locally — the DO only sends commands, never validates paths itself
// The CLI agent is the only security boundary for local filesystem access
G-SEC-04

postMessage Origin Allowlist — Shell Validates App Messages But Apps Never Validate Shell Messages

The Gap

postMessage Origin Allowlist — Shell Validates App Messages But Apps Never Validate Shell Messages The Operator Shell uses a `postMessage` protocol between the host shell (`app.naelao.dev`) and injected app iframes (`ui.naelao.app`). The spec shows the message type contract but does not show origin validation in the receiving iframe. The shell sends `CONTEXT`, `TOKEN_REFRESH`, and `THEME_CHANGE` messages to the iframe. If the iframe does not validate that `event.origin === 'https://app.naelao.dev'`, a malicious third-party page that embeds the app iframe can spoof these messages and inject a fake `TOKEN_REFRESH` payload with a forged JWT, granting the app iframe access to the malicious…

Required Fix

Required Fix All `window.addEventListener('message', handler)` calls in app iframe code must check `if (event.origin !== 'https://app.naelao.dev') return;`. This must be enforced in the `@naelao/portal-sdk` which all apps are required to use. The shell's `postMessage` handler for incoming `APP_ACTION` messages must verify the iframe's registered `panelUrl` origin matches `event.origin` before processing any action. Add a Content-Security-Policy on all app iframes: `frame-ancestors 'self' https://app.naelao.dev` to prevent third-party embedding of app panels. Severity: High — Missing origin validation in app iframes is a classic XSS via postMessage attack. A compromised or malicious app can spoof shell context and execute agent actions in arbitrary spaces. T-135 — Operator Shell Slot System

G-SEC-05

Workflow Path Validation — startsWith Check Vulnerable to Prefix Injection

The Gap

Workflow Path Validation — startsWith Check Vulnerable to Prefix Injection The Dynamic Workflow loadRunner validates the workflow path with: `if (!workflowPath.startsWith(`spaces/${spaceId}/`)) throw Error`. This check is incomplete. An attacker in Space A (ID: `abc-123`) could craft a workflow path like `spaces/abc-123-evil/workflows/backdoor.ts`. If there is a Space with ID `abc-123-evil` (created by the attacker in a different organization), the startsWith check passes and the backdoor workflow is loaded with Space A's context. The fix is using exact directory matching, not prefix matching.

Required Fix

Required Fix Replace startsWith with exact path structure validation: check that the path matches exactly `spaces/{spaceId}/workflows/{workflowName}.ts` or similar strict pattern, not just a prefix. Better: use path.parse() or similar to extract the embedded spaceId and compare to the metadata spaceId programmatically, not via string prefix. Severity: High — Attacker in Space A can load workflows from Space A-evil. Prefix injection via space ID spoofing bypasses isolation. Cross-space workflow execution possible. T-148 — Skills System

G-SEC-06

R2 Path Prefixes — No Filesystem-Level Isolation; Path Traversal via Crafted Keys

The Gap

R2 Path Prefixes — No Filesystem-Level Isolation; Path Traversal via Crafted Keys R2 organizes spaces by prefix: `spaces/{spaceId}/...`. There is no filesystem-level isolation — R2 is a flat key-value store. An agent running in Space A (ID: `abc-123`) could theoretically craft a path like `spaces/abc-123-../../../other-space/secret-file` and attempt to traverse out of its namespace. While modern S3-compatible APIs don't interpret `..` in keys (they're treated as literal characters), the risk is that agents could list prefixes and discover sibling spaces if the prefix matching is loose. For example, `SpaceR2.list('spaces/abc-123')` might match both `spaces/abc-123/` and…

Required Fix

Required Fix Add a trailing slash to all R2 path prefixes: `spaces/{spaceId}/` with a required trailing slash. Enforce this in the SpaceR2 helper — never allow a path that doesn't start with exactly `spaces/{spaceId}/`. In the listing function, check that returned keys match exactly the pattern `spaces/{spaceId}/*` and reject any keys with adjacent space IDs. Consider using R2 signed URLs with tight expiry windows instead of giving agents direct R2 access — this reduces the risk of path crafting entirely. Severity: Medium — R2 prefix isolation depends on strict string matching, not filesystem barriers. Malformed paths or prefix matching bugs could allow adjacent spaces to be listed or accessed. T-154 — ConcurrencyDO

G-SEC-07

Path Validation — '..' and Absolute Paths Checked Only in Skill Description, Not At Runtime

The Gap

Path Validation — '..' and Absolute Paths Checked Only in Skill Description, Not At Runtime The file-manager SKILL.md says: "IMPORTANT: All paths are relative to /workspace. Do NOT use absolute paths or paths starting with /. Do NOT use '..' in paths." This is a guideline in the skill description, but there is no runtime validation. An agent could call `read_file('/etc/passwd')` or `read_file('../../../etc/passwd')` and the skill would attempt to execute the request without checking. The SpaceR2 helper might still prevent access (if it prefixes with `spaces/{spaceId}/workspace/`), but the path validation relies on implicit string concatenation, not explicit validation.

Required Fix

Required Fix Add explicit path validation in the file-manager skill implementation before any R2 operation: reject paths containing '..', reject absolute paths (starting with /), reject paths with leading whitespace. Validate using a whitelist pattern: `/^[a-zA-Z0-9._/-]+$/` (allow only safe characters). Throw a clear error if validation fails: "Path must be relative, no '..', no leading '/'." Severity: Medium — Path validation is only in the skill description, not enforced at runtime. Agents could attempt to read files outside the workspace. T-159 — Prompt Engineering

G-SEC-08

Memory Context Injection — Max 20 Items; Older Memories Silently Discarded Without Archival

The Gap

Memory Context Injection — Max 20 Items; Older Memories Silently Discarded Without Archival The buildMemoryContext() function limits memory to 20 items: `memory.slice(0, 20)`. When an agent has more than 20 memories, the oldest ones are discarded from the prompt without any archival or notification. The agent won't know about these memories and can't access them. Over time, important memories (like "user's preferred coding style" or "previous project decisions") are lost silently. The 20-item limit is arbitrary and not tunable.

Required Fix

Required Fix Implement memory archival: when memory exceeds 20 items, move older items to a separate `archived_memory` table. The agent can explicitly query the archive if needed. Or, increase the limit and rely on token counting: calculate how many tokens 20 items uses, then allow as many items as fit in a token budget (e.g., 1000 tokens for memory). Add a memory summary: periodically summarize old memories into a single condensed item to preserve knowledge while saving tokens. Severity: Medium — Old memories are discarded silently. Important context is lost over time. No archival or recall mechanism. T-161 — naelao-mcp-hub

G-SEC-09

Skill 27-Pattern Scanner — Detects Obvious `process.env.` Patterns; Misses Obfuscated Variants

The Gap

Skill 27-Pattern Scanner — Detects Obvious `process.env.` Patterns; Misses Obfuscated Variants The launch checklist requires "27-pattern skill scanner active for all unverified skills." The scanner is mentioned but not implemented in the spec. Assuming it scans for patterns like `process.env.`, `require('`, `import('`, it catches obvious attempts to access secrets or execute code. However, it can be bypassed by obfuscation: `process['en' + 'v']`, `({}).constructor.prototype` (to access global), `atob('...')` to decode shell commands. The scanner would miss these obfuscated patterns.

Required Fix

Required Fix Implement AST-based analysis instead of regex patterns. Parse the SKILL.md as JavaScript/TypeScript and analyze the AST for dangerous API calls (process, require, import, eval, Function, etc). Sandbox skill execution: run unverified skills in a restricted V8 isolate with no access to process, require, or file system. This defense-in-depth approach catches both obvious and obfuscated attacks. Require code signing for unverified skills: skills must be signed by their author. If a signature check fails, the skill is automatically blocked. Severity: Medium — 27-pattern scanner uses simple regex matching. Obfuscated dangerous patterns bypass the filter. Unverified skills can still execute dangerous code. T-165 — Bootstrap Mode

G-SEC-10

Audit Query SQL Injection — Unparameterized Event Type Filter

The Gap

Audit Query SQL Injection — Unparameterized Event Type Filter The audit query endpoint constructs a SQL query with string interpolation: `AND blob1 = '${eventType}'`. The eventType comes from the query parameter and is not parameterized. An attacker could pass `eventType = "token_usage' OR blob1 = '"` to bypass the filter and retrieve audit logs from all event types, including security events and wallet transactions they shouldn't see. This is a classic SQL injection vulnerability.

Required Fix

Required Fix Use parameterized queries: `AND blob1 = ?` with eventType passed as a parameter to the SQL API. Validate eventType against a whitelist of known event types before using it in the query. Add logging of all admin audit queries to detect exploitation attempts. Severity: High — SQL injection in audit query endpoint. Attackers can bypass event type filters and access sensitive audit logs they shouldn't see. T-171 — naelao-triggers

G-SEC-11

Webhook Secret Validation — No Rotation Or Expiry; Compromised Secrets Never Invalidated

The Gap

Webhook Secret Validation — No Rotation Or Expiry; Compromised Secrets Never Invalidated Webhook secrets are stored in naelao-credentials and fetched on each webhook verification. Once set, they never expire or rotate. If a webhook secret is exposed (e.g., logged in an error message, leaked via a developer's GitHub repo), an attacker can forge valid webhooks indefinitely. There is no mechanism to rotate or expire the secret. A developer would have to manually generate a new secret in the UI and update the third-party provider's webhook configuration.

Required Fix

Required Fix Implement automatic secret rotation: every 90 days, generate a new secret and mark the old one as "accepting but deprecated" for 7 days (grace period). After 7 days, reject old secrets entirely. Add a "rotate secret now" button in the UI for manual emergency rotation. Log every secret rotation and every failed webhook signature verification to analytics for monitoring. Severity: Medium — Webhook secrets never expire. Compromised secrets accepted indefinitely. No rotation mechanism or forced expiry. T-172 — naelao-triggers

G-SEC-12

Manifest Signature Validation — Skipped If Signature Missing; Manifests Loaded Unsigned

The Gap

Manifest Signature Validation — Skipped If Signature Missing; Manifests Loaded Unsigned The provisioner fetches space type manifests from SpaceTypeRegistryDO. The spec says: "The manifest's Ed25519 signature is verified against the platform public key." However, the code doesn't explicitly show what happens if the signature is missing or validation fails. If SpaceTypeRegistryDO returns a manifest without a signature field, the validation code likely skips the check and loads the manifest as-is. This allows a compromised SpaceTypeRegistryDO (or a middle-layer attacker) to serve a modified manifest with malicious agent environment configs (e.g., disabledSkills: [], maxContextTokens: 1000000)…

Required Fix

Required Fix Require manifest.signature field to always be present. If missing, throw "Manifest signature required". Verify the signature before using ANY field from the manifest. A missing or invalid signature invalidates the entire manifest, not just a single field. Pin the public key in the code, not in a config. Rotating the key is a platform-wide event requiring code deployment. Severity: High — Missing signature validation on manifests. Malicious manifests can be loaded unsigned. Attackers can modify agent configs or disable safety features. T-177 — Provisioner

G-SEC-13

Portal Slug Uniqueness — 30s TTL Lock Not Sufficient; Race Allocates Duplicate Slugs

The Gap

Portal Slug Uniqueness — 30s TTL Lock Not Sufficient; Race Allocates Duplicate Slugs Slug reservation uses a KV lock with 30s TTL: `await env.PORTAL_ROUTES.put(\`slug-lock:${slug}\`, spaceId, { expirationTtl: 30 })`. Between the KV write and the return, two concurrent provisioning requests could both succeed at writing the lock. KV puts are eventually consistent in some Cloudflare configs, or the TTL could expire between the check and the write. Once provisioned, both Spaces would have the same slug. When a user visits the portal, it's ambiguous which Space to serve. The custom domain mapping breaks.

Required Fix

Required Fix Use a conditional put with compareAndSet semantics (if available in KV), or move slug allocation to SpaceDO SQLite with a UNIQUE constraint on (slug). Increase TTL to match max provisioning time (e.g., 5 minutes) to ensure locks don't expire prematurely. Add a periodic slug uniqueness audit: query all spaces, verify each slug is unique. Log and alert on duplicates. Severity: Medium — KV slug lock with 30s TTL allows race conditions. Concurrent provisions can allocate the same slug. Portal routing becomes ambiguous. T-179 — Provisioner

G-SEC-14

Product Slug Uniqueness — No UNIQUE Constraint; Concurrent Creates Can Allocate Duplicate Slugs

The Gap

Product Slug Uniqueness — No UNIQUE Constraint; Concurrent Creates Can Allocate Duplicate Slugs Product slugs are required to be unique (`slug TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE` in the schema), but the creation flow generates the slug in the application code and inserts it. Between the generation and the insert, two concurrent requests could generate the same slug (e.g., both hash the product name to "lexspace", both try to insert). The first INSERT succeeds, the second fails with a constraint violation. However, if the constraint isn't enforced or the application doesn't validate the slug upfront, duplicate slugs could be inserted. The constraint is there, but the error handling might swallow the…

Required Fix

Required Fix Ensure the UNIQUE constraint exists and is checked: `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_products_slug ON products(slug)`. In the application, catch the constraint violation error explicitly and return a user-friendly message: "This slug is already taken. Choose a different name." Or, pre-check slug availability and reserve it atomically (e.g., with a KV lock or a "pending" row). Severity: Medium — Product slugs lack UNIQUE constraint enforcement. Concurrent creates can generate duplicate slugs. Constraint errors may not be handled. T-183 — naelao-spaces Worker

G-SEC-15

SSO Config OIDC Secret — Encrypted In Secrets Store; No Key Rotation; Decryption Fails On Key Change

The Gap

SSO Config OIDC Secret — Encrypted In Secrets Store; No Key Rotation; Decryption Fails On Key Change OIDC client secrets are stored encrypted using Cloudflare Secrets Store. The encryption key is managed by Cloudflare and there's no explicit key rotation mechanism exposed to the application. If Cloudflare rotates the master encryption key (for security or compliance), secrets encrypted with the old key may become inaccessible. The application has no way to re-encrypt old secrets with the new key. Additionally, if the secret is compromised and needs to be rotated, there's no automated rotation workflow — the builder must manually update the config in the UI. During the re-configuration…

Required Fix

Required Fix Implement a "secret rotation" workflow: when a secret is updated, keep the old one available for a grace period (7 days) in case clients are using cached credentials. Log all rotations. Store secrets in a dedicated encrypted column in SpaceDO SQLite instead of relying on Cloudflare Secrets Store. Implement application-level key rotation (regenerate the data encryption key every 90 days, re-encrypt all secrets). Alert the builder when a secret is about to expire (30 days before) so they can proactively rotate it. Severity: Medium — SSO secrets encrypted in Cloudflare Secrets Store with no key rotation. If master key rotates, decryption fails. No secret rotation workflow. T-184 — naelao-spaces Worker

G-SEC-16

Conversation Access Approval — No Naelao Admin Enforcement; Builder Can Enable Without Review

The Gap

Conversation Access Approval — No Naelao Admin Enforcement; Builder Can Enable Without Review The spec requires that `conversationLogAccess` can only be enabled if: (a) plan is Enterprise, (b) builder has acknowledged legal obligations, (c) Naelao admin has approved. However, the enforcement is documented but not verified in the code. The naelao-spaces endpoint that updates the product config likely sets the flag based on the request body without checking if Naelao approval was granted. A builder could directly POST to the endpoint with `conversationLogAccess: true` and the flag would be set even though no admin approved it.

Required Fix

Required Fix Add an explicit check in the update endpoint: if the request tries to set `conversationLogAccess: true`, verify that `conversationAccessApprovedBy` is not null AND it points to a valid Naelao admin. If not, return 403: "conversationLogAccess requires Naelao platform approval." Only Naelao admin endpoints (naelao-admin Worker) can set `conversationAccessApprovedBy`. Builder endpoints cannot. Log every approval or rejection attempt with the builder ID for audit purposes. Severity: High — conversationLogAccess approval enforcement missing. Builders can enable without Naelao admin review. GDPR and privacy compliance at risk. T-185 — naelao-spaces Worker

G-SEC-17

Sub-Space Scenario Enforcement — No Runtime Check; Builders Violate Rules In API Calls

The Gap

Sub-Space Scenario Enforcement — No Runtime Check; Builders Violate Rules In API Calls The spec defines three scenarios (organizational, agency-child, user-workspace) with enforcement rules. Scenario A (organizational) should reject mixed space types. The code shows: `if (body.spaceType && body.spaceType !== parent.space_type && !parent.agency_shell) { return 400 }`. However, the scenario_type column is set during creation but never re-validated on subsequent updates. A builder could later enable agency_shell on a parent that was created as "organizational", violating the immutability guarantee. The scenario becomes ambiguous. Alternatively, a builder could PATCH the scenario_type column…

Required Fix

Required Fix Add a CHECK constraint: `ALTER TABLE spaces ADD CONSTRAINT chk_scenario_immutable CHECK (scenario_type NOT NULL)`. Once set, scenario_type cannot change. If scenario rules need to change (rare), require a migration Worker that validates the impact before allowing the change. Audit all PATCH endpoints that touch scenario-related columns (agency_shell, spaceType). Log every attempt to change them. Severity: Medium — Scenario type not immutable. agency_shell can be toggled post-creation. Space type enforcement becomes ambiguous. T-186 — naelao-spaces Worker

G-SEC-18

Agency Shell Parent/Child Isolation — Child Sub-Spaces Can Access Parent's R2 Prefix

The Gap

Agency Shell Parent/Child Isolation — Child Sub-Spaces Can Access Parent's R2 Prefix In the agency scenario, the parent is an internal admin shell and each child is a separate product. R2 prefixes are allocated per space: `workspace/{spaceId}/`. However, if a child sub-space agent is misconfigured or a child's R2 credentials are over-permissioned, the child could potentially read or write to the parent's prefix. The spec says parent and child "never render together in the same browser context" — but at the infrastructure level, if both use the same R2 bucket (which they do), there's no namespace isolation enforcing that a child's R2 client cannot access the parent's prefix. A malicious…

Required Fix

Required Fix Enforce R2 prefix isolation at the worker level: each space gets an R2 client bound to a specific prefix via a custom Worker that validates all requests: `if (!prefix.startsWith(`workspace/${spaceId}/`)) { throw 403 }`. Or, use separate R2 buckets per space type or per tier (parent bucket vs child bucket). Test: try to read parent's prefix from a child space's agent code. Should fail with 403 Forbidden. Severity: Medium — Agency child spaces share parent's R2 bucket. No namespace isolation. Child agents could access parent prefix. Data exfiltration risk. T-187 — naelao-spaces Worker

G-SEC-19

Cross-Sub-Space Grants — Race Between Grant Creation And Access Check; Users Bypass Expiry

The Gap

Cross-Sub-Space Grants — Race Between Grant Creation And Access Check; Users Bypass Expiry Cross-sub-space grants allow one space to grant read or full access to another. Grants can have an expiry. When a user from space A tries to access data from space B, the code checks: `SELECT * FROM cross_sub_space_grants WHERE granting_space_id = B AND receiving_space_id = A AND expires_at > NOW() AND revoked_at IS NULL`. However, between the grant check and the actual data access, the grant could expire (another request revoked it). The user has already been authenticated to access the data. Additionally, if the check uses a cached result (e.g., SpaceDO caches grants), an expired grant could be…

Required Fix

Required Fix Perform the grant check at data-access time, not at auth time. Every cross-space data read should verify the grant exists and hasn't expired. Or, use a short cache TTL (5 minutes) for grant checks to prevent stale cached grants from being used after revocation. Log every grant check failure. Alert on repeated attempts to access revoked grants. Severity: Medium — Grant expiry checked at auth, not at access. Cached grants may remain valid after expiry. Race between revocation and access. Over millions of credit deductions and wallet transactions, these rounding errors accumulate into real, visible discrepancies between what a customer was charged and what the ledger says. // Required: pre-deduction reserve pattern in sub-agent spawn
async function spawnSubAgent(
  parentRunId: string, agentId: string,
  estimatedCredits: number, env: Env, spaceId: string
): Promise<SubAgentResult> {

  // Step 1: Reserve credits BEFORE spawning — atomic in WalletDO
  const walletDO = getWalletDO(spaceId, env);
  const reserve = await walletDO.reserveCredits({
    amount: estimatedCredits,
    label: `sub-agent:${agentId}:${parentRunId}`,
    expiryMs: 5 * 60 * 1000  // reserve expires in 5min if sub-agent never starts
  });

  if (!reserve.success) {
    return { error: 'Insufficient credits for sub-agent spawn.', code: 'CREDITS_EXHAUSTED' };
  }

  try {
    // Step 2: Spawn only after successful reserve
    const result = await runSubAgent(agentId, parentRunId, env);

    // Step 3: Settle — convert reserve to actual deduction
    await walletDO.settleReserve(reserve.reserveId, result.actualCreditsUsed);
    return result;

  } catch (err) {
    // Step 4: Release reserve on failure — credits returned
    await walletDO.releaseReserve(reserve.reserveId);
    throw err;
  }
}
// WalletDO.reserveCredits() checks balance atomically (blockConcurrencyWhile)
// and holds the reservation so concurrent spawns can't double-spend the same balance

// Required: a billing identity unification layer
// A single canonical subscription record per user in SpaceDO,
// with source attribution (stripe | revenuecat | manual)

// SpaceDO billing schema addition:
// CREATE TABLE subscription_sources (
//   id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
//   user_id TEXT NOT NULL,
//   source TEXT NOT NULL,         -- 'stripe' | 'revenuecat_ios' | 'revenuecat_android'
//   external_id TEXT NOT NULL,    -- Stripe subscription ID or RevenueCat entitlement ID
//   status TEXT NOT NULL,         -- 'active' | 'cancelled' | 'expired'
//   plan TEXT NOT NULL,
//   UNIQUE(user_id, source)       -- one active subscription per source per user
// )

// On any subscription event (Stripe webhook OR RevenueCat webhook):
async function handleSubscriptionEvent(userId: string, source: string,
                                       externalId: string, plan: string, env: Env) {
  const spaceDO = getProductDO(userId, env);

  // Check if user already has an active subscription from ANY source
  const existing = await spaceDO.fetch(new Request('http://space/billing/active-subscription', {
    method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify({ userId })
  })).then(r => r.json());

  if (existing.hasActiveSubscription && existing.source !== source) {
    // User already subscribed via a different platform — log conflict, don't double-grant
    await logBillingConflict({ userId, existingSource: existing.source, newSource: source });
    return;
  }

  // Safe to provision — no duplicate
  await provisionSubscription(userId, plan, source, externalId, env);
}

The Gap

x402 AI Crawler Payment Gate — No Rate Limiting; Attackers Can Exhaust Wallet Via Repeated 402 Responses The x402 payment middleware on the Sites CF Pages deployment checks for a payment header and returns 402 Payment Required if missing. Each 402 response is routed through the wallet credit endpoint. There is no rate limiting on the 402 handler. An attacker can make thousands of requests to the same Sites page without the payment header, triggering thousands of 402 responses and wallet-credit attempts. These requests could: (a) exhaust the API rate limit quota if the wallet endpoint is rate-limited; (b) if not rate-limited, accumulate zero-amount credits in the wallet transaction log,…

Required Fix

Required Fix Add rate limiting to the 402 handler: e.g., max 10 requests per IP per minute. Return 429 Too Many Requests after the limit. Batch the wallet credit calls: don't call wallet-credit for every 402 response. Queue them and process in bulk every 5 minutes. Cache the 402 response for 30 seconds per IP + User-Agent combination to avoid repeated requests from the same crawler in the same minute. Severity: Medium — Attackers can flood the 402 handler and wallet credit endpoint. Legitimate crawler payments could fail under attack due to exhausted rate limits or unavailable wallet endpoint. G-BIL-09

Tier 5 Container Billing — Metered by Start Time, Not Actual Usage; Idle Containers Overcharge

The Gap

Tier 5 Container Billing — Metered by Start Time, Not Actual Usage; Idle Containers Overcharge Tier 5 containers are billed by the second they are allocated, not by CPU time. The spec says "metered by command duration." If an agent spins up a container to run `sleep 600` (10 minutes of idle sleep), the container is billed for 10 minutes of wall-clock time, even though zero CPU was used. For long-running agents that spawn containers for background tasks, this compounds: a container that allocates, waits 5 minutes for an external API to respond, then completes will be billed for 5+ minutes even if it used only 100ms of CPU.

Required Fix

Required Fix Use CF Container idle detection to pause billing while the container is idle (no CPU usage detected). Resume billing when computation resumes. Alternatively, require agents to implement request-response patterns, not long-lived container sessions. A container should start, do work, and exit quickly. For long-running tasks, use Dynamic Workflows (which have better pricing). Add a billing model choice to the container manifest: "per-wall-clock-second" (current) or "per-cpu-millisecond" (more fair). Default to fair billing. Severity: Medium — Containers metered by wall-clock time, not CPU time. Long waits (API calls, sleep, network I/O) increase costs without increasing computation. Agents are incentivized to use Tier 2 instead. T-151 — WalletDO

G-BIL-10

x402 Payments — Company Debit May Succeed While Creator Credit Fails; Atomicity Lost

The Gap

x402 Payments — Company Debit May Succeed While Creator Credit Fails; Atomicity Lost The x402 payment flow is a two-stage operation: (1) debit from company wallet, (2) credit to creator's WorkerDefinitionDO earnings. If step 1 succeeds and step 2 fails (e.g., the WorkerDefinitionDO is down, or the creator's space was deleted), the company has lost money but the creator receives no payment. The transaction is not atomic — there is no rollback. The code logs the x402_payment event to the analytics queue as step 3, which happens after both debits and credits, but if step 3 fails, the analytics event is lost and there's no audit trail of the failed payment.

Required Fix

Required Fix Implement a three-phase commit or saga pattern: (1) tentatively reserve funds in company wallet with status='pending', (2) credit creator wallet, (3) mark company wallet transaction as 'complete'. If step 2 fails, rollback step 1 in step 3. Store the x402 transaction attempt in both wallets' transaction history (not just analytics queue) so auditing is possible even if the analytics queue fails. For failed payments, retry them asynchronously via a queue, not synchronously via fetch(). Severity: High — x402 payments are not atomic. Company loses money even if creator never receives it. No rollback or retry mechanism. Audit trail is incomplete. T-153 — Schema & R2 Layout

G-BIL-11

Billing Cost Calculation — JavaScript Floats; Rounding Errors Accumulate Across Millions of Transactions

The Gap

Billing Cost Calculation — JavaScript Floats; Rounding Errors Accumulate Across Millions of Transactions The billing handler calculates cost in USD using JavaScript floating-point math: `(inputTokens / 1_000_000) * 3.00`. Floating-point arithmetic is imprecise — dividing by 1 million and multiplying by 3 introduces rounding errors. For 1,000,000 transactions, these rounding errors accumulate. Some transactions might be charged $0.0000000001 less, others $0.0000000001 more. Over millions of transactions, this could result in thousands of dollars of unaccounted revenue or under-billing. The billing system stores cost_usd as a DECIMAL (which is good) but calculates it with JavaScript floats…

Required Fix

Required Fix Use a decimal math library (decimal.js, big.js) for all cost calculations, not JavaScript's native float math. Alternatively, calculate cost in cents (integers) instead of dollars (floats): `(inputTokens * 3) / 1_000_000_000` then convert to cents as an integer, then divide by 100 only for display. Add a periodic reconciliation job that sums all recorded transactions and verifies the total matches the sum of individual costs. Severity: Medium — Floating-point rounding errors in cost calculation. Over millions of transactions, revenue discrepancies could reach thousands of dollars. T-157 — naelao-credentials

The Gap

Annotation Payments — No Refund On Rejection; Paid Annotations Then Discarded The bootstrap flow pays annotators for completed annotations via payAnnotator(). After payment, an LLM judge scores each annotation. If the score is below a quality threshold, the annotation is rejected and discarded. However, the annotator has already been paid. The spec doesn't mention refunding rejected annotations. If 20% of annotations are rejected, the bootstrap fund is partially wasted on low-quality work that won't be used for fine-tuning.

Required Fix

Required Fix Reverse payment flow: score the annotation first, then pay only if it passes quality threshold. This prevents waste. Or, implement a conditional hold: pay the annotator immediately, but flag low-quality annotations. If they remain flagged after 7 days (no appeal), deduct the payment. This gives annotators recourse to contest the score. Add analytics: track rejection rate per annotator. Systematically low-quality annotators can be deprioritized or removed from the pool. The Gap

The cron job snapshots all child spaces' usage at a point in time. However, agents in child spaces are running concurrently. Between the rollup cron reading the usage count and a child space writing a new usage record, the new usage is not captured in that day's rollup. The amount is attributed to the following day's invoice. For agencies managing many client spaces, this creates a billing accuracy problem. Over 100+ client spaces, the daily misattribution compounds to thousands of dollars of…

Required Fix

Required Fix Move to an event-driven model: every usage event writes an event to a queue, and billing is calculated by processing the event stream. Ensures every usage is captured in the correct period. Or, lock the parent space's billing period during the rollup: mark the period as "locked" before reading, so no new writes to child spaces can be attributed to that period. // Required: sweeper must release ConcurrencyDO slots when marking runs failed

// In naelao-sweeper cron:
async function cleanStaleConcurrencySlots(env: Env): Promise<void> {
  // Find all runs marked failed by the sweeper in the last 5 minutes
  const staleRuns = await getStaleRunsFromAnalytics(env);

  for (const run of staleRuns) {
    const concurrencyDO = env.NAELAO_CONCURRENCY_DO.get(
      env.NAELAO_CONCURRENCY_DO.idFromName(run.spaceId)
    );
    // Release the slot — idempotent (releasing a slot that's already released is a no-op)
    await concurrencyDO.releaseSlot(run.runId);
  }
}

// ConcurrencyDO.releaseSlot() must be idempotent:
async releaseSlot(runId: string): Promise<void> {
  const existing = this.db.exec('SELECT id FROM active_runs WHERE run_id = ?', runId).one();
  if (!existing) return; // already released — no-op
  this.db.exec('DELETE FROM active_runs WHERE run_id = ?', runId);
  // Also set a TTL-based auto-release as a second safety net:
  // Any active_run older than 1 hour is automatically released on next slot check
}

// When a definition is updated, a new version row is created.

interface WorkerDefinitionVersion {
  versionId: string;         // auto-generated UUID per update
  definitionId: string;
  code: string;              // R2 key for this version's code
  config: string;            // JSON

// WorkerInstanceDO stores the pinned versionId:
interface WorkerInstance {
  instanceId: string;
  definitionId: string;

  status: 'active' | 'updating' | 'stopped';

// Deployment locking via DO single-threaded execution:
// Both concurrent deployments hit the same WorkerInstanceDO (keyed by definitionId + subSpaceId).
// The DO's single-threaded nature serialises the two requests.
// Second request finds existing instance → returns existing instance, no duplicate created.
async deployToSubSpace(subSpaceId: string, versionId: string): Promise<WorkerInstance> {
  const existing = this.db.exec(
    'SELECT * FROM instances WHERE sub_space_id = ? AND status = ?', subSpaceId, 'active'
  ).one();
  if (existing) {
    // Already deployed — idempotent return
    return existing as WorkerInstance;
  }
  // Create new instance pinned to this version
  const instance = { instanceId: crypto.randomUUID(), pinnedVersionId: versionId, subSpaceId, status: 'active' };
  this.db.exec('INSERT INTO instances VALUES (?,?,?,?,?)', ...Object.values(instance));
  return instance;
}

KV Used for Locks and Counters — Eventual Consistency Breaks Both

The Gap

KV Used for Locks and Counters — Eventual Consistency Breaks Both The proposed rate-limiting fix (Vol. 4, T-44) and several idempotency checks in the spec use NAELAO_CONFIG_KV for counters and locks. Cloudflare KV is eventually consistent with global propagation that can take up to 60 seconds. A write in one region is not immediately visible in another. Using KV for a counter, a lock, or a rate limit produces wrong results under concurrent access — the exact scenario these mechanisms exist to handle. Why KV Cannot Be a Lock or Counter The Concurrency Failure Counter: Two requests read the rate-limit counter (both see 5), both increment, both write 6. The true count should be 7. KV has no…

Required Fix

Required: Durable Objects for Anything Needing Atomicity Durable Objects are single-threaded and strongly consistent by design — they are Cloudflare's only primitive for atomic counters, locks, and coordination. Anything that must be correct under concurrency must live in a DO, not KV. KV is correct only for read-heavy, write-rarely, eventual-consistency-tolerant data: configuration, cached schemas, feature flag values (where 60s propagation is acceptable and documented). // RIGHT: rate limiting in a DO (atomic, strongly consistent) export class RateLimitDO extends DurableObject { async checkAndIncrement(limit: number, windowMs: number): Promise<boolean> { const now = Date.now(); const windowStart = Math.floor(now / windowMs) * windowMs; // Single-threaded — no race possible let count =…

// RIGHT: rate limiting in a DO (atomic, strongly consistent)
export class RateLimitDO extends DurableObject {
  async checkAndIncrement(limit: number, windowMs: number): Promise<boolean> {
    const now = Date.now();
    const windowStart = Math.floor(now / windowMs) * windowMs;
    // Single-threaded — no race possible
    let count = (await this.ctx.storage.get<number>(`c:${windowStart}`)) ?? 0;
    if (count >= limit) return false;
    await this.ctx.storage.put(`c:${windowStart}`, count + 1);
    return true;   // exact count, every time
  }
}

// Rule: KV for config/cache/flags. DO for counters/locks/coordination.
// The spec's KV-based idempotency locks (notifications, x402) must move to DOs.

// Required: token_buffer cleanup + paginated replay

// 1. Cap the buffer — only keep last N tokens (configurable per Space tier)
const TOKEN_BUFFER_MAX_ROWS = 2000; // enough for ~2 reconnect scenarios

async bufferToken(runId: string, delta: string): Promise<void> {
  this.ctx.storage.sql.exec(
    'INSERT INTO token_buffer (run_id, delta) VALUES (?, ?)', runId, delta
  );
  // Keep buffer bounded — delete oldest if over limit
  this.ctx.storage.sql.exec(
    `DELETE FROM token_buffer WHERE run_id = ? AND id NOT IN (
       SELECT id FROM token_buffer WHERE run_id = ? ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT ?
     )`, runId, runId, TOKEN_BUFFER_MAX_ROWS
  );
}

// 2. Paginated replay (replace the current single-response approach)
// GET /agent/:id/replay?runId=X&after=0&limit=500
async replayBuffer(request: Request): Promise<Response> {
  const { runId, after = 0, limit = 500 } = await request.json();
  const tokens = this.ctx.storage.sql.exec(
    'SELECT id, delta FROM token_buffer WHERE run_id = ? AND id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ?',
    runId, after, limit
  ).toArray();
  const nextCursor = tokens.length === limit ? tokens[tokens.length - 1].id : null;
  return Response.json({ tokens: tokens.map(r => r.delta), nextCursor });
}

// naelao-agents queue consumer:
async function consumeAgentRun(message: Message<AgentRunMessage>): Promise<void> {
  const { runId } = message.body;
  const dedupKey = `agent-run-started:${runId}`;

  // Check if already started — KV TTL matches max agent run duration
  const alreadyStarted = await env.NAELAO_DEDUP_KV.get(dedupKey);
  if (alreadyStarted) {
    message.ack(); // silently drop the duplicate
    return;
  }

  // Mark as started before beginning work
  await env.NAELAO_DEDUP_KV.put(dedupKey, '1', { expirationTtl: 3600 }); // 1h TTL

  // Now start the actual agent run
  await dispatchAgentRun(message.body);
  message.ack();
}

The spec references Cloudflare's Tail Workers for logging but specifies no trace context schema, no correlation ID threading, and no way to reconstruct the causal chain of a failed run after the fact. This means every production incident is diagnosed by grepping logs across 22 separate Worker log streams…

Required: W3C Trace Context Propagation // Add to naelao-router: generate traceId on every inbound request // Then propagate via traceparent header (W3C Trace Context standard) // shared/tracing.ts — add to @naelao/shared package export interface TraceContext { traceId: string; // 32 hex chars — unique per request spanId: string; // 16 hex chars — unique per Worker hop runId?: string; // agentRunId if this is an agent run spaceId?: string; // scoping key } export function generateTraceId(): string { return crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, ''); } export function generateSpanId(): string { return crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, '').slice(0, 16); } // Format: traceparent: 00-{traceId}-{spanId}-01 export function makeTraceparent(ctx: TraceContext): string { return…

// Add to naelao-router: generate traceId on every inbound request
// Then propagate via traceparent header (W3C Trace Context standard)

// shared/tracing.ts — add to @naelao/shared package
export interface TraceContext {
  traceId: string;    // 32 hex chars — unique per request
  spanId: string;     // 16 hex chars — unique per Worker hop
  runId?: string;     // agentRunId if this is an agent run
  spaceId?: string;   // scoping key
}

export function generateTraceId(): string {
  return crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, '');
}

export function generateSpanId(): string {
  return crypto.randomUUID().replace(/-/g, '').slice(0, 16);
}

// Format: traceparent: 00-{traceId}-{spanId}-01
export function makeTraceparent(ctx: TraceContext): string {
  return `00-${ctx.traceId}-${ctx.spanId}-01`;
}

export function parseTraceparent(header: string): Partial<TraceContext> | null {
  const parts = header.split('-');
  if (parts.length < 4 || parts[0] !== '00') return null;
  return { traceId: parts[1], spanId: parts[2] };
}

// naelao-router: inject on every incoming request
app.use('*', async (c, next) => {
  const incoming = c.req.header('traceparent');
  const traceId = incoming
    ? parseTraceparent(incoming)?.traceId ?? generateTraceId()
    : generateTraceId();
  const spanId = generateSpanId();
  c.set('traceId', traceId);
  c.set('spanId', spanId);
  c.res.headers.set('traceparent', makeTraceparent({ traceId, spanId }));
  await next();
});

// Every Service Binding call MUST forward trace context:
// WRONG:
await env.NAELAO_BILLING.fetch(new Request('http://billing/charge', { body }));
// RIGHT:
await env.NAELAO_BILLING.fetch(new Request('http://billing/charge', {
  body,
  headers: { 'traceparent': makeTraceparent({ traceId, spanId: generateSpanId() }) }
}));

The Gap

The risk: a half-generated assistant message gets written to the thread as if it were complete. On the next turn, the agent reads its own truncated message as context and continues from a sentence that was cut off mid-word. The conversation becomes incoherent and there is no marker that the message was incomplete. The Missing Message Lifecycle States The spec stores messages with no explicit completion state.…

When a run's WAL entry is marked 'failed' or never reaches 'complete', any message it was streaming is marked 'interrupted' during the same recovery pass the sweeper already runs. // Required: explicit message status lifecycle
-- messages table addition:
status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'streaming'
  -- 'streaming'   = being generated right now
  -- 'complete'    = finished normally (stopReason: end_turn / tool_use)
  -- 'interrupted' = connection dropped or error mid-stream
  -- 'cancelled'   = user stopped generation

// On stream start: INSERT with status='streaming'
// On each token: UPDATE content (append), keep status='streaming'
// On clean finish: UPDATE status='complete'
// On disconnect/error: a watchdog (or next-run check) marks lingering
//   'streaming' messages older than 60s as 'interrupted'

// CRITICAL: context builder must handle interrupted messages:
function buildContext(messages: Message[]): Message[] {
  return messages.map(m => {
    if (m.status === 'interrupted') {
      // Append a marker so the LLM knows it was cut off — don't feed
      // a truncated sentence as if the agent chose to stop there
      return { ...m, content: m.content + '\n[message was interrupted]' };
    }
    return m;
  }).filter(m => m.status !== 'streaming'); // never feed an in-progress message
}

The Gap

Worker Subrequest Limit — Fan-Out Operations Hit the 1000-Subrequest Ceiling A single Cloudflare Worker invocation can make a maximum of 1000 subrequests (fetch calls, including Service Bindings, on the paid plan; 50 on free). The spec has several fan-out patterns that loop and make a subrequest per item: notifying N recipients, discovering tools from N installed apps, dispatching to N webhook targets, processing a batch of annotation tasks. Any of these that exceeds 1000 items in a single invocation throws and the whole operation fails — with no partial-progress recovery specified. The Fan-Out Hotspots Operation Subrequest per... Breaks when Notification fan-out (daily digest) recipient A…

Required Fix

The correct pattern is to enqueue the work: instead of looping and sending 5000 notifications inline, write 5000 messages to a Queue and let the queue consumer process them in batches across many invocations. The spec already has the queue infrastructure (naelao-notifications is a queue consumer) — but the producers in several places loop-and-send inline rather than enqueueing. Each fan-out site needs to be audited: if N can exceed ~500, it must go through a queue, not a loop. The queue also gives free retry and partial-progress recovery, which the inline loop lacks entirely. Gap T-64 — Medium
