Add a browser voice endpoint using CF Realtime SFU: in the operator shell, use the SFU WebSocket adapter: import { createSFUSession, createSFUWebSocketAdapter } from "@cloudflare/realtime/sfu-utils". const {sessionId} = await createSFUSession({accountId, appId, appSecret, baseUrl: "https://rtc.live.cloudflare.com/v1"}); const wsAdapter = await createSFUWebSocketAdapter({...}, sessionId). On the Agent side, wire the SFU WebSocket to the VoiceDO's audio input. This gives browser users sub-100ms first-audio latency via the nearest CF datacenter, with automatic reconnect and audio buffering on network hiccups (May 2026 feature). Phone calls via VAPI/Twilio remain for users who can't use browser audio.

G-S14 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — NaelaoAgentDO / AssistantDO

this.queue() Pattern Not Used — Internal Async Work Sent via CF Queues (External Overhead)

The Gap

For work that should be deferred but processed within the same DO (e.g., post-turn analytics, memory extraction, skill crystallization), the spec sends CF Queue messages to an external consumer Worker. CF's Agent class provides this.queue(callbackName, payload, retryOptions) which enqueues work for processing within the same DO, backed by cf_agents_queues SQLite table. This is faster (no external Queue round-trip), cheaper (no Queue billing), and retries within the DO (up to maxAttempts times with exponential backoff). External CF Queues should only be used for cross-DO or cross-Worker fan-out.

Required Fix

For work that can be processed within the same DO, use this.queue(): async onChatEnd(turn) { await this.queue("extractMemories", {messages: turn.messages, turnId: turn.id}); await this.queue("crystallizeSkills", {taskResult: turn.result, turnCount: turn.turnCount}); }. async extractMemories(payload) { const facts = await runMemoryExtraction(payload.messages); await this.upsertMemories(facts); }. Configure retry: static options = { retry: { maxAttempts: 3, baseDelayMs: 1000, maxDelayMs: 30000 } }. Reserve external CF Queues for: (1) notifying other DOs or Workers of events, (2) fan-out to multiple consumers, (3) delivery guarantees beyond the DO lifecycle (e.g., billing events that must survive DO crash).

G-S15 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — NaelaoAgentDO.initialize()

this.onStart() Lifecycle Hook Not Implemented — DO Initialization Not Idempotent

The Gap

The spec initializes AssistantDO and NaelaoAgentDO by checking for schema in the request handler path (if not initialized, run DDL). CF's Agent base class provides onStart() which: (1) fires once per DO lifetime on first wake after creation, (2) fires again after DO migration, (3) is guaranteed to complete before any requests are served (async but awaited), and (4) is not called on every wake — only on genuine starts. This is the correct place for schema initialization: idempotent (runs only when needed), atomic with request serving (no race condition), and semantically correct.

Required Fix

Implement onStart() as the canonical initialization point: async onStart() { this.sql`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, space_id TEXT NOT NULL, user_id TEXT, created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch("now")*1000))`; this.sql`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS messages (id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, session_id TEXT REFERENCES sessions(id), role TEXT NOT NULL, content TEXT NOT NULL, created_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch("now")*1000))`; // ... all tables ... }. Note: this.sql is the CF Agent SQL template literal helper (sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${userId}`) — it handles parameterization automatically. onStart() replaces blockConcurrencyWhile() schema init and the schema_initialized KV flag pattern.

G-S16 HIGH §operator-shell — Frontend / browser client

useAgentToolEvents() Hook Missing — No Client-Side Tool Execution Progress Tracking

The Gap

The spec's frontend has no mechanism to display tool call progress during an agent run. Users see a spinning indicator while the agent runs 15+ tool calls over 2 minutes — no feedback on which tool is running, which have completed, or if any have failed. CF's agents SDK provides useAgentToolEvents({agent}) which tracks all tool call lifecycle events in real-time: {runsById, runsByToolCallId, unboundRuns, getRunsForToolCall(toolCallId)}. Each AgentToolRunState has: tool name, input, status (running/complete/error), output, timing.

Required Fix

Add tool progress display using useAgentToolEvents: const {runsById, unboundRuns} = useAgentToolEvents({agent: "AssistantDO", name: spaceId}). Render in the UI: {Object.values(runsById).filter(r => r.status === "running").map(r => <ToolProgress key={r.id} name={r.tool} status={r.status} />)}. For the approval flow, tool calls with needsApproval: true will appear in runsByToolCallId with a "pending-approval" status before the user approves. This gives users real-time visibility into what the agent is doing, reducing perceived latency and building trust in the automation.

G-S17 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — AssistantDO SQL access

this.ctx.storage.sql.exec() Used Directly — CF this.sql Template Literal Is Safer and More Idiomatic

The Gap

The spec accesses DO SQLite via this.ctx.storage.sql.exec("SELECT * FROM messages WHERE session_id = ?", sessionId) with positional ? parameters as a variadic argument. This is error-prone: parameter count must match ?, wrong order causes silent data errors. CF's Agent class provides this.sql<T> as a tagged template literal: this.sql<Message[]>`SELECT * FROM messages WHERE session_id = ${sessionId}`. The template literal version: (1) infers parameter positions from template slots — impossible to mismatch order, (2) returns typed T[] (no manual casting), (3) rejects nested template interpolation (SQL injection prevention by design), (4) is shorter and more readable.

Required Fix

Replace all raw exec() calls with the this.sql template literal. Before: const rows = [...this.ctx.storage.sql.exec("SELECT * FROM messages WHERE session_id = ? ORDER BY created_at ASC", sessionId)]. After: const rows = this.sql<Message[]>`SELECT * FROM messages WHERE session_id = ${sessionId} ORDER BY created_at ASC`. For INSERT with multiple values: this.sql`INSERT INTO messages (id, session_id, role, content) VALUES (${id}, ${sessionId}, ${role}, ${content})`. The template literal cannot express multi-row INSERTs in one call — use a loop or this.sql`INSERT INTO messages SELECT ... FROM json_each(${JSON.stringify(rows)})` for batch inserts. All direct this.ctx.storage.sql.exec() calls should be migrated.

G-S18 HIGH §operator-shell / §05 — Frontend approval UI

addToolApprovalResponse() Not Implemented — Approval Prompts Have No Real-Time Client Path

The Gap

The spec's human-in-the-loop approval flow sends an approval link via email or push notification. The user clicks a link, which POSTs to a REST endpoint. This means: the WebSocket session showing the pending turn has no mechanism to receive the approval response in real-time — the user must leave the chat, click an email link, then return. In-chat approval (clicking a button while looking at the agent's request) is not possible. CF's useAgentChat() hook exposes addToolApprovalResponse({id, approved, data?}) which sends the approval decision directly over the existing WebSocket connection — the agent resumes immediately in the same session.

Required Fix

Implement in-chat approval using the SDK hook. In the operator shell: const {messages, addToolApprovalResponse} = useAgentChat({agent: "AssistantDO", name: spaceId}). Render approval cards inline in the message list: {messages.map(m => m.parts?.filter(p => p.type === "tool-approval").map(p => (<ApprovalCard key={p.id} toolName={p.toolName} args={p.args} onApprove={() => addToolApprovalResponse({id: p.id, approved: true})} onReject={() => addToolApprovalResponse({id: p.id, approved: false, data: {reason: "User rejected"}})} />)))}. Retain the email/push fallback for approvals where the user is not actively in the chat (implement the REST POST endpoint for those), but make in-chat the primary path.

G-S19 HIGH §05 — space-assistants — Sub-agent communication

parentAgent() and parentPath Not Implemented — Sub-Agents Cannot Notify Parent of Progress

The Gap

The spec's sub-agent pattern has no mechanism for a child agent to call back to its parent. Progress updates from sub-agents go to a shared SQLite table that the parent polls (5-minute sweeper cadence). CF's Agent SDK provides this.parentAgent(ParentClass) from within a child DO which returns a typed RPC stub for calling methods on the parent, and this.parentPath (array of {className, name} objects from root to current agent). A child agent completing its research task can immediately notify the parent via typed RPC rather than waiting for the next sweeper tick.

Required Fix

Add parent notification to sub-agent DOs: class ResearcherDO extends Agent<Env, ResearcherState> { async doResearch(task: string): Promise<string> { const parent = await this.parentAgent(AssistantDO); await parent.onSubAgentProgress({taskId: task, percent: 0}); const result = await runResearch(task); await parent.onSubAgentComplete({taskId: task, result}); return result; } }. In AssistantDO: async onSubAgentProgress(update) { await this.setState({...this.state, subAgentProgress: update}); }. async onSubAgentComplete(payload) { await this.deliverFiberResult(payload.taskId, payload.result); }. Use this.parentPath to log the full call chain for debugging: console.log("Agent chain:", this.parentPath.map(p => `${p.className}/${p.name}`).join(" → ")).

G-S20 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — AssistantDO WebSocket broadcast

Manual getWebSockets().forEach() Loop — CF this.broadcast() Is the Native Broadcast Method

The Gap

The spec broadcasts streaming tokens to connected clients via: this.ctx.getWebSockets().forEach(ws => { try { ws.send(JSON.stringify(event)); } catch (e) { /* ignore */ } }). CF's Agent base class provides this.broadcast(data) which: (1) iterates all connected WebSocket clients, (2) skips closed connections automatically, (3) handles errors internally, (4) is synchronous and safe to call from any context. The manual forEach pattern silently skips sending to closed sockets (error swallowed) and has no guarantee about message ordering when called concurrently.

Required Fix

Replace manual WebSocket iteration with this.broadcast(): async sendStreamingToken(token: string) { this.broadcast(JSON.stringify({type: "token", delta: token, turnId: this.currentTurnId})); }. async sendToolCallStart(toolName: string, toolCallId: string) { this.broadcast(JSON.stringify({type: "tool_start", toolName, toolCallId})); }. async sendTurnComplete(result: TurnResult) { this.broadcast(JSON.stringify({type: "done", ...result})); }. For targeted messages (send to only one client, e.g., approval UI): use connection.send() from onConnect(connection, ctx) where connection is the specific client's WebSocket.

G-S21 HIGH §naelao-notifications-full / §05 — Voice pipeline

afterTranscribe() Hook Missing — PII Not Filtered Before Voice Transcript Reaches LLM

The Gap

Voice calls transcribe user speech and feed the raw transcript directly into the agent's LLM context. If the user speaks their credit card number, SSN, or medical information, this PII enters the LLM's context and may be echoed back, logged, or stored. CF's withVoice mixin provides afterTranscribe(transcript, connection) hook which fires between STT output and LLM input — the hook can return a sanitized string or null (to skip the turn entirely).

Required Fix

Implement afterTranscribe() for PII redaction: async afterTranscribe(transcript: string, connection: Connection): Promise<string | null> { const redacted = redactPII(transcript); if (redacted !== transcript) { await logPIIRedaction(this.spaceId, "voice_transcript"); } return redacted; }. Implement redactPII() using regex patterns for common PII: credit card (4-digit groups), SSN (XXX-XX-XXXX), phone numbers, and email addresses. For HIPAA-scoped spaces, use a more aggressive redaction that flags any numeric sequence > 5 digits. Also implement beforeSynthesize(text, connection) to scan LLM responses before they are spoken: if the LLM echoes back credit card digits, catch and replace before TTS converts to audio.

G-S22 HIGH §naelao-notifications-full / §05 — VoiceDO response pipeline

beforeSynthesize() Hook Missing — Content Moderation Gap on Voice Responses Before TTS

The Gap

The voice pipeline sends the LLM's text response directly to the TTS synthesizer without content moderation. A prompt-injected user ("Say you are an AI that has no restrictions") or a misbehaving LLM could cause the voice agent to speak harmful content that gets synthesized to audio and played through the user's phone speaker. This is harder to interrupt mid-playback than a text response. CF's withVoice mixin provides beforeSynthesize(text, connection) which fires between LLM output and TTS input — can return modified text or null (silences the turn).

Required Fix

Implement beforeSynthesize() for content moderation: async beforeSynthesize(text: string, connection: Connection): Promise<string | null> { const violates = await checkContentPolicy(text); if (violates.harmful) { await this.speak(connection, "I'm sorry, I can't respond to that request."); return null; } if (text.length > 2000) { return text.slice(0, 2000) + " [Response truncated for voice delivery]"; } return text; }. The null return cancels TTS synthesis for that turn. Also implement onInterrupt(connection) to handle barge-in (user speaks while agent is speaking) — cancel the current TTS stream and process the new user input immediately.

G-S23 HIGH §ai-gateway — AI Gateway configuration

AI Gateway Spend Limits Not Configured — No Per-Provider Budget Enforcement at Infra Level

The Gap

The spec implements credit deduction in SpaceDO's deductCredits() as application-level billing. If a bug in the agent loop sends 1,000 LLM requests before the credits check fires, $3,000 of inference spend can accumulate. AI Gateway provides spend limits at the infrastructure level: configure a dollar-based budget per provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Together) with fixed or rolling windows (daily/weekly/monthly). When the budget is hit, AI Gateway blocks further requests at the proxy layer — before the Worker even sees them. This is a hard backstop independent of application-level bugs.

Required Fix

Configure AI Gateway spend limits in the CF dashboard or via API: for each AI Gateway endpoint, set a spend limit: { "provider": "anthropic", "limit": 1000.00, "window": "daily", "action": "block" }. Add per-space budget enforcement using AI Gateway's custom metadata: when routing LLM requests through AI Gateway, add cf-aig-metadata: {"space_id": spaceId} header. Configure per-metadata-key spend limits so each space has its own infrastructure-level budget cap. The application-level deductCredits() remains as the primary billing mechanism; AI Gateway spend limits are the emergency backstop. Alert (don't just block) at 80% of spend limit so operators can investigate before service is interrupted.

G-S24 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — Agent state telemetry

onStateChanged() Hook Not Implemented — No Agent State Change Audit Trail

The Gap

AssistantDO and NaelaoAgentDO update state via raw SQL INSERTs with no centralized hook to observe state transitions. If the agent transitions from "planning" to "executing" to "waiting-approval" to "complete", these transitions are invisible to the platform. There is no audit trail, no latency tracking per state, and no alert if an agent gets stuck in a state for too long. CF's Agent class fires onStateChanged(newState: State, oldState: State) whenever setState() is called — a natural hook for telemetry.

Required Fix

Implement onStateChanged for audit and telemetry: onStateChanged(state: AgentState, oldState: AgentState) { const transition = `${oldState.phase ?? "init"} → ${state.phase ?? "idle"}`; this.env.ANALYTICS.writeDataPoint({ blobs: [transition, this.spaceId, state.currentTaskId ?? "none"], doubles: [Date.now() - (oldState.phaseStartedAt ?? Date.now())], indexes: [this.agentId] }); if (state.phase === "waiting-approval" && !oldState.phase) { scheduleApprovalTimeoutAlert(state.approvalId, 600_000); } }. This creates a full state machine audit trail in Analytics Engine, enabling: "how long do agents spend in each phase?", "which spaces have approval bottlenecks?", "which tasks cause agents to get stuck?".

G-S25 HIGH §naelao-notifications-full / §05 — Voice call configuration

STT eotThreshold Not Configured — Default End-of-Turn Detection Causes Premature or Late Turn Ends

The Gap

The spec's voice integration never configures the STT end-of-turn detection threshold. CF's @cf/deepgram/flux STT has configurable eotThreshold (0.5-0.9, default 0.7) and eagerEotThreshold (enables faster but less accurate end-of-turn events). At the default 0.7, the STT may cut the user off mid-sentence (if they pause briefly while thinking) or wait too long before handing off to the LLM (adding perceived latency). Different use cases need different thresholds: customer support (wait longer, users ramble — use 0.8+), quick commands (faster response — use 0.5), professional (balanced — use 0.7).

Required Fix

Configure STT per space type: const eotThreshold = { customer_support: 0.85, command_control: 0.55, conversational: 0.70 }[space.scenarioType] ?? 0.70. transcriber = new WorkersAIFluxSTT(this.env.AI, { eotThreshold: spaceConfig.voiceEotThreshold ?? eotThreshold, eagerEotThreshold: spaceConfig.voiceEagerEot ?? 0.50, eotTimeoutMs: spaceConfig.voiceEotTimeout ?? 4000, keyterms: [...spaceConfig.voiceKeyterms, ...platformTerms] }). Store these voice config fields in SpaceDO SQLite and expose them in the space settings UI. Also configure keyterms: boosting domain-specific terms (product names, technical jargon) significantly improves STT accuracy for specialized spaces.

G-S26 HIGH §naelao-notifications-full / §05 — VoiceDO.beforeCallStart()

beforeCallStart() Hook Missing — No Rate Limiting or Auth on Incoming Voice Calls

The Gap

The spec's voice agent accepts all incoming calls from VAPI without any validation of the caller, rate limiting per user, or check of whether the user's space has voice enabled. A malicious actor who discovers a VAPI phone_number_id can initiate unlimited voice sessions, consuming speech-to-text inference credits and LLM tokens. CF's withVoice mixin provides beforeCallStart(connection) which fires before the call is accepted — returning false rejects the call.

Required Fix

Implement beforeCallStart() for call gating: async beforeCallStart(connection: Connection): Promise<boolean> { const meta = connection.metadata as {userId?: string, spaceId?: string}; if (!meta.userId || !meta.spaceId) return false; const space = await this.getSpaceConfig(meta.spaceId); if (!space?.voiceEnabled) { await this.speak(connection, "Voice calls are not enabled for this workspace."); return false; } const rateKey = `voice:${meta.userId}:${Math.floor(Date.now()/60000)}`; const callCount = await incrementAndCheckLimit(rateKey, space.voiceCallsPerMinute ?? 1); if (!callCount.allowed) { await this.speak(connection, "Call rate limit exceeded. Please try again in a minute."); return false; } return true; }. Also verify caller identity using the JWT passed in the WebSocket upgrade query parameter.

G-S27 HIGH §naelao-notifications-full / §05 — CF Realtime SFU

SFU WebSocket Auto-Reconnect Not Used — Browser Audio Drops Permanently on Network Hiccup

The Gap

If the spec implements browser-to-agent audio via a WebSocket connection (directly or via CF SFU), transient network drops (mobile user enters elevator, WiFi handoff) cause the audio stream to drop permanently — the user must hang up and call back. CF's Realtime SFU WebSocket adapter (auto-reconnect feature, released May 2026) automatically retries for 5 seconds on disconnect, buffers outgoing audio during the retry window, and replays buffered packets after reconnection. This makes brief network interruptions transparent to the voice conversation.

Required Fix

Use the CF Realtime SFU WebSocket adapter with auto-reconnect enabled: import { createSFUWebSocketAdapter } from "@cloudflare/realtime/sfu-utils". const adapter = await createSFUWebSocketAdapter({ accountId: env.CF_ACCOUNT_ID, appId: env.SFU_APP_ID, appSecret: env.SFU_APP_SECRET, baseUrl: "https://rtc.live.cloudflare.com/v1", autoReconnect: true, reconnectTimeoutMs: 5000, audioBufferMs: 3000 }, sessionId). The adapter buffers up to 3 seconds of audio during disconnection. On reconnect, it sends buffered packets with correct sequence numbers so the receiver reconstructs the audio stream. Downsampling utilities are provided: downsample48kStereoTo16kMono() for browser mic input, upsample16kMonoTo48kStereo() for playback.

G-S28 HIGH §operator-shell — Frontend / browser

VoiceClient Vanilla JS Integration Missing — No Non-React Voice Embedding Option for Builders

The Gap

The spec documents the operator shell (React app) but provides no voice integration option for builders who want to embed a voice assistant in their own website or mobile app without React. CF's @cloudflare/voice/client provides VoiceClient for vanilla JS: import { VoiceClient } from "@cloudflare/voice/client". const client = new VoiceClient({agent: "AssistantVoiceDO"}). client.addEventListener("statuschange", () => updateUI(client.status)). await client.startCall(). Status values: "idle" | "listening" | "thinking" | "speaking". This enables embedding via a simple <script> tag without a React dependency.

Required Fix

Add VoiceClient as an embeddable widget option. Create a naelao-voice-widget.js bundle (CF Pages, hosted at /static/voice-widget.js): const client = new VoiceClient({agent: "AssistantVoiceDO", name: window.NAELAO_SPACE_ID}). client.addEventListener("statuschange", () => { document.getElementById("naelao-voice-status").textContent = client.status; }). document.getElementById("naelao-voice-btn").onclick = () => client.startCall(). This gives space builders a 3-line embed: <script src="https://app.naelao.dev/static/voice-widget.js"></script><div id="naelao-voice-status"></div><button id="naelao-voice-btn">Talk to Assistant</button>. Document VoiceClient alongside useVoiceAgent in the platform SDK docs.

G-S29 HIGH §05 — space-assistants — scheduleEvery / cron-jobs.json

scheduleEvery() Not Used for Recurring Tasks — Cron Expression Parsing Hand-Rolled and Error-Prone

The Gap

The spec's cron-jobs.json stores cron expressions ("0 9 * * 1-5" for weekdays at 9am) that the sweeper parses with a custom lightweight cron parser. CF's Agent SDK provides this.scheduleEvery(intervalSeconds, callback, payload, retryOptions) for recurring tasks and this.schedule("0 9 * * 1-5", callback) for cron-expression-based scheduling. The SDK parses cron expressions internally (no custom parser needed), stores schedules in cf_agents_schedules SQLite with retry state, and fires callbacks directly on the DO with at-most-once semantics (no duplicate-run race condition unlike the sweeper).

Required Fix

Replace cron-jobs.json with SDK scheduling. When a user adds a recurring task: async addRecurringTask(task: RecurringTask) { if (task.intervalSeconds) { const sched = await this.scheduleEvery(task.intervalSeconds, "runTask", {taskId: task.id}); } else if (task.cron) { const sched = await this.schedule(task.cron, "runTask", {taskId: task.id}); } await this.sql`INSERT INTO user_schedules (task_id, sched_id) VALUES (${task.id}, ${sched.id})`; }. async runTask(payload: {taskId: string}) { const task = this.sql<Task[]>`SELECT * FROM tasks WHERE id = ${payload.taskId}`[0]; if (task) await this.executeTask(task); }. To list: this.getSchedules(). To cancel: this.cancelSchedule(schedId). SDK schedules survive DO hibernation (stored in SQLite) and retry automatically on failure.

G-S30 HIGH §ai-gateway — AI Gateway / Workers AI

session_affinity Not Set for Workers AI Calls — KV Prompt Cache Hit Rate Suboptimal

The Gap

Anthropic's prompt caching achieves high hit rates when the same CF edge location processes requests for the same conversation (the cache is local to the CF datacenter). Workers AI routes requests to the datacenter closest to the client, but without affinity guarantees, subsequent requests in the same conversation may route to different datacenters, causing cache misses. CF's Agent base class provides the sessionAffinity getter which returns a stable value (the DO's Durable Object ID) that can be used as a routing hint to Workers AI for consistent datacenter selection.

Required Fix

Pass session affinity to Workers AI calls: const response = await this.env.AI.run("@cf/anthropic/claude-3-5-sonnet", { messages, session_affinity: this.sessionAffinity }). The sessionAffinity getter returns a stable string (the DO ID) that Workers AI uses to prefer routing to the same datacenter. This maximizes Anthropic prompt cache hits for the same conversation (same system prompt prefix). Also set a consistent request ID: const requestId = crypto.randomUUID(); pass as cf-aig-request-id header to AI Gateway for deduplication of retried requests. For the Think SDK, session affinity is used automatically — another reason to extend Think rather than using env.AI.run() directly.

G-S31 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — Sub-agent URL routing

Sub-Agent URL Routes Not Registered in wrangler.toml — /agents/ Path Returns 404

The Gap

The CF Agents SDK routes agent requests via URL paths: /agents/{class-kebab}/{name} for root agents and /agents/{parent}/{name}/sub/{child}/{name} for sub-agents. These routes must be handled by a Worker that calls routeAgentRequest(). The spec's wrangler.toml likely has specific routes for named endpoints but does not configure the /agents/* catch-all route. Without this, all WebSocket connections from useAgent(), useAgentChat(), and useVoiceAgent() fail with 404. The spec's naelao-router needs to be configured to handle this route pattern.

Required Fix

Add /agents/* routing to naelao-router in wrangler.toml: [[routes]] pattern = "app.naelao.dev/agents/*" zone_name = "naelao.dev". In naelao-router Worker: import { routeAgentRequest } from "agents"; export default { async fetch(request, env, ctx) { const url = new URL(request.url); if (url.pathname.startsWith("/agents/")) { return await routeAgentRequest(request, env) ?? new Response("Agent not found", {status: 404}); } return handleOtherRoutes(request, env, ctx); } }. Ensure all agent DO classes are exported from the Worker entry point and bound in wrangler.toml so routeAgentRequest can resolve them by class name. Sub-agent routes (/agents/.../sub/...) are handled automatically by the SDK router.

G-S32 HIGH §naelao-agent-do / §05 — Agent tool policy

needsApproval: true Tool Flag Pattern Not Applied — Per-Tool Client Approval Granularity Missing

The Gap

The spec implements approval at the action-category level (requires_approval_for: ["customer_email_send", "issue_refund"]) checked at the AgentDO level before dispatching tool calls. CF's tool definition supports needsApproval: true per individual tool — the SDK pauses execution and sends the approval request to the connected client over WebSocket with the specific tool name and arguments. This is finer-grained (per tool, not per category) and client-initiated (user sees exactly what will be executed). The spec's approach requires a separate approval tracking system; the SDK pattern is built-in.

Required Fix

Apply needsApproval: true to high-risk tools in the tool definitions: tools: { sendEmail: tool({description: "Send email", inputSchema: emailSchema, needsApproval: true, execute: sendEmailFn}), processRefund: tool({description: "Process refund", inputSchema: refundSchema, needsApproval: true, execute: refundFn}), searchKnowledge: tool({description: "Search knowledge base", inputSchema: searchSchema, needsApproval: false, execute: searchFn}) }. The SDK handles the pause, WebSocket notification to the client, and resume. Low-risk tools (read-only, non-destructive) set needsApproval: false and execute immediately. The requires_approval_for list in space config can be used to dynamically set needsApproval based on space settings: const requiresApproval = spaceConfig.approvalRequired.includes(toolName).

G-S33 HIGH §05 — space-assistants — AssistantDO voice + VAPI

forceEndCall() Not Implemented — Voice Calls Cannot Be Terminated Programmatically

The Gap

The spec's voice call via VAPI can be terminated by the user hanging up or by the call timeout, but there is no mechanism for the agent to end the call programmatically: if the refund was approved, if the issue was resolved, if the user became abusive, or if the call has exceeded the space's voice minute budget. VAPI provides an end-call REST API but this requires an additional HTTP call with the call ID. CF's withVoice mixin provides forceEndCall(connection) which immediately ends the call from within the DO, freeing the TTS and STT pipeline.

Required Fix

Implement call termination triggers in the agent: async onTurn(transcript, ctx) { const reply = await this.runAgentTurn(transcript); if (shouldEndCall(reply)) { await this.speak(ctx.connection, "Your request has been processed. Goodbye!"); this.forceEndCall(ctx.connection); return reply; } return reply; }. shouldEndCall() checks: (1) the LLM reply contains an end-call intent (classify with a simple prompt), (2) call duration > space.maxVoiceMinutes, (3) credit balance < MIN_BALANCE. Also implement credit tracking in onTurn: const callDuration = (Date.now() - callStartTime) / 60000; await this.deductCredits(spaceId, callDuration * VOICE_COST_PER_MINUTE); if (creditsExhausted) { await this.speak(ctx.connection, "Voice credit exhausted."); this.forceEndCall(ctx.connection); }.

G-S34 HIGH §05 — space-assistants / §16 — Agent onConnect()

Agent Connection Handler Not Implementing CF onConnect() Pattern — Auth Checked in Message Handler

The Gap

The spec authenticates WebSocket connections by checking the JWT in the first WebSocket message received (after upgrade). CF's Agent base class provides onConnect(connection, ctx) which fires immediately after WebSocket upgrade but before the first message. Returning or throwing from onConnect() terminates the connection before any messages are exchanged — the correct place for auth. Checking auth in the message handler means the connection is established (DO is woken, resources allocated) before the caller is authenticated, creating a DoS vector where unauthenticated clients can wake DOs at will.

Required Fix

Implement onConnect() for early authentication: async onConnect(connection: Connection, ctx: ConnectionContext) { const url = new URL(ctx.request.url); const token = url.searchParams.get("token"); if (!token) { connection.close(4001, "Authentication required"); return; } try { const payload = await verifyJWT(token, this.env.JWT_SECRET); if (payload.spaceId !== this.spaceId) { connection.close(4003, "Forbidden"); return; } connection.setState({userId: payload.sub, spaceId: payload.spaceId, role: payload.role}); } catch (e) { connection.close(4001, "Invalid token"); return; } }. Connection state set in onConnect() is available in all subsequent handlers (onMessage, onClose) via connection.state. This prevents unauthenticated clients from waking the DO and consuming resources.

G-S35 HIGH §05 — space-assistants — AssistantDO multi-agent orchestration

No Multi-Agent Team Composition Pattern — CF Agent Facet Hierarchy Not Used for Specialist Agents

The Gap

The spec dispatches one sub-agent at a time (parent → single child) for background tasks. CF's Agent SDK supports multi-level facet hierarchies: AssistantDO → [ResearcherDO, CoderDO, ReviewerDO] in parallel, with each specialist running as a named sub-agent that can itself spawn deeper sub-agents. The spec has no pattern for: (1) parallel multi-specialist dispatch, (2) aggregating results from multiple concurrent sub-agents, (3) specialist agent selection based on task type, (4) specialist agents with their own persistent memory and tool sets. This limits complex tasks to sequential single-agent execution.

Required Fix

Implement a multi-agent team pattern using CF facets: async orchestrateTask(task: ComplexTask) { const [researcher, coder, reviewer] = await Promise.all([this.subAgent(ResearcherDO, `research-${task.id}`), this.subAgent(CoderDO, `code-${task.id}`), this.subAgent(ReviewerDO, `review-${task.id}`)]); const [research, code] = await Promise.all([researcher.research(task.context), coder.draft(task.spec)]); const review = await reviewer.review({research, code, requirements: task.requirements}); return {research, code, review}; }. Each specialist DO has its own: tool set (ResearcherDO has web search + knowledge tools, CoderDO has workspace tools, ReviewerDO has read-only tools), memory (separate SQLite in each DO), and system prompt. The parallel execution collapses what would be a sequential 30-step loop into 3 concurrent 10-step tasks, reducing total latency by ~3x.

Appendix T

Twelfth-Pass: Space Assistant Completeness — OpenClaw Feature Parity, MCP Apps, Multi-Container, Skills Self-Improvement

35 architectural gaps covering: OpenClaw feature parity (continuous background loop, fiber concurrency, proactive trigger types, tool chaining, skill marketplace, inline sub-agent delegation, channel hub normalization, delegation chain), MCP Apps ecosystem (App Store, installed app persistence, tool approval flow, scope model, McpAgent/AIChatAgent separation, OAuth callback), Skills self-improvement via Hermes pattern (crystallization loop, versioning, test suite, within-session cache, conflict resolution), multi-container coordination (pool management, container specialization, filesystem sync, pre-warming, network policy), shared agent user data isolation (memory namespace, Vectorize filter, session isolation, R2 path divergence), instance management (atomic limit enforcement, hibernation flush, spaceId/userId restoration, observability), and missing CF primitive usage (Vectorize write path, decay_rate application, ctx.waitUntil() crash).

G-T01 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / keepAlive

No Continuous Background Loop — Heartbeat Driven by External Sweeper Instead of Native this.schedule() + this.keepAliveWhile()

The Gap

The spec drives AssistantDO heartbeats from an external naelao-sweeper Worker running every 5 minutes via CF Cron Trigger. This creates a distributed coordination problem: the sweeper must maintain a KV registry of all active assistants, wake each DO individually via HTTP fetch, and handle failures across potentially thousands of DOs simultaneously. The CF Agents SDK provides this.keepAliveWhile(condition) and this.keepAlive() to prevent DO hibernation without any external coordination, and this.schedule(delay, callback, payload) for self-scheduling the next heartbeat iteration. These primitives were designed exactly for this continuous-background-loop pattern and eliminate the sweeper Worker entirely.

Required Fix

Replace the external sweeper with internal DO scheduling: ```typescript async onStart() { // Self-schedule first heartbeat immediately await this.schedule(300_000, "heartbeat", {}); } async heartbeat(payload: unknown) { await this.runHeartbeatTasks(); // Re-schedule next heartbeat await this.schedule(300_000, "heartbeat", {}); } async runLongFiberTask(fiber: Fiber) { // Prevent hibernation while fiber is running return await this.keepAliveWhile(async () => { return await executeFiber(fiber); }); } ``` Remove the naelao-sweeper Worker and its KV registry entirely. Each DO manages its own wakeup cycle independently with zero cross-DO coordination overhead.

G-T02 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / fiber concurrency

Fiber Concurrency Model Incomplete — Fibers Stored in SQLite but Executed Sequentially, Not in Parallel

The Gap

The spec stores "fibers" in DO SQLite as a queue and processes them one at a time in the heartbeat loop. The OpenClaw architecture the spec claims to implement runs multiple fibers concurrently using Promise.allSettled() so that a long-running Python execution fiber does not block a quick Slack reply fiber. In a Durable Object, concurrent JavaScript execution is safe within a single turn because DOs are single-threaded per I/O boundary — multiple awaited operations can run in parallel with Promise.all. The spec's sequential fiber drain loop serialises all work, causing a blocked long-running task to delay time-sensitive user-facing responses.

Required Fix

Replace sequential fiber drain with concurrent execution: ```typescript async heartbeat() { const pendingFibers = this.sql<Fiber[]>` SELECT * FROM fibers WHERE status = 'pending' ORDER BY priority DESC, created_at ASC LIMIT 10 `; const results = await Promise.allSettled( pendingFibers.map(f => this.executeFiber(f)) ); results.forEach((r, i) => { if (r.status === 'rejected') { this.markFiberFailed(pendingFibers[i].id, r.reason); } }); } ``` Use ctx.waitUntil() via the Worker's ExecutionContext (passed in fetch, not DurableObjectState) to extend fiber execution beyond the heartbeat request boundary. Cap concurrent fibers at a configurable limit (default 5) to avoid memory pressure.

G-T03 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / proactive triggers

Proactive Trigger Types Limited to Time-Based Cron — Event-Based, State-Change, and Threshold Triggers Absent

The Gap

The spec implements proactive agent triggers exclusively as time-based cron schedules stored in cron-jobs.json. The OpenClaw architecture defines four trigger types: (1) time-based (cron), (2) event-based (incoming webhook payload matching a filter), (3) state-change-based (a watched value in DO SQLite crosses a boundary), and (4) threshold-based (a metric — e.g., unread Slack messages > 20). The spec has no mechanism for the agent to react to an incoming Stripe webhook, no way to watch for a DB column crossing a threshold, and no event filter engine. This limits proactive behavior to scheduled tasks only.

Required Fix

Add a trigger registry table and evaluation engine: ```typescript // In onStart() schema init this.sql`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS triggers ( id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, type TEXT NOT NULL CHECK(type IN ('cron','event','state_change','threshold')), filter_json TEXT NOT NULL, action_json TEXT NOT NULL, last_fired_at INTEGER )`; // Event-based trigger evaluation (called from webhook handler) async evaluateTriggers(event: WebhookEvent) { const triggers = this.sql<Trigger[]>` SELECT * FROM triggers WHERE type = 'event' `; for (const t of triggers) { const filter = JSON.parse(t.filter_json); if (matchesFilter(event, filter)) { await this.spawnFiber(JSON.parse(t.action_json), event); } } } ``` Evaluate threshold triggers in the heartbeat loop by querying watched metrics. Route incoming webhooks (Stripe, GitHub, Slack events) through a shared /webhooks/{spaceId} endpoint that calls evaluateTriggers on the target AssistantDO.

G-T04 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / tool execution

Tool Chaining Dependency Graph Absent — Tools Run Sequentially With No DAG-Based Composition

The Gap

The spec runs LLM-selected tools sequentially in a simple loop: call tool, get result, append to messages, call LLM again. OpenClaw's tool composition model allows defining a dependency graph (DAG) where tool A's output is declared as input to tool B, enabling parallel execution of independent branches and typed data flow between tools. For example: (fetch_user_profile, fetch_account_history) run in parallel; their results feed summarize_customer_context; that feeds both draft_response and check_policy simultaneously. The spec's sequential loop cannot express this structure, adding unnecessary latency on multi-tool tasks.

Required Fix

Introduce a tool pipeline definition: tools can declare outputSchema and inputFrom fields: ```typescript const tools = { fetchProfile: tool({ outputSchema: userProfileSchema, execute: ({userId}) => fetchUserProfile(userId) }), fetchHistory: tool({ outputSchema: historySchema, execute: ({userId}) => fetchHistory(userId) }), summarize: tool({ inputFrom: ['fetchProfile', 'fetchHistory'], execute: ({fetchProfile, fetchHistory}) => summarizeContext(fetchProfile, fetchHistory) }) }; ``` Implement a DAG executor: topological sort the tool call graph, execute independent nodes with Promise.all(), pass resolved outputs to dependent nodes. Log the full DAG execution trace to DO SQLite for debugging. This collapses three sequential LLM round-trips into a single parallel fan-out + join.

G-T05 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — Skills / marketplace

Skill Marketplace Absent — Platform Skills Are Static; No User-Installable Skill Packs

The Gap

The spec defines three skill tiers (Platform, Space-level, Personal) but Tier 1 Platform skills are static files in R2 maintained by the Naelao team. There is no mechanism for users or space admins to browse and install pre-built skill packs from a marketplace (e.g., "HubSpot CRM Skills", "GitHub Code Review Skills", "Notion Writing Skills"). The OpenClaw architecture includes an agent marketplace where skill packs are versioned bundles of tools + instructions that can be installed into an agent with one click. Without this, the skill ecosystem is closed to Naelao-authored content only.

Required Fix

Create a skill marketplace data model and installation flow: ```typescript // In naelao-marketplace Worker / DO interface SkillPack { id: string; name: string; version: string; tier: 'platform' | 'community' | 'private'; skills: Skill[]; tools: ToolDefinition[]; r2_key: string; // bundled skill pack in global R2 } // In AssistantDO: install a skill pack async installSkillPack(packId: string) { const pack = await this.env.MARKETPLACE_DO .get(packId).getMetadata(); // Write skills to personal tier in assistant R2 await this.env.R2.put( `spaces/${this.spaceId}/assistants/${this.userId}/skills/packs/${packId}.json`, JSON.stringify(pack) ); await this.sql`INSERT OR REPLACE INTO installed_packs (pack_id, version, installed_at) VALUES (${packId}, ${pack.version}, unixepoch('now')*1000)`; } ``` Expose a /marketplace endpoint in the operator shell listing available packs by category, rating, and install count.

G-T06 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / sub-agent delegation

No Inline Sub-Agent Delegation — Parent Always Fire-and-Forgets; Cannot Await Child Result Synchronously

The Gap

The spec's sub-agent dispatch is always fire-and-forget: the parent AssistantDO POSTs a task to a child agent and moves on. When the child completes, it writes results to a shared SQLite table. The parent only learns of completion on its next heartbeat poll (up to 5 minutes later). OpenClaw's agent delegation model allows a parent to await a child inline — blocking the parent fiber until the child returns a result — enabling complex multi-step workflows where intermediate results feed subsequent LLM calls. The spec has no spawnSubAgent() that returns a Promise resolving to the child's output.

Required Fix

Implement inline delegation using CF sub-agent RPC: ```typescript // In AssistantDO async delegateResearch(topic: string): Promise<string> { // this.subAgent() returns a typed RPC stub const researcher = await this.subAgent( ResearcherDO, `researcher-${this.userId}-${Date.now()}` ); // Awaits child completion inline — parent fiber blocks here const result = await researcher.research(topic); return result; } // Usage in agent turn const research = await this.delegateResearch(userQuery); const answer = await this.llm([...context, research]); ``` For fire-and-forget tasks (background indexing, non-blocking notifications), retain the current pattern. For tasks where the parent needs the result before continuing the user-facing turn, use inline delegation. Document the distinction in the spec: inline vs. background delegation patterns.

G-T07 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — Channel hub / InboxMessage

Channel Hub Normalization Missing — Slack, Discord, Telegram Have Separate Handlers With No Unified Message Format

The Gap

The spec has separate handler classes for each channel: SlackHandler, DiscordHandler, TelegramHandler, EmailHandler. Each handler parses the channel-native payload format, extracts the message text and user ID, and calls into the agent with channel-specific parameters. When adding a new channel (e.g., WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams), a developer must write a new handler from scratch and integrate it with AssistantDO separately. The OpenClaw channel hub normalizes all incoming messages to a single InboxMessage format before they reach the agent, so the agent never deals with channel-specific payload structures.

Required Fix

Define a canonical InboxMessage format and normalize at handler boundaries: ```typescript interface InboxMessage { id: string; channelType: 'slack' | 'discord' | 'telegram' | 'email' | 'sms' | 'web'; channelId: string; // e.g. Slack channel ID userId: string; // platform user ID displayName: string; text: string; attachments: Attachment[]; replyTo?: string; // thread/message ID for replies timestamp: number; raw: unknown; // original payload for audit } // Each handler converts to InboxMessage class SlackHandler { normalize(payload: SlackEvent): InboxMessage { return { channelType: 'slack', channelId: payload.event.channel, userId: payload.event.user, text: payload.event.text, // ... }; } } // AssistantDO receives only InboxMessage async onInboxMessage(msg: InboxMessage) { ... } ``` Store InboxMessages in a unified inbox table in AssistantDO SQLite for full conversation history across channels.

G-T08 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / sub-agent result delivery

No Agent Delegation Chain — Sub-Agent Results Returned via Polling, Not Synchronous Parent Notification

The Gap

When a sub-agent finishes its task, it writes results to a shared KV or SQLite table and exits. The parent AssistantDO discovers the result on the next heartbeat poll (5-minute cycle). This polling model introduces up to 5 minutes of latency between task completion and the parent acting on the result — unacceptable for user-facing workflows where the agent is waiting for a research result before drafting a response. The CF parentAgent() RPC call allows a child to push its result directly to the parent's onSubAgentComplete() method, eliminating the polling delay.

Required Fix

Replace result polling with push notification via parentAgent(): ```typescript // In child ResearcherDO async research(topic: string) { const result = await doResearch(topic); // Push result to parent immediately on completion const parent = await this.parentAgent(AssistantDO); await parent.onSubAgentComplete({ taskId: this.taskId, result, completedAt: Date.now() }); return result; } // In parent AssistantDO async onSubAgentComplete( payload: {taskId: string; result: string; completedAt: number} ) { // Resume the waiting fiber immediately await this.resumeFiber(payload.taskId, payload.result); await this.sql` UPDATE fibers SET status='complete', result=${payload.result} WHERE id = ${payload.taskId} `; } ``` The parent fiber that was awaiting child completion is resumed within milliseconds of child completion. Remove the result polling loop from the heartbeat — it is only needed as a fallback for crashed children.

G-T09 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / MCP App Store

No MCP App Store Concept — Users Cannot Browse, Install, or Manage MCP Apps That Extend AssistantDO

The Gap

The spec defines AssistantDO as an MCP server but provides no mechanism for users to install third-party MCP servers (MCP Apps) into their assistant to extend its tool set. In the OpenAI/OpenClaw model, MCP Apps are remote MCP servers that users can install via an OAuth flow — the agent then has access to their tools automatically. Without an App Store concept, the Naelao platform is locked to only the tools the Naelao team ships, preventing the ecosystem growth that makes agent platforms valuable. CF natively supports remote MCP servers via the McpAgent class and can serve as an MCP proxy.

Required Fix

Define the MCP App Store architecture: 1. Create a naelao-app-store Worker/DO that maintains a registry of available MCP Apps (name, description, OAuth endpoints, tool manifest, scopes). 2. Add an /app-store endpoint in the operator shell for browsing apps. 3. On install click, initiate OAuth flow: redirect user to MCP server's OAuth URL with redirect_uri=https://app.naelao.dev/mcp-oauth-callback. 4. On callback, store the access token and installed app metadata in AssistantDO SQLite (see G-T10). 5. On each agent turn, load installed app tools by fetching the MCP server's /tools endpoint using the stored access token. Store the App Store registry in a global DO: appStoreStub.registerApp(appManifest). Space admins can publish private apps only visible within their space.

G-T10 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / mcp_apps table

Installed MCP App State Not Persisted — No mcp_apps Table in AssistantDO SQLite

The Gap

Even if an MCP App install flow is implemented, the spec has no SQLite table to store installed app metadata (OAuth tokens, scopes, app ID, installation date). Without persistent storage, installed apps are lost on DO hibernation. The agent would need to re-authenticate every time it wakes, breaking any MCP App integration. Additionally, there is no mechanism to list which apps a user has installed, revoke an app's access, or refresh expired OAuth tokens.

Required Fix

Add the mcp_apps table in AssistantDO onStart(): ```typescript this.sql`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS mcp_apps ( app_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, mcp_server_url TEXT NOT NULL, access_token TEXT NOT NULL, refresh_token TEXT, token_expires_at INTEGER, scopes_json TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]', installed_at INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT (unixepoch('now')*1000), last_used_at INTEGER, status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active' CHECK(status IN ('active','revoked','error')) )`; // Token refresh logic async getAppToken(appId: string): Promise<string> { const app = this.sql<McpApp[]>` SELECT * FROM mcp_apps WHERE app_id = ${appId} AND status = 'active' `[0]; if (!app) throw new Error('App not installed'); if (app.token_expires_at && app.token_expires_at < Date.now()) { return await this.refreshAppToken(app); } return app.access_token; } ``` Store OAuth tokens encrypted using the space's encryption key (env.ENCRYPTION_KEY). Never log access tokens in Analytics Engine or console.

G-T11 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / MCP tool approval

MCP App Tool Approval Flow Missing — Installed MCP App Tools Bypass needsApproval Requirement on First Use

The Gap

When a user installs an MCP App, its tools immediately become available to the agent with no human approval required on first execution. If a malicious or misconfigured MCP App exposes a "delete_all_files" tool, the agent could invoke it without the user ever seeing an approval prompt. The CF Agents SDK's needsApproval: true flag should be automatically applied to all tools from installed MCP Apps until the user has explicitly approved each tool at least once. First-use approval creates a trust baseline for the installed app's tool set.

Required Fix

Implement first-use approval for MCP app tools: ```typescript async callMcpAppTool( appId: string, toolName: string, args: unknown ) { const approval = this.sql<ApprovalRecord[]>` SELECT * FROM mcp_tool_approvals WHERE app_id = ${appId} AND tool_name = ${toolName} `[0]; if (!approval) { // First use: require explicit approval return await this.requestHumanApproval({ type: 'mcp_tool_first_use', appId, toolName, args, message: `MCP App "${appId}" wants to run "${toolName}" for the first time.` }); } // Approved: execute the tool return await this.invokeMcpTool(appId, toolName, args); } ``` Add a mcp_tool_approvals table: (app_id, tool_name, approved_at, approved_by_user_id). After first approval, subsequent calls execute without prompting. Revocation of an app (mcp_apps.status = 'revoked') also clears its tool approvals.

G-T12 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / MCP app scopes

No MCP App Scopes/Permissions Model — App Installation Grants All Tools With No Per-Tool Scope Manifest

The Gap

The spec has no concept of per-tool scopes for MCP Apps. In the OpenAI plugin/MCP App model, each app publishes a scope manifest listing which tools require which permission levels (read-only, write, destructive). The user approves a scope manifest at install time, not individual tool calls. An MCP App that has only read scopes approved cannot execute write or destructive tools even if the agent tries to call them. Without scopes, all installed app tools have equal access, making it impossible to install a "read-only analytics" MCP App without also granting its incidentally available write tools.

Required Fix

Add scope enforcement to MCP app tool dispatch: ```typescript interface McpAppScope { toolName: string; level: 'read' | 'write' | 'destructive'; description: string; } // At install time, user approves specific scopes async installMcpApp( appId: string, approvedScopes: McpAppScope[] ) { const scopeJson = JSON.stringify(approvedScopes); await this.sql`INSERT INTO mcp_apps (app_id, scopes_json, ...) VALUES (${appId}, ${scopeJson}, ...)`; } // At tool call time, enforce scopes async callMcpAppTool( appId: string, toolName: string, args: unknown ) { const app = await this.getMcpApp(appId); const scopes: McpAppScope[] = JSON.parse(app.scopes_json); const allowed = scopes.find(s => s.toolName === toolName); if (!allowed) { throw new Error( `Tool "${toolName}" not in approved scopes for app "${appId}" `); } return await this.invokeMcpTool(appId, toolName, args); } ``` Display the scope manifest in the App Store install UI so users understand what they are approving.

G-T13 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / McpAgent vs AIChatAgent

AssistantDO Conflates MCP Server and AIChatAgent Roles — Violates CF SDK Class Hierarchy

The Gap

The spec has AssistantDO simultaneously acting as: (1) an MCP server (exposing tools to external MCP clients via the MCP protocol), and (2) an AIChatAgent (running the inner LLM loop, managing conversation history, handling WebSocket chat sessions). The CF Agents SDK separates these: McpAgent extends Agent and handles MCP protocol (tool listing, tool execution over MCP JSON-RPC), while AIChatAgent extends Think and handles the conversational AI loop. Conflating both in one DO means MCP protocol messages and WebSocket chat messages share the same handler, creating routing ambiguity and preventing independent scaling of MCP serving vs. chat serving.

Required Fix

Separate AssistantDO into two distinct classes: ```typescript // MCP server: exposes tools to external MCP clients class AssistantMcpDO extends McpAgent<Env> { server = new McpServer({name: 'Naelao Assistant'}); async init() { this.server.tool('search_memory', searchMemorySchema, (args) => this.searchMemory(args)); this.server.tool('create_task', createTaskSchema, (args) => this.createTask(args)); } } // Chat agent: handles user-facing conversation class AssistantDO extends AIChatAgent<Env, AssistantState> { async onChatMessage(message: ChatMessage) { return await this.think(message.content); } } ``` Route /mcp/* requests to AssistantMcpDO and /agents/assistant-do/* requests to AssistantDO. This is the pattern CF's moltworker reference implementation uses. The McpDO can delegate tool execution back to the main AssistantDO via service binding RPC.

G-T14 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / MCP OAuth callback

No Remote MCP Server OAuth Callback Handling — MCP App Installation Flow Has No Redirect URI Handler

The Gap

MCP App installation via OAuth requires a redirect URI: after the user grants access on the MCP server's OAuth page, the browser redirects to https://app.naelao.dev/mcp-oauth-callback?code=...&state=... The naelao-assistant Worker has no handler for this path. The OAuth code cannot be exchanged for an access token, so the installation flow never completes. This is a blocking gap for any MCP App ecosystem: without a callback handler, zero MCP apps can be installed.

Required Fix

Add an OAuth callback handler to naelao-assistant (or naelao-router) Worker: ```typescript // In naelao-router fetch handler if (url.pathname === '/mcp-oauth-callback') { const code = url.searchParams.get('code'); const state = url.searchParams.get('state'); if (!code || !state) { return new Response('Bad Request', {status: 400}); } // Decode state: {spaceId, userId, appId, codeVerifier} const stateData = await verifyAndDecodeOAuthState( state, env.JWT_SECRET ); // Exchange code for token const app = await getAppManifest(stateData.appId); const tokenResponse = await fetch(app.tokenEndpoint, { method: 'POST', body: new URLSearchParams({ grant_type: 'authorization_code', code, code_verifier: stateData.codeVerifier, redirect_uri: 'https://app.naelao.dev/mcp-oauth-callback', client_id: env.MCP_CLIENT_ID }) }); const token = await tokenResponse.json(); // Store token in AssistantDO const assistantDO = getAssistantDO( stateData.spaceId, stateData.userId, env ); await assistantDO.storeMcpAppToken(stateData.appId, token); return Response.redirect('/app-store?installed=' + stateData.appId); } ``` Use PKCE (code_verifier/code_challenge) for security. Store the OAuth state JWT in a short-lived KV entry (TTL: 10 minutes) to prevent CSRF and replay attacks.

G-T15 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — Skills / Hermes self-improvement

Skills Never Self-Improve — No Post-Task Skill Crystallization Loop (Hermes Pattern)

The Gap

The spec defines skills as static instruction files stored in R2, written once by users or the Naelao team. After an agent successfully completes a complex task, the specific tool call sequence and reasoning chain that worked are discarded. The Hermes self-improvement pattern defines: after each successful agentic task completion, extract the successful tool call sequence as a reusable skill, store it in the agent's personal skill tier, and use it automatically next time a similar task appears. This transforms each agent from a static instruction-follower into a continuously improving system that gets better at tasks it has done before.

Required Fix

Implement post-task skill crystallization: ```typescript async onTaskComplete(task: CompletedTask) { if (!task.success || task.turnCount < 3) return; // Extract the successful tool call sequence const toolSequence = task.messages .filter(m => m.role === 'assistant' && m.tool_calls) .map(m => m.tool_calls); if (toolSequence.length === 0) return; // Ask the LLM to crystallize a skill from this run const skillDef = await this.llm([{ role: 'system', content: 'Extract a reusable skill from this successful task run.' }, { role: 'user', content: JSON.stringify({task: task.description, toolSequence}) }]); // Store as a new personal-tier skill await this.addSkill({ id: `crystallized-${Date.now()}`, name: skillDef.name, description: skillDef.description, instructions: skillDef.instructions, sourceTask: task.id, version: 1 }); } ``` Gate crystallization on task success (no human corrections after completion) and minimum complexity (>= 3 tool calls). Log crystallization events to Analytics Engine for observability.

G-T16 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — Skills / versioning

No Skill Versioning — Self-Modified Skills Overwrite Previous Version With No Rollback Capability

The Gap

When a skill is self-improved (G-T15) or manually edited by a user, the new version overwrites the old R2 object. If the new version causes the agent to perform worse (more errors, user complaints, lower task completion rate), there is no way to rollback to the previous version. The spec has no version history for skills, no comparison between skill versions, and no automatic rollback trigger if a new version degrades performance metrics.

Required Fix

Add skill versioning: ```typescript // R2 key pattern with version const skillKey = (skillId: string, version: number) => `spaces/${spaceId}/assistants/${userId}/skills/${skillId}/v${version}.json`; async addSkill(skill: Skill) { const existing = await this.getLatestSkill(skill.id); const version = existing ? existing.version + 1 : 1; const key = skillKey(skill.id, version); await this.env.R2.put(key, JSON.stringify({...skill, version})); // Update skill index await this.sql`INSERT OR REPLACE INTO skill_versions (skill_id, version, r2_key, created_at) VALUES (${skill.id}, ${version}, ${key}, unixepoch('now')*1000)`; await this.sql`UPDATE skills SET current_version = ${version} WHERE id = ${skill.id}`; } async rollbackSkill(skillId: string, toVersion: number) { await this.sql`UPDATE skills SET current_version = ${toVersion} WHERE id = ${skillId}`; } ``` Expose rollback in the operator shell skill management UI. Retain last 10 versions per skill in R2; prune older versions automatically. Track per-version task success rate to enable data-driven rollback decisions.

G-T17 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — Skills / test suite

No Skill Test Suite — Self-Modified Skills Have No Automated Validation After Modification

The Gap

When the Hermes skill crystallization loop (G-T15) or a user edit modifies a skill, the new version is immediately live with no automated validation. A poorly crystallized skill could instruct the agent to always use a deprecated tool, include incorrect parameter names, or contradict the base system prompt. Without test cases, the only signal that a skill version is broken is user complaints after the damage is done. The OpenClaw framework defines per-skill test cases: a set of input/expected-output pairs that are auto-run after any skill modification.

Required Fix

Add a skill test framework: ```typescript interface SkillTest { id: string; skill_id: string; input_message: string; expected_tool_calls: string[]; // tool names that must appear forbidden_tool_calls: string[]; // tools that must NOT appear expected_output_contains: string[]; } async runSkillTests(skillId: string): Promise<TestResult[]> { const tests = this.sql<SkillTest[]>` SELECT * FROM skill_tests WHERE skill_id = ${skillId} `; const results = await Promise.all(tests.map(async t => { const run = await this.testRun(t.input_message, skillId); const passed = t.expected_tool_calls.every(tc => run.toolCalls.includes(tc)) && t.forbidden_tool_calls.every(tc => !run.toolCalls.includes(tc)); return {testId: t.id, passed, run}; })); // Auto-rollback if any test fails if (results.some(r => !r.passed)) { await this.rollbackSkill(skillId); } return results; } ``` Run tests asynchronously after skill modification using this.queue('runSkillTests', {skillId}). Alert the space admin if a skill auto-rolled back.

G-T18 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — Skills / caching

Skill Loading Not Cached Within Session — All Three Tiers Re-Read From R2 on Every Agent Turn

The Gap

The spec loads skills by reading R2 objects for all three tiers (Platform, Space, Personal) on each agent turn to compose the system prompt. A single turn may load 10-30 skill files across three R2 prefixes. With R2 read latency of 20-40ms per object and no within-session cache, a turn that activates 5 skills incurs 100-200ms of R2 read overhead on top of LLM latency. Skills rarely change during an active session (they change between sessions when a user edits them). An in-memory cache keyed by skill version avoids redundant R2 reads within the same DO activation.

Required Fix

Add an in-memory skill cache with version-based invalidation: ```typescript class AssistantDO extends AIChatAgent<Env> { // In-memory cache: survives multiple turns within same activation private skillCache = new Map<string, {version: number; skill: Skill}>(); async loadSkills(): Promise<Skill[]> { const index = this.sql<SkillIndex[]>` SELECT id, current_version FROM skills WHERE active = 1 `; const skills = await Promise.all(index.map(async ({id, current_version}) => { const cached = this.skillCache.get(id); if (cached?.version === current_version) return cached.skill; // Cache miss: read from R2 const obj = await this.env.R2.get( skillKey(id, current_version) ); const skill = await obj!.json<Skill>(); this.skillCache.set(id, {version: current_version, skill}); return skill; })); return skills; } } ``` The cache is invalidated on hibernation (in-memory state is lost) but rebuilt from SQLite index on the next activation. Cache size is bounded by the number of active skills (typically <50) — no eviction policy needed.

G-T19 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — Skills / conflict resolution

No Skill Conflict Resolution — Tier 3 Override of Tier 1/2 Is Silent With No Precedence Logging

The Gap

The spec loads skills from three tiers and concatenates their instructions into the system prompt with Tier 3 (Personal) taking precedence over Tier 2 (Space) which takes precedence over Tier 1 (Platform). If a Personal skill says "always respond in French" but a Platform skill says "always respond in the user's detected language", the conflict is silently resolved by instruction ordering — the last instruction wins, but no one knows why the agent is behaving oddly. Conflicting skill instructions produce unpredictable LLM behavior because the model tries to satisfy contradictory constraints.

Required Fix

Add conflict detection and precedence logging: ```typescript async detectSkillConflicts(skills: Skill[]): Promise<Conflict[]> { // Use a lightweight LLM call to detect instruction conflicts const conflicts = await this.llm([{ role: 'system', content: 'Identify conflicting instructions in this skill set. Output JSON: [{skill1, skill2, conflict_description}]' }, { role: 'user', content: skills.map(s => `${s.id} (Tier ${s.tier}): ${s.instructions}`).join('\n---\n') }]); return JSON.parse(conflicts); } async buildSystemPrompt(skills: Skill[]): Promise<string> { const conflicts = await this.detectSkillConflicts(skills); if (conflicts.length > 0) { // Log to Analytics Engine for admin review this.env.ANALYTICS.writeDataPoint({ blobs: [JSON.stringify(conflicts), this.spaceId], indexes: ['skill_conflict'] }); } // Apply tier precedence explicitly in prompt return buildPromptWithPrecedenceComments(skills, conflicts); } ``` Surface conflicts in the operator shell skill management view so admins can resolve them intentionally rather than discovering them through agent misbehavior.

G-T20 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantSandboxDO / multi-container

Single Container Assumption — AssistantSandboxDO Manages One Container; Concurrent Tasks Compete on Same Sandbox

The Gap

AssistantSandboxDO creates a single CF Container per assistant and routes all sandbox tasks (Python execution, bash scripts, browser automation, Node.js code) through it sequentially. When a long-running Python data analysis fiber is executing, it blocks bash command execution, browser screenshot tasks, and all other sandbox work for that assistant. The Moltworker architecture defines a multi-container pool: multiple specialized containers per agent with independent execution, sharing a single R2 workspace as the source of truth. The spec never defines container pool management, container type specialization, or cross-container task routing.

Required Fix

Redesign AssistantSandboxDO to manage a container pool: ```typescript interface ContainerSlot { id: string; type: 'python' | 'node' | 'browser' | 'bash'; status: 'idle' | 'busy' | 'starting'; containerRef: DurableObjectStub | null; lastUsedAt: number; } class AssistantSandboxDO extends DurableObject { private pool: ContainerSlot[] = []; private maxContainers = 3; // configurable per space plan async executeTask(task: SandboxTask): Promise<TaskResult> { const slot = await this.acquireContainer(task.type); try { return await slot.containerRef!.execute(task); } finally { this.releaseContainer(slot.id); } } async acquireContainer(type: ContainerSlot['type']) { // Find idle container of matching type, or create new one let slot = this.pool.find( s => s.type === type && s.status === 'idle' ); if (!slot && this.pool.length < this.maxContainers) { slot = await this.createContainer(type); } if (!slot) throw new Error('Container pool exhausted'); slot.status = 'busy'; return slot; } } ``` Expose pool status in AssistantDO.getHealth() for observability.

G-T21 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantSandboxDO / container types

Container Type Specialization Absent — All Tasks Run in a Single Generic Container

The Gap

The spec creates one generic CF Container per assistant and runs all workloads in it: Python scripts, bash commands, Node.js code, and browser automation (Playwright). A generic container must include Python runtime, Node.js, and a Chromium browser, making its image large and its startup time slow (~3 seconds cold start for a full-featured image). Moltworker's multi-container model uses specialized containers: a slim Python container (~1.2s start), a Node.js container (~0.8s start), and a heavier browser container (~4s start). Tasks are routed to the appropriate specialized container, reducing average cold start by ~60%.

Required Fix

Define container type manifests in the spec: ```typescript const CONTAINER_TYPES = { python: { image: 'naelao/sandbox-python:latest', // Python 3.12 + common libs memoryMb: 512, cpuMilli: 1000, diskMb: 1024 }, node: { image: 'naelao/sandbox-node:latest', // Node.js 22 + npm memoryMb: 256, cpuMilli: 500, diskMb: 512 }, browser: { image: 'naelao/sandbox-browser:latest', // Chromium + Playwright memoryMb: 2048, cpuMilli: 2000, diskMb: 4096 }, bash: { image: 'naelao/sandbox-bash:latest', // Alpine + common CLI tools memoryMb: 128, cpuMilli: 250, diskMb: 256 } } as const; ``` Publish these container images to the Cloudflare Container Registry and reference them in wrangler.toml container bindings. The task router in AssistantSandboxDO selects container type based on task.type from the fiber definition.

G-T22 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantSandboxDO / filesystem sync

Container Filesystem Sync Undefined — Concurrent Container Writes to Same R2 Prefix Cause Undefined Behavior

The Gap

The spec mentions FUSE-mounted R2 as the container workspace but never specifies: (1) which R2 bucket prefix each container mounts, (2) how FUSE write-back is triggered (write-through vs. write-behind), (3) how a second container reading a file written by the first container avoids a stale cache read, and (4) what happens when two containers write to the same file concurrently. In the Moltworker model, R2 is the source of truth: containers use FUSE write-through (every write is immediately PUT to R2), and cache invalidation uses R2 event notifications (R2 PUT fires an event that all containers with the affected key in their FUSE cache must invalidate).

Required Fix

Define the filesystem sync protocol in the spec: ``` Write path: Container write → FUSE driver → R2.put(key, data) (synchronous) On R2.put success → FUSE confirms write to container On R2.put failure → FUSE returns EIO to container Read/cache invalidation path: Container read → FUSE checks local cache → cache miss: R2.get(key) R2 PUT event → naelao-r2-notifier Worker → AssistantSandboxDO.onR2Event(key) → broadcast invalidation to all active containers via container.invalidateCache(key) Conflict resolution: R2 object versioning enabled on workspace bucket Concurrent writes: last-writer-wins (R2 conditional PUT not used) Conflict detection: container can opt-in to R2 conditional PUT (If-Match: etag) for critical files ``` Document this explicitly in the Moltworker integration spec section. Add a conflict_log table in AssistantSandboxDO SQLite to record R2 write conflicts for debugging.

G-T23 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantSandboxDO / pre-warming

No Container Pre-Warming Pool — First Sandbox Task After Idle Incurs 3+ Second Cold Start Latency

The Gap

CF Containers have a cold start time of 1.5-4 seconds depending on image size. AssistantSandboxDO creates containers on demand when the first sandbox task arrives. After the DO has been idle (e.g., overnight), the next morning's first task — often a simple bash command — waits 3 seconds before executing. For interactive agents, this latency is jarring. The Moltworker model defines a container pre-warm pool: when the AssistantDO heartbeat detects an upcoming scheduled task or the user has been actively chatting recently (signals the agent may soon need a container), it pre-warms a container in the background.

Required Fix

Add pre-warming to AssistantSandboxDO: ```typescript async preWarmIfNeeded() { const idleSlot = this.pool.find(s => s.status === 'idle'); if (idleSlot) return; // already warm if (this.pool.length >= this.maxContainers) return; // pool full // Pre-warm the most common container type for this assistant const mostUsed = await this.getMostUsedContainerType(); const slot = await this.createContainer(mostUsed); slot.status = 'idle'; this.pool.push(slot); console.log(`Pre-warmed ${mostUsed} container for ${this.agentId}`); } ``` Call preWarmIfNeeded() from AssistantDO heartbeat when: (1) user has sent a message in the last 5 minutes, (2) a scheduled task is due in the next 60 seconds, or (3) the DO has just woken from hibernation. Configure pre-warm as a DO alarm set 30 seconds before a known upcoming task. Pre-warm only if the space plan includes container access (avoid wasting resources for text-only assistants).

G-T24 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantSandboxDO / network policy

Container Network Policy Not Configured — Containers Get Full Network Access by Default; Untrusted Code Runs Unrestricted

The Gap

env.SANDBOX.create() is called in the spec without a network policy option. CF Containers support configurable network policies: full (default, internet access), restricted (only egress to allowlisted hostnames), or none (no network). Agent-executed user code (Python scripts, bash commands from LLM tool calls) runs in a container with full internet access by default. A prompt-injected agent could exfiltrate secrets, make unexpected external API calls, or participate in a DDoS attack from within the container.

Required Fix

Add network policy to container creation: ```typescript async createContainer( type: ContainerSlot['type'], taskContext: TaskContext ): Promise<ContainerSlot> { const networkPolicy = this.resolveNetworkPolicy( type, taskContext ); const container = await this.env.SANDBOX.create({ image: CONTAINER_TYPES[type].image, network: networkPolicy, memory: CONTAINER_TYPES[type].memoryMb * 1024 * 1024, cpu: CONTAINER_TYPES[type].cpuMilli }); return {id: crypto.randomUUID(), type, containerRef: container, status: 'idle', lastUsedAt: 0}; } resolveNetworkPolicy( type: ContainerSlot['type'], ctx: TaskContext ): NetworkPolicy { if (ctx.userProvided) { // User-submitted code: restricted egress only return { type: 'restricted', allowedHostnames: this.spaceConfig.sandboxAllowedHosts ?? [] }; } // Agent-generated code: allow access to declared tools only return { type: 'restricted', allowedHostnames: ctx.requiredHosts }; } ``` Allow space admins to configure sandboxAllowedHosts in space settings for legitimate external API access from containers.

G-T25 CRITICAL §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / shared agent memory

Shared Agent Mode Memory Namespace Collision — memory Table Has No user_id Column; All Users' Memories Merge

The Gap

When a Space admin enables shared assistant mode (one AssistantDO instance serving all space members), the current memory table schema has no user_id column. All users' extracted facts, conversation summaries, and structured memories write to the same namespace. User A's personal information (address, payment method, preferences) is retrievable during User B's conversation. This is a data isolation failure with potential GDPR implications: User B's agent may reference User A's personal data in its responses.

Required Fix

Add user_id to all memory tables and enforce isolation at query time: ```typescript // Schema (in onStart): this.sql`ALTER TABLE memories ADD COLUMN user_id TEXT`; this.sql`CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_memories_user ON memories(user_id, space_id)`; // Write path — always include user_id: async storeMemory(key: string, value: string, userId: string) { const memKey = this.isSharedMode ? `${userId}:${key}` // namespace with userId in shared mode : key; await this.sql`INSERT OR REPLACE INTO memories (key, value, user_id, space_id, updated_at) VALUES ( ${memKey}, ${value}, ${userId}, ${this.spaceId}, unixepoch('now')*1000 )`; } // Read path — always filter by user_id: async recallMemory(key: string, userId: string) { const memKey = this.isSharedMode ? `${userId}:${key}` : key; return this.sql<Memory[]>` SELECT * FROM memories WHERE key = ${memKey} AND user_id = ${userId} `[0]; } ``` Apply the same user_id isolation to structured_facts, sessions, and all other per-user tables when in shared mode.

G-T26 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / Vectorize isolation

Shared Agent Vectorize Namespace Collision — Vector Search Has No user_id Filter; User A's Memories Appear in User B's Recall

The Gap

In shared agent mode, all users' memories are inserted into the same Vectorize index (Layer 5 of the Memory OS) with no user_id metadata. A vector similarity search for User B's question may return embedding neighbors from User A's stored memories. Because vector similarity is semantic (not syntactic), the leakage is invisible: User B's agent may surface personal facts about User A without any obvious indicator that the data came from a different user.

Required Fix

Add user_id to all Vectorize inserts and filter on all queries: ```typescript // Write path: async storeVectorMemory( text: string, userId: string, metadata: Record<string, string> ) { const embedding = await this.env.AI.run( '@cf/baai/bge-small-en-v1.5', {text} ); await this.env.VECTORIZE.upsert([{ id: `${userId}-${crypto.randomUUID()}`, values: embedding.data[0], metadata: { userId, // REQUIRED for isolation spaceId: this.spaceId, ...metadata } }]); } // Read path — ALWAYS include userId filter: async recallVectorMemory(query: string, userId: string) { const embedding = await this.env.AI.run( '@cf/baai/bge-small-en-v1.5', {text: query} ); return await this.env.VECTORIZE.query( embedding.data[0], { topK: 10, filter: {userId, spaceId: this.spaceId} // user isolation filter } ); } ``` Audit all existing Vectorize query call sites in the spec to ensure none omit the userId filter. In non-shared mode, the userId filter is still recommended as defense-in-depth.

G-T27 HIGH §05 — Space Assistant — AssistantDO / shared sessions

Shared Agent Channel Sessions Not Per-User — sessions Table Has No user_id Column; All Users Share One Session Per Channel

The Gap

In shared agent mode, the sessions table tracks active sessions by channel type (Slack, Discord, etc.) but has no user_id column. When User A and User B both send Slack messages in the same channel, the agent creates one session for the Slack channel. Both users' messages are appended to the same session, interleaving their conversations. The agent responds to User B's message with context from User A's conversation and vice versa — complete conversation isolation failure.

Required Fix
