(2) Batch Analytics Engine writes using the batch write API (up to 25 events per write request, reducing per-event overhead). (3) Add a per-space analytics tier: free-tier spaces get sampled-only analytics; paid spaces get full fidelity. (4) Run monthly cost projection in the ops dashboard: current_events_rate × days_remaining × $0.25/M. Alert when projected monthly cost > $10K. Consider migrating high-volume diagnostic events to CF Logpush (cheaper) or Axiom at scale.

G-AC16 HIGH §ops — space registry hot DO

Space Registry DO Becomes a Hot Read-Only Bottleneck Under Millions of Concurrent Space Lookups

The Gap

Every Worker request that needs to route to a space (naelao-router → find SpaceDO for spaceId) may consult a central registry to validate that the space exists and load its routing metadata. If this registry is a single DO, it serialises all lookups. At millions of concurrent requests across millions of products, the registry DO becomes the single most-accessed DO in the system. Unlike SpaceDOs which scale horizontally (one per product), the registry has no sharding plan.

Required Fix

Eliminate the registry DO for the hot path. Encode space existence and routing metadata in a signed JWT embedded in the subdomain or URL: e.g., `{spaceId}.naelao.com` → naelao-router reads KV cache (spaceId → metadata JSON) with 60-second TTL. KV read latency is ~1ms at edge (vs 10-50ms DO call). On KV miss, fetch from SpaceMetaDO and repopulate KV. The SpaceMetaDO only receives cold-start or cache-miss traffic (rare). For security, sign the metadata with an HMAC so Workers verify it without a round-trip. Registry DO is then only needed for space creation/deletion (write-rare operations).

G-AC17 HIGH §ops — RateLimitDO hot spot

RateLimitDO Is Itself a Serialisation Bottleneck — All Concurrent Rate Checks Queue on One DO Per Key

The Gap

Replacing KV rate limiting with a DO-based token bucket (G-AC11) solves consistency but introduces a new problem: a single RateLimitDO per rate-limit key serialises all concurrent requests for that key. A popular product with 1000 concurrent users all sending messages simultaneously creates 1000 queued DO calls. Each DO call takes 5-15ms minimum. 1000 × 15ms = 15 seconds of queued rate-check latency before any user gets a response. DO-based rate limiting at this scale is worse than no rate limiting.

Required Fix

Use a sharded RateLimitDO topology: 16 shards per rate-limit key, addressed as `rl:{key}:{hash(requestId) % 16}`. Each shard holds a fraction (1/16) of the total bucket allowance. Requests are routed to a shard by request ID hash. Over-counting (a shard allowing more than its share due to imbalanced traffic) is bounded at 16× the shard replenishment rate, which at typical rates means <1% burst overage — acceptable for rate limiting. For strict rate limits (auth endpoints), use a 2-phase check: fast DO shard check followed by a KV-written idempotency key to prevent retried requests from double-consuming.

G-AC18 HIGH §ops — sweeper O(N) scale

Cron-Based Sweepers Iterate O(N) Over All Products — Will Not Complete Within 1-Minute Cron Window at Scale

The Gap

Multiple cron jobs in the spec iterate over all spaces: billing sweeper (check for overdue spaces), canary promotion checker (advance rollouts), container cleanup (terminate idle containers), archive sweeper (move cold conversations to R2). Each cron job runs once per minute and scans all spaces. At 1M products, even a 1ms-per-space scan takes 1000 seconds — 16× longer than the 60-second cron interval. Sweepers start running before the previous run finishes. The spec addresses duplicate sweeper runs for single operations (G-AA42) but not the fundamental O(N) scale problem.

Required Fix

Replace full-scan sweeper crons with event-driven and alarm-based patterns: (1) Billing overdue: set a DO alarm for each space at renewal_date + 3 days. The alarm fires only for that space. (2) Canary promotion: set a DO alarm at canary_start + stabilization_window for each active deployment. (3) Container cleanup: containers register a TTL alarm on start; they clean themselves up. (4) Archive sweeper: each SpaceDO sets an alarm when its SQLite storage exceeds 8GB (80% of 10GB). The alarm triggers only that space's archive job. This converts O(N) crons to O(1) event dispatch — each space manages its own lifecycle via alarms.

G-AC19 HIGH §ops — sub-space user registry scale

SpaceDO User Registry Grows Without Bound in SaaS Products With Millions of End-Users

The Gap

For SaaS tenancy products, SpaceDO's coordinator role includes a user registry: a table recording all end-users who have joined the product, their roles, credits, and activity timestamps. At 1M end-users per SaaS product, this table has 1M rows in SpaceDO's 10GB SQLite budget. Each user row (id, email_hash, role, credits, last_active_at, settings_json) might be 500 bytes. 1M users × 500 bytes = 500MB for just the user registry, consuming 5% of the SpaceDO 10GB budget. At 10M users, the user registry alone exhausts the budget.

Required Fix

Extract the user registry from SpaceDO to a dedicated UserRegistryDO (one per product) backed by Turso when user count > 100K. UserRegistryDO handles: user lookup by id, role assignment, credit balance (delegated to WalletDO), and activity tracking. SpaceDO coordinator only stores aggregate counts and a routing pointer (which UserRegistryDO shard handles userId X). Implement UserRegistryDO sharding: 16 shards addressed by `${spaceId}:users:${hash(userId) % 16}`, each holding ~62K users per shard. Provision additional shards automatically when any shard exceeds 80% capacity.

G-AC20 HIGH §pricing — infrastructure cost model

Builder Pricing Tiers Do Not Account for Turso, Analytics Engine, R2 Egress, or Container Costs

The Gap

The Naelao billing model (spec §billing, Appendix Y BillingStrategy) prices builder plans around AI token consumption and feature access. It does not factor in: (1) Turso per-DB cost ($0.20-0.75/month per product DB, or per-user DB at 1M users = $200K/month). (2) Analytics Engine volume (up to $375K/month at 1M users as G-AC15). (3) R2 egress costs for file downloads, screenshots, and exports (typically $0.09/GB, significant for document-heavy spaces). (4) CF Container compute costs for code execution sandboxes. Naelao is currently selling token-based credits while silently absorbing all infrastructure costs, which are non-linear and will cause the platform to lose money at scale.

Required Fix

Model the infrastructure cost per space type per tier: (a) Calculate expected Analytics Engine events per active user per day by space type (research agent = ~200 events, simple chatbot = ~20 events). (b) Add an infra_cost_factor to each pricing tier that scales with usage. (c) At builder product creation, select a cost category (lightweight / standard / compute-heavy) that maps to a wholesale credit rate. (d) Run a monthly infrastructure cost reconciliation: if a builder's product consumes more infrastructure than their plan's infra_cost_factor predicts, auto-upgrade them or apply an overage charge. This prevents subsidised pricing from becoming a loss leader at scale.

G-AC21 CRITICAL §db — Turso topology decision

Turso Topology Decision Is Undocumented — Per-Product vs Per-User DB Choice Left Implicit

The Gap

Appendix Z recommends Turso (libSQL) as the solution for multi-tenant database scaling past the SpaceDO 10GB SQLite limit. However the spec does not record the architectural decision: is Turso provisioned per builder product (one DB per SpaceDO, all end-users as rows within it) or per end-user (one DB per user within a SaaS product, giving hard data isolation)? These are fundamentally different topologies with different cost profiles, isolation guarantees, and migration paths. Without a documented decision, different parts of the codebase may implement conflicting assumptions.

Required Fix

Document the canonical Turso topology decision: (1) DEFAULT: per-product DB (one Turso DB per SpaceDO / builder product). End-users are rows isolated by user_id and tenant-level RLS. This is cost-efficient (1 DB per product regardless of user count) and scales to millions of users via SQLite's read concurrency. (2) ENTERPRISE OPT-IN: per-user DB (one Turso DB per end-user, provisioned by child-DO or UserRegistryDO). Selected via storageTopology: "turso-per-user" in the manifest. Required for HIPAA BAA, GDPR data deletion by physical DB drop, or customer-managed encryption. (3) The manifest storageTopology field encodes this choice; the DO bootstrap code branches on it at space creation.

G-AC22 HIGH §db — Turso routing table

No Routing Table Schema for spaceId/userId to Turso Endpoint and Auth-Token Mapping

The Gap

When a Worker or DO needs to connect to a space's Turso DB, it must know the Turso database URL and authentication token for that space. The spec recommends "store endpoint + auth-token in a secrets store" (G-Z03 Required Fix) but does not define: what secrets store (Doppler? Vault? KV? DO SQLite?), what the routing table schema looks like, how the DO retrieves the endpoint for a given spaceId at runtime, or how this lookup is cached to avoid a secrets-store round-trip on every query. Without this, the entire Turso integration is hand-waved.

Required Fix

Define the Turso connection registry: a TursoRegistryDO (one per account) that holds turso_connections(space_id, db_url, auth_token_encrypted, db_name, created_at, last_used_at) in its SQLite. auth_token is encrypted with the per-space DEK. At space creation, the bootstrap flow: (1) calls Turso Management API to create the DB, (2) stores the returned url + auth-token via TursoRegistryDO.register(spaceId, url, encryptedToken). At runtime, DOs call TursoRegistryDO.getConnection(spaceId) → decrypted url + token. Cache the connection object in DO in-memory state (re-fetch only after DO eviction). Never store Turso credentials in KV (eventual consistency) or R2 (no access control).

G-AC23 HIGH §db — Turso migration mechanics

No Zero-Downtime Migration Saga from SpaceDO SQLite to Turso — Data Stranded at Switchover

The Gap

The spec identifies the migration path as "dump via storage.sql.exec → import into libSQL" (G-Z08) but provides no handling for: (a) writes that arrive during migration (the space is live, users are active), (b) ensuring consistency between the in-progress dump and the live SQLite that is still accepting writes, (c) the cutover moment (when does the DO start reading/writing from Turso instead of local SQLite?), (d) rollback if the Turso import fails partway through. This is a live migration of a production database under active load.

Required Fix

Implement a dual-write migration saga: (1) Phase 1 (dual-write): DO writes to both local SQLite and Turso simultaneously (via @libsql/client). Reads still come from local SQLite. (2) Phase 2 (bulk sync): export current SQLite snapshot to Turso via batch INSERT (in 1000-row chunks via CF Workflow steps). (3) Phase 3 (read switchover): after bulk sync completes, flip a feature flag in DO in-memory state to read from Turso. (4) Phase 5 (write switchover): after 24h of successful reads, stop writing to local SQLite. (5) Phase 6 (cleanup): purge local SQLite via storage.deleteAll() after validation. Each phase is a CF Workflow step with compensating rollback.

G-AC24 HIGH §db — Turso cold-start HTTP latency

@libsql/client Cold-Start HTTP Latency Stacks on LLM Latency — No Connection Warm-Up Strategy

The Gap

@libsql/client in CF Workers makes HTTP requests to the Turso edge replica. Every DB query opens a new HTTP connection (CF Workers have no persistent TCP connections between invocations). A cold Worker invocation that needs to query Turso adds: TLS handshake (10-50ms) + HTTP round-trip (5-20ms from CF edge to Turso edge) = 15-70ms overhead before the first query result. In a typical agent turn with 3-5 DB queries (read memory, check credentials, write conversation), this adds 45-350ms of pure HTTP overhead on top of the 2-5 second LLM latency. The spec cites this as G-Z10 but provides no mitigation.

Required Fix

Adopt HTTP/2 keep-alive for @libsql/client: configure the client to use the `fetch` transport with `Connection: keep-alive` and set the CF Worker's `fetch` flag to allow connection reuse across requests (CF Workers in the same isolate reuse HTTP connections via the underlying `fetch` cache). Add a connection warmup in the DO's blockConcurrencyWhile init: run a `SELECT 1` query to establish the Turso connection before the first user request. Cache the @libsql/client instance in the DO in-memory state (do not recreate on every request — only after DO eviction). Target Turso's edge replica in the same CF region using the `sync_url` to a CF-co-located endpoint.

G-AC25 HIGH §db — Turso pricing at per-user scale

Turso Per-User DB Pricing Not Modeled — 1M Users × $0.20/DB/Month Is an Unexpected Cost Cliff

The Gap

The per-user Turso topology (storageTopology: "turso-per-user", G-AC21) provisions one Turso database per end-user within a SaaS product. At $0.20/month per Turso DB on the Turso Scaler plan (the minimum plan supporting unlimited DBs), a SaaS product with 1M users incurs $200,000/month in Turso DB fees alone — before any data storage or query costs. This cost is not reflected in the Naelao builder pricing tiers and would make per-user DB isolation economically impossible for most builders.

Required Fix

Limit per-user DB topology to enterprise-tier products with the data isolation requirement explicitly acknowledged. In the manifest, storageTopology: "turso-per-user" requires an enterprise plan and triggers an explicit cost acknowledgment: "This configuration provisions one dedicated database per end-user. At 1M users, Turso fees are approximately $200,000/month. Your Naelao enterprise plan includes a cost credit of $X toward managed database fees." For standard and pro plans, only per-product DB is available. Alternatively, negotiate a volume discount with Turso for DB counts > 100K: Turso's enterprise pricing moves to flat-rate per-account rather than per-DB.

G-AC26 MEDIUM §db — Turso backup strategy

Turso DB Backup Strategy Not Documented — Unclear Whether Naelao Relies on Turso Built-In or Must Implement Its Own

The Gap

The spec's backup and PITR recommendations (G-AB31, G-Z06) describe WAL streaming for SpaceDO SQLite. Turso has its own built-in replication and backup system (Turso automatically replicates to multiple replicas and provides point-in-time recovery via their platform). However the spec does not document: (a) whether Naelao relies on Turso's managed backup, (b) how Naelao would restore a Turso DB in a disaster scenario, (c) what the Turso-side RPO/RTO is, or (d) how a builder triggers a restore if they accidentally delete data.

Required Fix

Document the Turso backup contract: (1) Naelao relies on Turso's built-in daily snapshots and 7-day PITR (available on Scaler+ plans). (2) Add `POST /builder/products/{productId}/db/restore { targetTimestamp }` that calls Turso Management API's restore endpoint. (3) For critical data (wallet transactions, agent definitions), maintain a separate append-only event log in R2 that can be replayed over a restored DB for gap-filling. (4) Test restore procedure quarterly by spawning a Turso DB clone from a 7-day-old snapshot and running the test suite against it. Document RPO = 1 hour (Turso WAL streaming), RTO = 30 minutes (restore + replay).

G-AC27 HIGH §db — Turso credential security

Turso Auth-Token Storage, Rotation, and Per-DB Scoping Are Not Defined

The Gap

Each Turso database requires an auth-token for access. The spec says "store endpoint + auth-token in a secrets store" but does not define: what secrets store is used, whether each DB gets a unique auth-token or all share one account-level token, what the token rotation cadence is, how rotation is performed without downtime (old token still valid for in-flight requests during rotation), and what happens if a Turso auth-token is leaked (it grants full access to that DB including all tenant data). A leaked shared account-level token gives access to ALL tenant DBs.

Required Fix

Use per-DB auth-tokens: when creating a Turso DB via the Management API, generate a DB-scoped token (not the account-level token) with readonly=false. Store the token encrypted with the space's DEK in TursoRegistryDO. Rotate tokens on a 90-day cadence: (1) generate a new token via Turso API, (2) store new token as pending, (3) deploy a flag so new DO instances use the new token, (4) after 24h, revoke the old token. Implement a token compromise response: POST /admin/security/turso-rotate/{spaceId} that immediately generates a new token and revokes the old one. Log all rotation events to the security audit log.

G-AC28 MEDIUM §db — conversation archival path

Cold Conversation Archival from SpaceDO SQLite to R2 Has No Defined Threshold, Format, or Search Path

The Gap

SpaceDO's SQLite fills with conversation messages over time. The spec references a pattern of archiving cold messages to R2 to extend the effective storage beyond the 10GB SQLite budget. However the spec does not define: (a) at what threshold archival is triggered (80% of 10GB? messages older than 90 days?), (b) what format R2 archives use (JSONL per thread? per month? per space?), (c) how archived messages are made searchable (re-loaded into SQLite on demand? queried via Vectorize?), or (d) how the DO knows which messages are in R2 vs live SQLite when assembling conversation history.

Required Fix

Define the archival contract: (1) Trigger: when SpaceDO SQLite > 7GB (70% of limit), the archival alarm fires. (2) Selection: archive messages older than 90 days (configurable per space plan). (3) Format: write to R2 at `spaces/{spaceId}/archive/messages/{year}/{month}.jsonl.gz` — one JSONL line per message, gzipped. (4) Index: write an archive_index(thread_id, month_key, r2_path, min_created_at, max_created_at, message_count) row to SQLite. On conversation history load, check archive_index for the thread, fetch the relevant monthly file from R2, decompress, and merge with live SQLite rows. (5) Search: Vectorize stores a summary embedding per archived thread for context assembly.

G-AC29 CRITICAL §billing — credit atomicity cross-hop

Credit Read-Check-Deduct Is Not Atomic Across Service Binding Hops — Overdraft Is Possible at Scale

The Gap

The credit enforcement pattern requires: (1) NaelaoAgentDO checks balance, (2) if sufficient, calls naelao-billing via Service Binding to deduct, (3) naelao-billing calls WalletDO.deduct(). Steps 1 and 2 are in separate DOs — not atomic. Two concurrent agent turns for the same space can both pass the balance check (both read balance = 100, both see "enough credits") before either deduction executes. Both turns run and both deduct, resulting in an overdraft. At scale with thousands of concurrent turns per popular product, this overdraft vulnerability is routinely exploitable and represents direct financial loss.

Required Fix

Move the credit check inside WalletDO so it is atomic: WalletDO.checkAndDeduct(amount: number): { success: bool, newBalance: number }. This single DO call atomically checks and deducts within the DO's single-threaded execution — no race possible. NaelaoAgentDO calls WalletDO directly via Service Binding before starting the turn; if { success: false }, reject with 402. Remove the separate balance-check step from NaelaoAgentDO entirely. Add a pre-authorization pattern for long-running turns: WalletDO.reserve(estimatedCost) → reservationId, then WalletDO.settle(reservationId, actualCost) on completion, refunding any over-reservation.

G-AC30 CRITICAL §billing — Analytics Engine event loss

Analytics Engine Write Failure Means Free Tokens — Token Consumption Not Rolled Back on Billing Event Loss

The Gap

Billing events (token usage, tool call costs, credit deductions) are written to CF Analytics Engine for metering and reconciliation. If the Analytics Engine write fails (quota exceeded, transient error, Worker CPU limit hit), the credit deduction from WalletDO has already succeeded but the billing event is lost. The tokens were consumed and the LLM call was made, but the usage is not recorded anywhere permanent. At scale with millions of events, Analytics Engine write failures are not rare edge cases — they are normal traffic patterns that must be handled gracefully.

Required Fix

Decouple billing event persistence from Analytics Engine: write billing events to a CF Queue first (durable, at-least-once delivery) before emitting to Analytics Engine. The Queue consumer writes to Analytics Engine and, on failure, retries with exponential backoff. For authoritative billing records, write the event synchronously to WalletDO's SQLite as a wallet_transactions row (the DO write is durable and atomic). Analytics Engine is then a derived view of wallet_transactions, not the source of truth. Reconcile monthly: query wallet_transactions for the billing period and compare to Analytics Engine aggregates; the delta surfaces lost events.

G-AC31 HIGH §billing — Stripe API rate limits at scale

No Batch Strategy for Stripe API Calls — Rate Limit (100 req/sec) Creates a Bottleneck at Millions of Events

The Gap

Stripe's default API rate limit is 100 requests/second in live mode (higher on negotiated enterprise plans). At millions of simultaneous billing events (token consumption, subscription renewals, metered usage reports), naelao-billing will exceed this limit, resulting in 429 errors from Stripe. The spec handles individual Stripe failures with retry logic, but does not batch subscription events, does not implement Stripe Meters batch reporting, and does not queue Stripe API calls through a rate-limited dispatch worker.

Required Fix

Implement a StripeBatchProcessor CF Workflow: (1) Usage events from WalletDO are written to a "stripe_pending" Queue. (2) The Queue consumer reads up to 100 events per batch, groups them by subscription_id, and calls Stripe Meters.create({ meter_event }) for each group — Stripe Meters batch API accepts multiple events per call. (3) Renewal operations are scheduled via SpaceDO alarms (one alarm per subscription) to spread renewals across the billing period rather than all hitting at midnight on the 1st. (4) Add a StripeRateLimiterDO that tracks the current Stripe call rate and queues calls that would exceed 80 req/sec, releasing them as capacity opens.

G-AC32 HIGH §billing — Analytics → Stripe reconciliation

No Documented Process to Reconcile Analytics Engine Usage Data Against Stripe Invoices

The Gap

The platform uses Analytics Engine to record usage (token consumption, API calls) and Stripe to generate invoices. These two systems can drift: Analytics Engine events may be lost (G-AC30), Stripe webhooks may fail (G-G03), or clock skew between systems may cause events to fall in the wrong billing period. There is no documented monthly reconciliation process to detect and correct these discrepancies. A builder on usage-based billing may be over- or under-charged by up to several percent without either party knowing.

Required Fix

Implement a monthly RevenueReconciliationWorkflow triggered on the 1st of each month: (1) Query Analytics Engine: SELECT sum(tokens_consumed) as ae_total WHERE space_id = X AND period = LAST_MONTH. (2) Query WalletDO SQLite: SELECT sum(amount) FROM wallet_transactions WHERE type = "debit" AND period = LAST_MONTH. (3) Query Stripe: retrieve the closed invoice for the subscription for last month. (4) Compare ae_total vs wallet_total vs stripe_invoice_amount. If delta > 2%, flag for manual review; if delta < 0.1%, auto-approve. Write reconciliation results to billing_reconciliation(space_id, period, ae_total, wallet_total, stripe_total, delta_pct, status) for audit.

G-AC33 HIGH §billing — two-sided ledger

Two-Sided Ledger Has No Trace ID Linking Wholesale and Retail Sides — Reconciliation Is Impossible

The Gap

Naelao operates a two-sided ledger (Appendix Y, G-Y23): wholesale (builder pays Naelao for platform access) and retail (end-user pays builder for product access). When an end-user's API call triggers a token consumption event, it simultaneously touches the retail ledger (end-user's credit balance with the builder's product) and the wholesale ledger (builder's credit balance with Naelao). These two debits must be traceable to the same originating event. The spec does not define a trace ID or correlation structure linking the two ledger entries.

Required Fix

Add a billing_correlation_id (UUID generated at turn start) to every credit deduction. When an agent turn fires: (1) AssistantDO generates billing_correlation_id. (2) Retail debit: WalletDO.checkAndDeduct(endUserBillingPlan.cost, { correlationId }). (3) Wholesale debit: BuilderWalletDO.deduct(wholesaleCost, { correlationId }). Both wallet_transactions rows carry the same correlationId. Analytics Engine event also carries correlationId as blob1. Expose GET /billing/reconcile/{correlationId} returning both ledger entries, the Analytics Engine event, and the originating turn_id — the full money trail from end-user click to Naelao revenue in one query.

G-AC34 HIGH §billing — sub-space billing rollup race

Sub-Space Billing Rollup Cron Loses Usage Accrued Between Snapshot Read and Next Write

The Gap

For products with sub-spaces (team tenancy, SaaS with user sub-spaces), billing is rolled up from child spaces to the parent product by a daily cron. The cron reads each child space's usage since last_rollup_at, sums it, and writes the aggregate to the parent billing ledger. Any usage that accrues in a child space between the moment the cron reads it and when the next cron runs is silently dropped from the current billing period and either attributed to the next period or lost entirely. Over thousands of child spaces, this gap compounds to significant revenue leakage.

Required Fix

Replace cron-based rollup with event-driven billing: each WalletDO.deduct() in a child space publishes a billing_event({ spaceId, parentSpaceId, amount, timestamp, correlationId }) to a CF Queue. The Queue consumer processes events in real time and updates the parent's billing aggregate in BuilderWalletDO. This is event-sourced billing: the parent's ledger is always up to date because events flow to it as they happen. Remove the cron rollup entirely. For analytics (daily/monthly aggregates), derive totals by querying Analytics Engine using the parent_space_id filter rather than relying on a cron-computed rollup.

G-AC35 MEDIUM §billing — builder revenue reconciliation

Builder Revenue Share Monthly Reconciliation Process Is Undefined — Publishers May Never Be Paid

The Gap

The marketplace model (§13) promises builders a revenue share (e.g., 80% of end-user payments flow to the builder's Naelao wallet as publisher_earnings). However the process by which a builder converts their wallet balance to an actual Stripe payout is not specified. How does a builder request a withdrawal? Is there a minimum threshold? What is the payout schedule? How is the Naelao platform fee subtracted? Is there a tax form (1099, VAT invoice) generated? Without this, builders earn credits they cannot monetise, making the marketplace non-viable as an income stream.

Required Fix

Define the builder revenue lifecycle: (1) Revenue accumulates in BuilderWalletDO.publisher_earnings_credits. (2) Monthly on the 15th, a PayoutWorkflow runs for all builders with earnings > $25 (minimum payout threshold). (3) PayoutWorkflow: compute gross_earnings (sum of publisher_earnings events), subtract platform_fee_pct from manifest BillingStrategy, generate a remittance statement PDF, call Stripe Connect to initiate a payout to the builder's connected bank account. (4) Write payout_records(builder_id, period, gross_earnings, platform_fee, net_payout, stripe_transfer_id, status). (5) Send the builder a payout notification email with the remittance PDF attached.

G-AC36 HIGH §billing — concurrent debit queue

Millions of Simultaneous Debit Events Cannot All Be Processed Synchronously in WalletDO

The Gap

At peak load (millions of concurrent agent turns across millions of products), WalletDO instances across the platform each receive thousands of debit() calls per second per hot product. Each WalletDO handles one product, so its debit queue depth equals the number of concurrent agent turns for that product. A viral product with 100K concurrent users each starting a turn simultaneously would queue 100K debit calls at WalletDO, each waiting for the previous to complete. At 5ms per debit, the queue drains in 500 seconds — effectively halting all agent operations for 8 minutes.

Required Fix

Implement a credit reservation queue pattern to pipeline debits without blocking: (1) Before starting an agent turn, issue a WalletDO.reserve(estimatedCost) — this takes 5ms and acquires a reservation token. (2) The agent turn runs concurrently with other reserved turns (credit is pre-committed). (3) On turn completion, issue WalletDO.settle(reservationId, actualCost) — this corrects any over/under-estimate. (4) WalletDO processes settle calls in batch at 100ms intervals (batch_settle), averaging 1ms overhead per settle. Net result: turns are parallel, WalletDO processes reservations in 1 batch per 100ms regardless of concurrency. Add a reservation expiry (30 min) to handle abandoned turns.

G-AC37 HIGH §websocket — no WebSocket gateway layer

No WebSocket Gateway Layer — All Long-Lived Connections Terminate Directly at DOs Without Connection Management

The Gap

Every Naelao product WebSocket connection (streaming agent responses, real-time collaboration, live updates) is accepted directly by a DO via ctx.acceptWebSocket(). DOs must hold the connection alive for the duration of a conversation session, which can span minutes to hours. There is no intermediary WebSocket gateway, connection proxy, or fan-out broker. This means: (a) connection count per DO is unbounded, (b) connection metadata (authentication, rate limits, session state) must be re-verified on every message by the DO, (c) there is no cross-DO connection routing (a user cannot seamlessly switch between agent DOs in a session).

Required Fix

Introduce a WebSocket gateway Worker (naelao-ws-gateway) that handles connection acceptance, authentication, and message routing. The gateway: (1) accepts the WebSocket upgrade, validates the JWT, and establishes the authenticated session. (2) Forwards messages to the appropriate DO based on message type (route conversation messages to ConversationShardDO, tool results to AgentDO, billing events to WalletDO). (3) Handles connection fan-out: one client can subscribe to events from multiple DOs (e.g., watch conversation + watch billing + watch agent status). (4) Implements per-connection rate limiting at the gateway layer before any DO is touched. This decouples connection management from business logic.

G-AC38 MEDIUM §websocket — DO connection capacity unknown

DO WebSocket Connection Capacity Is Undocumented — Platform Has No Known Scale Ceiling for Simultaneous Connections Per Product

The Gap

The CF DO WebSocket hibernation API allows a DO to hold many WebSocket connections while hibernated. However the spec does not document: (a) what the CF-platform-imposed maximum connections per DO instance is, (b) whether connection count affects DO eviction frequency, (c) the memory overhead per connection (in hibernation vs active state), or (d) at what connection count a DO becomes too slow to process messages due to the forEach broadcast loop. A product with 50,000 simultaneous users would have 50,000 WebSocket connections on their SpaceDO — this may be fine or may silently fail.

Required Fix

Instrument WebSocket connection count metrics: in each DO's periodic alarm (every 60 seconds), call this.ctx.getWebSockets().length and emit to Analytics Engine as double1: ws_connection_count. Alert if any single DO exceeds 10,000 connections (an assumed safe threshold). Implement connection sharding for high-connection products: when ws_connection_count > 5,000, spin up a WebSocketShardDO (addressed as `${spaceId}:ws:${shardIndex}`) and redirect new connections to the least-loaded shard. Implement a lightweight connection-count load balancer that returns the target shard address on WebSocket upgrade.

G-AC39 HIGH §websocket — DO hibernation connection drop

DO Hibernation Drops WebSocket Connections Without Graceful Client Handoff or Reconnect Guidance

The Gap

CF DO hibernation (used for idle DOs to reduce costs) terminates all in-memory state but preserves WebSocket connections in a hibernated state — messages trigger wake-up. However if the DO is evicted (not just hibernated) due to memory pressure, all WebSocket connections are forcibly closed. Clients receive a 1001 "Going Away" close frame with no explanation, no reconnect endpoint, and no session token to resume from. The reconnect logic is entirely client-side and must re-authenticate, re-load context, and re-establish streaming state from scratch, creating a jarring user experience.

Required Fix

Implement a graceful reconnect protocol: (1) Before the DO terminates (use the DO beforeunload equivalent or the first message after eviction detection), broadcast a { type: "DO_EVICTING", reconnectAfterMs: 2000, sessionToken: resumeToken } frame. (2) The client WebSocket error handler checks for this frame and schedules a reconnect with the session token after the specified delay. (3) On reconnect, the DO uses the session token to restore conversation context from SpaceDO SQLite (message history, agent state). (4) Add jitter to the reconnectAfterMs (randomize ±1000ms across clients) to prevent reconnect storms (G-AC40).

G-AC40 HIGH §websocket — reconnect storm not implemented

Reconnect Storm Jitter Strategy Is Documented (G-X16) But Not Implemented in DO Hydration Code

The Gap

G-X16 explicitly identified and documented the reconnect storm problem: a DO eviction with 200 connected clients causes 200 simultaneous reconnect attempts, each triggering DO hydration (SQLite reads, KV reads, possibly Vectorize queries) and exceeding the 1000-subrequest-per-Worker limit. The fix — jitter delay of Math.random() * 10000ms per client, capped concurrent DO instantiations to 5 via a KV semaphore — is proposed in the gap's Required Fix section. However no code implementing this fix appears in the spec. The documentation of the gap exists; the remediation does not.

Required Fix

Implement the G-X16 reconnect storm mitigation: (1) Client-side: in the WebSocket onclose handler, replace immediate reconnect with: setTimeout(reconnect, Math.random() * 10000). (2) Server-side: in naelao-router, wrap DO stub acquisition with a ReconnectSemaphoreDO (one per space) that allows at most 5 concurrent DO hydrations (blockConcurrencyWhile pattern). Requests beyond 5 are queued with a 200ms poll. (3) DO hydration order: reconnect requests initialize only the minimum state (schema check, session validation) before accepting WebSocket; full hydration (Vectorize, KV, memory) is deferred until the first user message.

G-AC41 HIGH §websocket — state sync quadratic scaling

WebSocket State Sync Broadcasts Full State Object on Every Change — Quadratic Memory and Bandwidth at Scale

The Gap

The platform uses this.setState() / this.broadcast() (CF Agents SDK) to sync DO state to all connected clients. The spec acknowledges this creates quadratic scaling: state_size × update_frequency × client_count bytes sent per second. In token-streaming mode, the agent emits a state update containing the full accumulated response on every token (potentially 500 updates × 50KB state × 1000 clients = 25GB/second of bandwidth for one busy DO). No delta/patch-only state sync is documented.

Required Fix

Replace full-state broadcasts with delta patches: (1) Assign a monotonic sequence number to each state mutation. (2) In the broadcast, send only { seq, patch: [{ op, path, value }] } (JSON Patch RFC 6902) instead of the full state. Clients apply patches to their local state. (3) For new connections or clients that fall behind (seq gap > 50), send a full-state snapshot. (4) In token-streaming, emit a minimal patch: { op: "append", path: "/currentResponse/text", value: tokenChunk } rather than a full state object. This reduces per-token broadcast payload from ~50KB to ~100 bytes — a 500× reduction at the cost of client-side patch application logic.

G-AC42 HIGH §websocket — geographic WebSocket routing

WebSocket Upgrade Requests Are Not Routed to a Regionally Co-Located DO — Global Users Suffer Additive Latency

The Gap

A WebSocket upgrade request from a Tokyo user reaches the nearest CF edge Worker (Tokyo PoP, ~5ms). The Worker then resolves the SpaceDO stub. If the SpaceDO is pinned to a US data centre (where it was first created), the WebSocket is established over a US-connected DO — meaning every message from the Tokyo user travels: Tokyo client → Tokyo Worker → US DO → Tokyo Worker → Tokyo client. This round-trip adds 200-300ms per message. The WebSocket connection itself is persistent, but every DO-processed event (agent response, tool result) traverses the trans-Pacific link.

Required Fix

At WebSocket upgrade time, the naelao-ws-gateway should select a regionally optimal DO: (1) Check the space's preferredRegion from SpaceMetaDO (set at space creation based on the builder's location hint). (2) If the requesting user's CF-Connecting-IP geolocation (available via request.cf.country) is in a different continent from the DO's pinned region, create a regional session relay: a lightweight SessionRelayDO (hint: locationHint matching user's region) that proxies messages to the canonical SpaceDO. The relay adds ~10ms (same-region relay) vs 200ms (cross-region DO). (3) For reads (conversation history, agent status), serve from the relay's local cache. Writes still go to the canonical DO.

G-AC43 MEDIUM §websocket — CF Smart Placement for DOs

CF Smart Placement Is Not Configured for DOs — DOs Are Pinned at First Access With No Ongoing Optimisation

The Gap

CF Smart Placement is a Cloudflare feature that monitors the geographic origin of incoming requests to a DO and automatically migrates the DO to the region where most traffic originates, minimising round-trip latency. Without Smart Placement, a DO created from a US-based builder remains in the US even if the builder's product gains 90% of its users in Southeast Asia. locationHint (G-N01) helps at creation time but does not adapt to shifting user geography after launch.

Required Fix

Enable CF Smart Placement for all SpaceDOs, AssistantDOs, and ConversationShardDOs in wrangler.toml: [durable_objects.smart_placement] mode = "auto". Document the tradeoff: Smart Placement may move a DO between regions, which could conflict with data residency requirements (G-AA47). For spaces with data residency constraints (jurisdiction: "EU"), pin to a specific region using locationHint and disable Smart Placement via mode = "off". For all other spaces, enable Smart Placement and accept that DO location adapts to user geography over time. Monitor DO region via CF API metrics and alert if a data-residency-constrained DO migrates outside its jurisdiction.

G-AC44 HIGH §cf-limits — sub-agent parallelism ceiling

Sub-Agent Fan-Out Has No Account-Level Parallelism Ceiling — Recursive Spawning Creates Exponential Workflow Instances

The Gap

DynamicOrchestrator (§mini-agi) can spawn up to 16 parallel sub-agents (CF platform limit). Each sub-agent can spawn 16 more, and so on. A 3-level deep orchestration spawns up to 16³ = 4096 concurrent CF Workflow instances for one user request. At thousands of simultaneous user requests, this becomes millions of concurrent Workflow instances. CF Workflows have per-account concurrency limits that are not documented in the spec. A single misbehaving or prompt-injected orchestration request could exhaust the entire account's Workflow concurrency budget.

Required Fix

Implement an OrchestrationBudgetDO (one per space) that tracks active sub-agent spawns using a counter in SQLite. Before spawning a sub-agent, DynamicOrchestrator calls OrchestrationBudgetDO.request(depth, fanout) which checks: (1) total active agents for this space < plan.maxConcurrentAgents (free=2, pro=10, enterprise=50), (2) current depth < plan.maxOrchestrationDepth (free=1, pro=3, enterprise=5), (3) total Workflow instances spawned by this orchestration < 256. If any limit is exceeded, return { allowed: false, reason } and the orchestrator falls back to sequential execution. Release budget slots when sub-agents complete.

G-AC45 HIGH §cf-limits — CF Queue per-account limits

Millions of Products With Dedicated Queues May Hit Undocumented CF Queue Per-Account Ceiling

The Gap

The spec allocates dedicated CF Queues per product for various purposes: the agent task queue, the billing event queue, the DLQ, the notification queue. If each product has 4 dedicated queues, 1M builder products = 4M CF Queues. CF's documentation does not publish a per-account Queue count limit but does note that accounts are resource-bounded. Hitting an undocumented limit would silently prevent new space creation (queue creation fails) or cause existing queues to behave abnormally, with no clear error message.

Required Fix

Replace per-product dedicated Queues with shared namespaced Queues: instead of one Queue per product per function, use a single Queue per function type (naelao-agent-tasks, naelao-billing-events, naelao-notifications, naelao-dlq) with the spaceId encoded in the message body. Consumers filter messages by spaceId. This reduces Queue count from 4×N_products to a fixed 4 Queues regardless of product count. For high-volume spaces that need dedicated throughput, implement a QueueShardDO that multiplexes messages across a pool of pre-provisioned Queues (one pool per region) using consistent hashing on spaceId.

G-AC46 HIGH §ops — conversation archive threshold

SpaceDO Conversation Data Has No Defined Archival Threshold or Cleanup Path — Storage Grows Without Bound

The Gap

SpaceDO SQLite accumulates conversation messages, tool results, agent traces (G-AB11), and LLM call logs (G-AB12) indefinitely. There is no defined storage threshold at which archival is triggered, no archival process implementation (only a conceptual mention), and no way for a builder to manage their storage budget. A product with 10K daily active users each exchanging 20 messages generates 200K rows per day. At 500 bytes per row, that's 100MB per day, and the SpaceDO 10GB limit is exhausted in ~100 days with no warning.

Required Fix

Implement tiered storage lifecycle in SpaceDO: (1) Hot tier (SQLite): messages from the last 30 days. (2) Warm tier (R2 with metadata in SQLite): messages 30-365 days old. (3) Cold tier (R2 Glacier-equivalent via Infrequent Access storage class): messages > 365 days. Trigger archival alarm when SQLite > 7GB. The archival CF Workflow: SELECT and batch-INSERT old messages to R2 JSONL, DELETE from SQLite, update archive_index. Add a storage dashboard widget in the builder portal: "Storage: 4.2GB / 10GB | Next archival in 8 days." Alert builder at 80% and 95% with options to upgrade plan (higher Turso limit) or adjust retention policy.

G-AC47 MEDIUM §ops — custom domain routing

No Custom Domain Routing for Builder Products — Builders Cannot Map myapp.com to Their Naelao Space

The Gap

The spec describes builder products as accessible via Naelao-hosted subdomains (e.g., product.naelao.com) but does not document how a builder maps their own domain (myapp.com) to their Naelao Space. Custom domains require: (a) DNS CNAME configuration guidance, (b) a CF Workers Custom Domain or CF for SaaS integration that routes the custom domain to the correct SpaceDO, (c) automatic TLS certificate provisioning, (d) a verification mechanism to prove domain ownership before the mapping is activated. Without custom domains, builders cannot white-label their products.

Required Fix

Implement CF for SaaS (Cloudflare's platform for custom hostname management): (1) Builder adds a CNAME record: myapp.com → {spaceId}.naelao.com (documented in onboarding). (2) Builder calls POST /builder/products/{productId}/custom-domain { hostname: "myapp.com" }. (3) Naelao calls CF API to create a custom_hostname on the naelao.com zone: CF for SaaS issues a TXT DNS challenge for domain ownership verification. (4) Builder adds the TXT record; Naelao polls CF API until status = "active." (5) naelao-router receives requests with Host: myapp.com, looks up the custom_hostname → spaceId mapping in KV (TTL 60s), and routes to the correct SpaceDO. Emit a CF Cache-Control: private to prevent edge caching of user-specific responses.

G-AC48 HIGH §ops — space creation throughput

Simultaneous Mass Space Creation Floods SpaceDO SQLite Schema Init — No Creation Rate Throttle

The Gap

When a new space is created, the SpaceDO constructor runs blockConcurrencyWhile(async () => initSchema()) which applies 40+ CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS statements to initialize the SQLite schema. This is a cold-start database initialization that takes 50-200ms per space. If a large enterprise signs up and bulk-creates 10,000 spaces via the API (e.g., provisioning one space per employee), 10,000 simultaneous SQLite schema inits fire against the CF account's DO infrastructure simultaneously. CF may throttle or rate-limit this pattern, causing creation failures with no retry logic documented.

Required Fix

Add a space creation rate limiter: POST /spaces is rate-limited to 10 concurrent creations per account per minute. Excess requests are queued via a SpaceCreationQueue (CF Queue). The Queue consumer processes one creation at a time per space namespace. For bulk creation (enterprise onboarding), expose POST /spaces/bulk { count, template } that spawns a CF Workflow that provisions spaces in batches of 10 with 500ms delays between batches. Add a creation_status field to the space record: "provisioning" → "active" → "failed". Expose GET /spaces?status=provisioning for bulk creation monitoring. Add exponential backoff retry logic in the creation Workflow for transient DO init failures.

G-AC49 MEDIUM §ops — cross-platform aggregate analytics

Naelao Has No Cross-Platform Aggregate Analytics — Cannot See Total Users, Revenue, or Churn Across All Spaces

The Gap

The Naelao platform team has no internal analytics dashboard showing: total active users across all builder products, total platform revenue (wholesale), top-growing spaces, churn by product category, infrastructure cost vs revenue by space, or anomalous spaces (unusually high credit consumption, possible abuse). Without this data, the Naelao team cannot make pricing decisions, identify at-risk customers, or detect platform-wide abuse patterns.

Required Fix

Create a PlatformAnalyticsDO (singleton, accessed by a fixed key) that aggregates daily stats across all spaces. Each SpaceDO emits a daily heartbeat event to Analytics Engine: { index1: "platform", blob1: spaceId, blob2: planId, double1: dau, double2: credits_consumed, double3: agent_runs, double4: storage_bytes }. A daily CF Cron reads the last 30 days from Analytics Engine via the SQL API and writes aggregates to PlatformAnalyticsDO SQLite. Expose /admin/analytics/* routes (admin-only) for the Naelao team. Include: top 100 spaces by growth, bottom 20 spaces by retention (churn risk), spaces where infra_cost > revenue (loss leaders), and spaces with anomalous credit consumption spikes.

G-AC50 HIGH §ops — hot SpaceDO fallback

No Circuit Breaker or Fallback for a Hot SpaceDO Under Viral Traffic — Platform Has No Load Shedding

The Gap

If a builder's product goes viral (e.g., featured on Product Hunt, a social media share drives 500K users to a space in one hour), the SpaceDO for that product receives a surge of operations it cannot process fast enough. CF will queue requests to the DO, but the queue is unbounded (no documented queue limit or timeout). Other spaces on the same CF account are unaffected (DOs are isolated), but the viral space's users experience 30+ second response times or 503 errors as the DO queue backs up. The spec has no traffic shaping, load shedding, or graceful degradation plan for this scenario.

Required Fix

Implement a SpaceDO circuit breaker: a HealthMonitorDO per space that tracks the p95 request latency for the SpaceDO over the last 60 seconds. If p95 > 5000ms for 3 consecutive 20-second windows, HealthMonitorDO opens the circuit: (1) New conversation starts return a 503 with Retry-After: 30 and a "high demand" message. (2) In-flight conversations continue (no mid-stream interruption). (3) New connections are queued via a WaitingRoomDO (displays estimated wait time). (4) HealthMonitorDO triggers auto-scaling: notifies the Naelao ops team to request emergency CF account limit increases. (5) Circuit resets when p95 < 2000ms for 2 consecutive windows.

Appendix AD — Twenty-Second Pass

Auth & Sessions · RAG Depth · GDPR Deletion & Crypto Ops · Container & MCP Lifecycle · Tracing/Migration/Idempotency · Voice/Collab/Webhooks/SDK

G-AD01 HIGH §auth — refresh token rotation

No Refresh Token Rotation or Reuse Detection — A Stolen Refresh Token Grants Indefinite Access

The Gap

The spec issues JWTs but does not document a refresh token mechanism with rotation. Without rotation, a refresh token, once issued, is valid until expiry; if stolen (XSS, malware, log leak), the attacker can mint access tokens indefinitely with no detection. There is no reuse-detection: if both the legitimate user and an attacker present the same refresh token, the platform cannot tell that the token was compromised and should be revoked.

Required Fix

Implement rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection. On each token refresh: (1) issue a new access token + a new refresh token, (2) mark the old refresh token as used in a RefreshTokenDO (one per user) keyed by token family ID. (3) If a refresh token that is already marked "used" is presented again, treat it as theft: revoke the entire token family and force re-authentication. Store refresh tokens hashed (SHA-256), never plaintext. Set access token TTL short (15 min) and refresh token TTL longer (30 days) with sliding expiration.

G-AD02 CRITICAL §auth — session revocation consistency

Session Revocation Uses Eventually-Consistent KV — Revoked Tokens Stay Valid for Up to 60 Seconds Across Regions

The Gap

Token revocation (logout, account suspension, role downgrade, security incident) is checked against a KV blocklist. CF KV is eventually consistent with up to 60-second cross-region propagation. After an admin revokes a compromised session or downgrades a malicious user, that user's token continues to work for up to a minute in other regions — a critical window during a security incident. For a platform with millions of sessions, this is an exploitable hole.

Required Fix

Move the revocation check to a strongly-consistent store. Maintain a token version counter per user in the UserRegistryDO (or SpaceDO member record). Embed token_version in the JWT at issuance. On every authenticated request, the auth Worker reads the current token_version from the DO (strongly consistent) and rejects the token if jwt.token_version < current. Incrementing the user's token_version atomically revokes ALL their tokens instantly with no propagation delay. Cache the version in-Worker for 5 seconds to bound DO load; accept a 5-second worst-case revocation window instead of 60.

G-AD03 MEDIUM §auth — multi-device sessions

No Multi-Device Session Registry — Users Cannot See or Revoke Sessions on Other Devices

The Gap

The spec has no concept of a session registry that tracks which devices a user is logged in on. Users cannot view their active sessions ("logged in on iPhone, Chrome on MacBook, unknown device in another country"), cannot revoke a single device without logging out everywhere, and cannot detect unauthorized access. This is table-stakes security UX that every modern platform provides (Google, GitHub, Stripe all show active sessions).

Required Fix

Add user_sessions(session_id, user_id, device_label, ip_geo, user_agent, created_at, last_active_at, refresh_token_family_id) to UserRegistryDO. On login, create a session row with parsed device/geo info. Expose GET /auth/sessions (list active sessions) and DELETE /auth/sessions/{id} (revoke one device by invalidating its refresh token family). Add a "log out all other devices" action that revokes all sessions except the current. Surface "new device login" email notifications with the device/geo details.

G-AD04 HIGH §auth — JWT signing key rotation

JWT Signing Key Has No Rotation Mechanism (JWKS) — A Leaked Signing Key Cannot Be Retired Without Logging Everyone Out

The Gap

The spec signs JWTs with a signing key but does not document key rotation. If the signing key is compromised, the only remediation is to change the key, which instantly invalidates every outstanding JWT across the entire platform — a mass logout of all users. There is no key ID (kid) in the JWT header, no JWKS endpoint exposing multiple valid keys, and no overlap window where old and new keys are both accepted during rotation.

Required Fix

Implement JWKS-style key rotation: (1) Each signing key has a kid (key ID) included in the JWT header. (2) Maintain a set of valid keys (current + previous) in a SigningKeyDO, with the current key used for signing and both accepted for verification. (3) Expose GET /.well-known/jwks.json for public-key verification (if moving to RS256/ES256). (4) Rotate the signing key every 90 days: generate a new key, mark it current, keep the old key valid for the JWT max-TTL window, then retire it. (5) On compromise, rotate immediately and shorten the overlap window. This allows key rotation without mass logout.

G-AD05 HIGH §auth — end-user auth provider abstraction

End-User Authentication Provider Is Not Abstracted Per Product — Each Builder Product Cannot Choose Its Own Auth Method

The Gap

In the multi-tenant model, end-users of a builder's product authenticate to that product, not to Naelao directly. Different builder products need different auth: a consumer SaaS wants Google/Apple social login, an enterprise team product wants SAML/SSO, a simple tool wants email magic links. The spec assumes Naelao-native JWT auth but does not abstract the end-user auth provider so each builder product can configure its own identity source via the manifest.

Required Fix

Add an authProvider block to the product manifest: { type: "naelao" | "oauth" | "saml" | "magic-link" | "byo-jwt", config: {...} }. Implement an AuthProviderAdapter interface with implementations per type. naelao-auth resolves the product's configured provider at login time and delegates: OAuth providers use the standard authorization-code flow; SAML uses a WorkOS/Stytch integration (per G-AA01); byo-jwt validates JWTs signed by the builder's own IdP against a configured JWKS URL. The resulting identity is normalized into a Naelao end-user record. Constrain provider choice by plan (SAML = enterprise only).

G-AD06 HIGH §auth — password reset flow

Password Reset and Account Recovery Flow Is Unspecified — No Secure Token Generation, Expiry, or Single-Use Enforcement

The Gap

The spec mentions password-based auth but does not document the password reset flow. A broken reset flow is a top breach vector: reset tokens that don't expire, are guessable, are reusable, or leak via referrer headers all lead to account takeover. There is no specification for: reset token generation (cryptographic randomness), token expiry (typically 1 hour), single-use enforcement, rate limiting on reset requests, or account-recovery for users who lose access to their email.

Required Fix

Implement a secure password reset flow: (1) POST /auth/forgot-password generates a cryptographically random 32-byte token, stores its SHA-256 hash in a password_resets table with expires_at = now + 1h and used = false. (2) Email a link with the raw token (never store raw). (3) POST /auth/reset-password validates the token hash, checks not-expired and not-used, atomically marks used = true, updates the password (PBKDF2/Argon2), and revokes all existing sessions (G-AD02). (4) Rate-limit forgot-password to 3 requests per email per hour. (5) Use generic responses ("if an account exists, an email was sent") to prevent account enumeration. Document an account-recovery path (support-verified) for lost-email cases.

G-AD07 MEDIUM §auth — auth edge caching

Auth Verification Hits naelao-auth on Every Request — Single Point of Failure and Latency Tax at Scale

The Gap

The router auth middleware calls naelao-auth (or a central auth DO) on every authenticated request to validate the JWT and resolve the user's role/space membership. At millions of requests per second, this makes naelao-auth a hot path and a single point of failure: if naelao-auth degrades, the entire platform becomes unauthenticated. Every request also pays the latency of an extra Worker-to-Worker hop.

Required Fix

Make JWT verification stateless at the edge: the router verifies the JWT signature locally (using the cached public key / JWKS, G-AD04) without calling naelao-auth — signature verification is pure crypto and needs no network call. Embed the user's role and space memberships as signed claims in the JWT (refreshed on each token refresh). Only consult the DO-based revocation check (G-AD02) which is a fast cached read. This removes naelao-auth from the per-request hot path entirely; it is only called at login/refresh time. Falls back gracefully: signature + revocation version are sufficient for authorization decisions.

G-AD08 MEDIUM §auth — session fixation

No Session Fixation Protection — Session Identifier Is Not Regenerated After Privilege Change

The Gap

When a user authenticates or elevates privilege (e.g., logs into an admin role, completes MFA), the spec does not regenerate the session identifier. Session fixation attacks work by setting a victim's session ID before they authenticate, then using that same (now-authenticated) session ID. Without session regeneration on privilege boundaries, a fixed session ID set pre-auth remains valid post-auth.

Required Fix

Regenerate the session/token on every privilege boundary: (1) On successful login, issue a fresh token with a new session_id — never reuse a pre-auth session. (2) On MFA completion (step-up auth), issue a new token with an elevated claim and a new session_id. (3) On role change, force token refresh. Invalidate the prior session_id immediately. For WebSocket sessions, require re-authentication with the new token after any privilege change rather than carrying the old connection forward.

G-AD09 HIGH §rag — hybrid search

RAG Uses Pure Vector Search With No Keyword (BM25) Hybrid — Exact-Term and Acronym Queries Fail

The Gap

The knowledge retrieval pipeline uses only Vectorize semantic (vector) search. Pure vector search is weak at exact-term matching: product SKUs, error codes, acronyms, proper nouns, and rare technical terms often have poor embedding representations and get out-ranked by semantically-similar-but-wrong chunks. A user asking about "error E4017" may get chunks about general errors rather than the exact one. There is no keyword/BM25 component blended with vector results.

Required Fix

Implement hybrid retrieval: (1) Run vector search via Vectorize (semantic recall) AND a keyword search in parallel. For keyword search, maintain an FTS5 (SQLite full-text search) virtual table in the SpaceDO/Turso DB over chunk text, or use a lightweight BM25 scorer. (2) Merge the two result sets using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF): score = Σ 1/(k + rank_i) across both rankings. (3) Return the top-N fused results to the reranker (G-AD10). Hybrid search reliably surfaces both semantically-relevant and exact-term-matching chunks. Make the vector/keyword weight configurable per space.

G-AD10 MEDIUM §rag — cross-encoder reranking

No Cross-Encoder Reranking Stage — Top-K Vector Results Are Used Raw Without Relevance Re-Scoring

The Gap

After retrieval, the top-K chunks from Vectorize are injected into the LLM context in vector-similarity order. Bi-encoder vector similarity is a coarse relevance signal; the most relevant chunk is frequently not ranked first. Without a reranking stage, the LLM receives chunks in suboptimal order, and context-window budget is wasted on lower-relevance chunks that crowd out the best ones. This directly degrades answer quality, especially for large knowledge bases.

Required Fix

Add a cross-encoder reranking stage between retrieval and context assembly: (1) Retrieve a larger candidate set (top-30) via hybrid search. (2) Score each candidate against the query using a cross-encoder reranker — either Cohere Rerank API, a Workers AI reranking model (@cf/baai/bge-reranker-base), or an LLM-as-reranker for small candidate sets. (3) Select the top-8 reranked chunks for the context window. Log retrieval_set and reranked_set to the trace (G-AB11) for debugging "why was this chunk retrieved." Make the candidate-set size and final-K configurable per space plan.

G-AD11 HIGH §rag — batch embedding fan-out

Document Embedding Is Generated Sequentially — Ingesting a Large Document Set Is O(N) Slow and Blocks

The Gap

The ingestion pipeline embeds chunks in a sequential loop (chunk → embed → upsert, one at a time). Ingesting a large knowledge base (a 500-page PDF = ~2000 chunks, or a 10,000-document corpus) takes thousands of sequential embedding API calls. At ~100ms per embedding call, 2000 chunks = 200 seconds of blocking ingestion, which exceeds Worker CPU/wall-clock limits and gives builders a multi-minute "indexing" wait with no progress indication.

Required Fix

Parallelize embedding generation: (1) Use the embedding API's batch endpoint (Workers AI and OpenAI both accept arrays of inputs per call) — embed 100 chunks per API call instead of 1. (2) Run ingestion as a CF Workflow: each step embeds and upserts one batch of 100 chunks, so a 2000-chunk document is 20 parallel-friendly steps with checkpointing. (3) Emit ingestion progress events (chunks_embedded / total) to the builder dashboard. (4) Use a Queue to decouple upload from indexing so the upload returns immediately and indexing happens asynchronously with a status field (pending → indexing → ready).

G-AD12 MEDIUM §rag — embedding cost tracking

No Per-Space Embedding Cost Tracking or Quota — Knowledge Base Ingestion Is an Unmetered Cost Sink

The Gap

Every document ingested generates embeddings (a paid API call or Workers AI compute). The spec tracks LLM token consumption for chat but does not track or bill embedding generation cost. A builder who bulk-uploads a 100,000-document corpus incurs significant embedding cost that Naelao absorbs silently. There is no per-space embedding quota, no cost attribution, and no limit preventing a single space from running up enormous ingestion bills.

Required Fix

Track embedding generation as a billable event: on each batch embedding call, record embedding_events(space_id, chunk_count, tokens_embedded, cost_credits, created_at). Debit the space's wallet for embedding cost (or count against an included ingestion quota per plan). Add per-plan ingestion limits: free = 1000 chunks/month, pro = 100K, enterprise = unlimited (metered). Surface "knowledge base size: X chunks, Y embeddings this month" in the builder dashboard. Block ingestion with a clear 402 when the quota is exhausted, offering an upgrade path.

G-AD13 MEDIUM §rag — semantic chunking

Fixed-Size Chunking Splits Mid-Sentence and Mid-Structure — Degrades Retrieval Quality on Structured Documents

The Gap

The chunker splits documents into fixed-size windows (e.g., 512 tokens) regardless of document structure. This splits sentences, paragraphs, table rows, and code blocks arbitrarily across chunk boundaries, so a single coherent idea is fragmented and neither fragment embeds well. Structured documents (Markdown with headings, tables, code, legal documents with numbered clauses) suffer badly: a chunk may contain the end of one section and the start of another, embedding to a meaningless midpoint.

Required Fix

Implement structure-aware (semantic) chunking: (1) Parse document structure first — split on Markdown headings, paragraph boundaries, list items, table rows, and code-block boundaries before applying size limits. (2) Keep semantic units intact: never split a sentence; prefer splitting at paragraph then sentence boundaries. (3) Add configurable chunk overlap (e.g., 64 tokens / 12.5%) so context spanning a boundary appears in both adjacent chunks. (4) Attach structural metadata to each chunk (heading path, section number) for citation. (5) For code, chunk by function/class boundaries using a lightweight AST or brace-matching, not token count.

G-AD14 CRITICAL §privacy — multi-store erasure saga

GDPR Erasure Has No Atomic Multi-Store Saga With Retry and Verification — Deletion Partially Fails Silently

The Gap

A GDPR right-to-erasure (Article 17) request must delete user data from every store: SpaceDO/Turso SQLite, R2 (files, screenshots, archives), Vectorize (embeddings), KV (caches), Analytics Engine (events), and any backup. The spec mentions an erasure flow but it lacks transactionality: if the Vectorize deleteByIds succeeds but the R2 archive deletion fails, the request is marked complete while personal data persists in R2. There is no retry, no per-store verification, and no erasure certificate proving completion.

Required Fix

Implement an ErasureSaga as a CF Workflow with a step per store, each idempotent and retried: (1) SpaceDO/Turso: DELETE user rows. (2) R2: list and delete all objects under the user's prefix + archived JSONL lines mentioning the user. (3) Vectorize: deleteByIds for all vectors with the user's metadata. (4) KV: delete cached entries by key prefix. (5) Analytics Engine: crypto-shred (delete the user's HMAC key so events become unattributable) since per-row deletion is unsupported. (6) Backups: enqueue backup-purge (G-AD15). After all steps, run a VERIFICATION pass that queries each store for residual data and fails the saga if any is found. Issue a signed erasure certificate with per-store confirmation timestamps.

G-AD15 CRITICAL §privacy — backup deletion

Deleted Data Persists in Backups Indefinitely — Restoring a Backup Resurrects "Erased" Personal Data

The Gap

The backup/PITR strategy (G-AB31, WAL streaming to R2) captures all data including data that is later erased. The erasure flow deletes from live stores but never touches backups. A backup from before an erasure request still contains the user's personal data, and restoring it (after a disaster, or maliciously) resurrects "deleted" data — a GDPR violation. The spec has no backup retention policy coordinated with erasure and no mechanism to purge erased records from existing backups.

Required Fix

Coordinate backups with erasure: (1) Set a bounded backup retention window (e.g., 35 days). Erasure requests are guaranteed complete across all backups within retention + 1 day, documented in the privacy policy. (2) Encrypt every backup with the per-space DEK (G-AD17); on erasure of an entire space, crypto-shred by deleting the DEK, rendering all backups of that space unrecoverable instantly. (3) For per-user erasure within a live space, maintain an erasure_tombstones log; on any backup RESTORE, replay tombstones to re-erase the affected records before the restored data is brought online. (4) For Turso PITR, call the Turso Management API to purge snapshots older than the erasure (G-AD16).

G-AD16 HIGH §privacy — Turso PITR deletion

Turso Point-in-Time-Recovery Snapshots Are Not Purged on Erasure — Personal Data Recoverable From Turso Backups

The Gap

When a space migrates to Turso (G-AC21), Turso maintains its own automatic PITR snapshots (typically 7-30 days). The Naelao erasure flow deletes rows from the live Turso DB but has no coordination with Turso's backup layer. A user's erased data remains recoverable from Turso's PITR snapshots for the full retention window with no Naelao-side control or visibility.

Required Fix

Document and enforce the Turso backup-deletion contract: (1) For full-space deletion, call the Turso Management API to delete the database entirely, which removes all its snapshots. (2) For per-user erasure within a shared Turso DB, accept the PITR window as the maximum erasure-completion SLA and document it in the privacy policy (e.g., "erasure completes within 30 days including all backups"). (3) Where stricter erasure is required (enterprise/HIPAA), use the per-user Turso DB topology so each user's data is a separate database that can be dropped (with its snapshots) on erasure. Record the Turso DB deletion confirmation in the erasure certificate.

G-AD17 HIGH §security — DEK rotation

Per-Space Data Encryption Keys Have No Rotation Policy or Re-Encryption Workflow

The Gap

The spec proposes per-space DEKs derived from a master key (G-W11) but provides no operational key-rotation policy: no rotation cadence, no procedure to re-encrypt existing ciphertext under a new DEK without downtime, no detection of DEK compromise, and no revocation path. Encryption keys that never rotate violate SOC 2 / PCI requirements and mean a single leaked DEK exposes all of a space's historical encrypted data forever.

Required Fix

Implement DEK versioning and rotation: (1) Store a key_version with every ciphertext (prepended to the encrypted blob). (2) Maintain multiple DEK versions per space; encrypt new data with the current version, decrypt old data with its stored version. (3) Run a lazy re-encryption process: on read, if a record uses an old DEK version, re-encrypt it under the current version (re-encrypt-on-access), plus a background Workflow that sweeps and re-encrypts cold data. (4) Rotate DEKs every 365 days or immediately on suspected compromise. (5) On compromise, rotate the DEK and force re-encryption of all of that space's data, isolating blast radius to the one affected space (not the platform).

G-AD18 HIGH §security — master key rotation

Master Key Rotation Has No Ceremony or Versioning — A Compromised Master Key Cannot Be Retired Without Re-Encrypting Everything

The Gap

All per-space DEKs are derived from a single NAELAO_MASTER_KEY via HKDF. The master key has no version, so rotating it (after compromise or per policy) would invalidate every derived DEK simultaneously, requiring re-encryption of all encrypted data across all spaces in one operation — operationally impossible at scale. A leaked master key cannot be compartmentalized: it exposes every space's DEK and therefore all encrypted data platform-wide.

Required Fix

Move to envelope encryption with master-key versioning: (1) Each space's DEK is randomly generated (not derived) and stored wrapped (encrypted) by the master key. (2) The wrapped DEK records which master-key version wrapped it. (3) Maintain master-key versions in a KMS (CF Secrets Store, AWS KMS, or Vault). (4) Rotate the master key by re-wrapping each space's DEK under the new master version (a cheap operation — only the small DEKs are re-wrapped, not the bulk data). This decouples master rotation from data re-encryption. On master compromise, re-wrap all DEKs under a fresh master; bulk ciphertext is untouched because the DEKs themselves did not change.

G-AD19 HIGH §security — credential access audit log

No Audit Log of Credential/Secret Decryption — SOC 2 and GDPR Art. 32 Cannot Be Satisfied

The Gap

When an agent, workflow, or human operator decrypts a stored credential (BYOK API key, OAuth token, MCP secret), this access is not logged. A compliance auditor cannot answer "who accessed which secret and when," which is a hard requirement for SOC 2 (CC6) and GDPR Article 32. Without this log, a credential breach cannot be scoped (which secrets were accessed by the compromised component?).

Required Fix

Add an append-only credential access audit log: every decrypt operation writes credential_access_log(id, space_id, credential_id, accessor_type, accessor_id, purpose, trace_id, accessed_at) to a dedicated store. The log is append-only (no UPDATE/DELETE) and hash-chained (each entry includes the hash of the previous entry) so tampering is detectable (G-AD20). Stream the log to an immutable sink (R2 with object-lock, or an external SIEM). Expose admin queries: "all accesses to credential X," "all credentials accessed by component Y in the last 24h." Alert on anomalous access patterns (a component reading credentials it never read before).

G-AD20 MEDIUM §security — audit log immutability

Audit Logs Are Stored in Mutable Tables — No Tamper-Evidence or Append-Only Guarantee

The Gap

Security and billing audit logs are written to ordinary SQLite tables that support UPDATE and DELETE. An attacker who compromises a DO (or a malicious insider) can rewrite or delete audit history to cover their tracks. Compliance frameworks require audit logs to be tamper-evident and append-only; mutable audit tables fail this requirement and undermine the trustworthiness of every other security control.

Required Fix

Make audit logs tamper-evident: (1) Hash-chain entries: each row includes prev_hash = SHA-256(previous row's canonical serialization), forming a verifiable chain where altering any historical entry breaks all subsequent hashes. (2) Periodically (hourly) write the latest chain head hash to an external append-only store (R2 with Object Lock / WORM, or a transparency-log service) so even a fully-compromised DO cannot rewrite history undetectably. (3) Provide a verifyAuditChain(spaceId) function that recomputes the chain and reports the first broken link. (4) Never expose UPDATE/DELETE on audit tables in any code path.

G-AD21 MEDIUM §privacy — soft vs hard delete

Soft-Delete vs Hard-Delete Lifecycle Is Undefined — Unclear When Data Is Recoverable vs Permanently Gone

The Gap

The spec uses "delete" ambiguously. It is unclear whether deleting a space, user, or document marks it deleted_at (soft, recoverable) or physically removes it (hard). This matters for: accidental-deletion recovery (users expect an undo window), GDPR erasure (which requires actual removal), and storage reclamation. Without a defined lifecycle, some data may be soft-deleted forever (never reclaimed, GDPR-violating) while other data is hard-deleted instantly (no undo, support nightmares).

Required Fix

Define a uniform deletion lifecycle: (1) DELETE → soft-delete (set deleted_at, hide from all queries via a default WHERE deleted_at IS NULL) with a 30-day recovery window. (2) During the window, expose POST /{resource}/{id}/restore. (3) After 30 days, a cleanup Workflow hard-deletes and triggers the cascade (G-AD14) across all stores. (4) GDPR erasure requests bypass the soft-delete window and trigger immediate hard-delete + cascade (legal obligation overrides convenience). (5) Document the lifecycle clearly so users and auditors know exactly when data becomes unrecoverable. Distinguish "user-initiated delete" (soft, recoverable) from "erasure request" (hard, immediate).

G-AD22 HIGH §containers — image build pipeline

Container Image Build, Versioning, and Publish Pipeline Is Unspecified

The Gap

The container marketplace lists images and the runtime binds to them, but there is no specification for how container images are built, tested, versioned, and published. How does a community developer submit an image? What build environment compiles it? How is it tagged and versioned? How are updates rolled out to spaces using the image? Without a build pipeline, the container ecosystem cannot grow safely or reproducibly.

Required Fix

Define a container image pipeline: (1) Submit: developer pushes a Dockerfile + manifest to a build endpoint. (2) Build: a sandboxed build runner (CF Containers or an external builder) builds the image reproducibly, runs the developer's declared tests, and rejects on failure. (3) Scan: run a vulnerability scan (G-AD23) and reject images with critical CVEs. (4) Version: tag images with semver + an immutable content digest; store in the Cloudflare Container Registry. (5) Publish: after review, list the image with its version. (6) Rollout: spaces pin to a version range; new versions are opt-in or canary-rolled (per G-AB10/G-AB50 patterns). Record build provenance (SLSA attestation) for supply-chain security.

G-AD23 HIGH §containers — image vulnerability scanning

Container Images Are Not Vulnerability-Scanned Before Listing — Supply-Chain Risk in the Marketplace

The Gap

Container images submitted to the marketplace (or built by builders) are not scanned for known vulnerabilities (CVEs) in OS packages, language dependencies, or embedded secrets. A malicious or simply outdated image with a critical CVE (e.g., a vulnerable openssl, an exposed crypto miner, a leaked AWS key baked into a layer) can be listed and run inside the platform, endangering every space that uses it.

Required Fix

Add a mandatory image-scanning gate in the build pipeline (G-AD22): (1) Scan every image with Trivy / Grype (open-source) or Snyk Container for OS + dependency CVEs. (2) Run a secret scanner (gitleaks/trufflehog) across all layers to detect baked-in credentials. (3) Block listing if any CRITICAL/HIGH CVE or any secret is found; surface the findings to the submitter. (4) Re-scan listed images weekly against updated CVE databases; auto-flag and notify maintainers when a previously-clean image develops a new critical CVE. (5) Display a security badge (last scanned, CVE count) on each marketplace listing.

G-AD24 CRITICAL §containers — FUSE-R2 write consistency

FUSE-R2 Filesystem Has No Concurrent-Write Conflict Resolution — Two Containers Writing the Same File Corrupt It

The Gap

The sandbox workspace is an R2 bucket mounted as a filesystem via FUSE. R2 is an eventually-consistent object store with last-write-wins semantics and no file locking. If two containers (or two fibers in a multi-container task) write the same file, or one reads while another writes, the result is silent corruption or lost updates. The spec describes the FUSE-R2 sync path but does not address concurrent access, write ordering, or conflict resolution.

Required Fix

Add a coordination layer for FUSE-R2 writes: (1) Route all writes for a given workspace path through a per-workspace WorkspaceLockDO that grants advisory locks (path → holder, TTL). A container acquires the lock before writing and releases on completion. (2) Use R2 conditional writes (If-Match on ETag) to detect lost updates: if the ETag changed since read, the write fails and the caller re-reads and retries (optimistic concurrency). (3) On container crash mid-write (G-AD25), the lock TTL expires and a recovery checks R2 object integrity. (4) Document that the workspace is single-writer per path; concurrent multi-container tasks must partition their file namespaces.

G-AD25 HIGH §containers — crash mid-write rollback

Container Crash Mid-FUSE-Write Leaves Partial/Corrupt R2 Objects With No Rollback

The Gap

When a container crashes (OOM, timeout, eviction) while a FUSE write is in flight, the R2 object may be left partially written or in an inconsistent state. There is no transaction boundary, no write-ahead intent log, and no recovery process to detect and roll back partial writes. The next container to read that file gets corrupt data with no error.

Required Fix

Implement write durability for FUSE-R2: (1) Write to a temp object (path.tmp.{writeId}) first, then atomically "commit" by copying to the final path via R2 server-side copy (atomic) and deleting the temp.
