A crash before commit leaves only an orphaned temp, never a corrupt final object. (2) Maintain a write-intent log in the WorkspaceLockDO: { path, writeId, started_at }. On container restart/recovery, scan for incomplete intents and either complete (if temp is valid) or roll back (delete temp). (3) Run a periodic sweeper to GC orphaned temp objects older than 1 hour. (4) Checksum objects (store CRC in R2 metadata) and verify on read to detect any residual corruption.

G-AD26 HIGH §containers — egress allow-list

Container Outbound Network Egress Has No Allow-List — Sandboxed Code Can Exfiltrate Data or Attack Internal Services

The Gap

Containers run agent-generated or builder-provided code and can make arbitrary outbound network requests. The spec blocks RFC-1918 (internal) ranges in places but does not implement a configurable egress allow-list. Sandboxed code can POST a space's data to an attacker-controlled domain, reach cloud metadata endpoints, or scan/attack arbitrary internet hosts from Naelao's infrastructure (reputational and legal risk). This is the SSRF/exfiltration vector at the container layer.

Required Fix

Implement egress control for containers: (1) Default-deny outbound network; require an explicit egressAllowlist in the manifest (list of allowed domains/CIDRs). (2) Route all container egress through a forward proxy (a Naelao-controlled Worker or Squid-style proxy) that enforces the allow-list, blocks RFC-1918 + link-local (169.254.0.0/16) + cloud metadata IPs, and logs all egress for audit. (3) For agents that need general web access, route through the existing browser/fetch tool (which has its own SSRF guards, G-AB35) rather than raw container egress. (4) Rate-limit and bandwidth-cap egress per space to bound exfiltration and cost. (5) Alert on egress to newly-seen domains.

G-AD27 MEDIUM §containers — container network isolation

Containers in a Shared Pool Have No Network Isolation From Each Other

The Gap

Multi-container tasks (AssistantSandboxDO container pools) run multiple containers that may share a network namespace or be reachable from one another. Without network isolation between containers belonging to different spaces (or different tasks), a compromised container could scan and attack sibling containers, accessing their in-flight data or interfering with their execution. The spec does not specify per-container network namespacing.

Required Fix

Enforce per-task network isolation: (1) Each container (or each task's container group) runs in its own network namespace with no route to other tasks' containers. (2) Containers belonging to different spaces are never co-resident on a shared network. (3) Inter-container communication within a single task (if needed) goes through an explicit, authenticated channel (a task-scoped bridge), not flat L2 reachability. (4) Apply default-deny iptables/network-policy rules; only the egress proxy (G-AD26) and the FUSE-R2 mount are reachable. (5) Verify isolation with an integration test that attempts cross-container connection and asserts it is refused.

G-AD28 HIGH §mcp — MCP OAuth callback

Remote MCP Server OAuth Flow Has No Callback Handler or Token-Exchange Implementation

The Gap

Connecting to a remote MCP server that requires OAuth (most SaaS MCP integrations: GitHub, Google, Slack MCP servers) requires an OAuth authorization-code flow: redirect the user to the provider, receive a callback with an auth code, exchange it for tokens, and store them. The spec mentions an OAuth redirect but does not implement the callback handler, the code-for-token exchange, the state parameter (CSRF protection), or token storage/refresh for MCP connections.

Required Fix

Implement the full MCP OAuth flow: (1) GET /mcp/{server}/connect generates a state token (stored in KV with the space/user context, 10-min TTL) and redirects to the provider's authorize URL. (2) GET /mcp/oauth/callback validates state (CSRF), exchanges the code for access + refresh tokens via the provider's token endpoint, encrypts them with the space DEK, and stores them in the MCP credential store. (3) On MCP tool calls, use the access token; on 401, refresh using the refresh token and retry. (4) Track token_expires_at and proactively refresh before expiry. (5) Expose a "disconnect" action that revokes the token at the provider and deletes it locally.

G-AD29 MEDIUM §mcp — MCP connection pooling

MCP Hub Opens a Fresh Connection Per Tool Call With No Pooling or Keepalive — High Latency and Connection Churn

The Gap

The naelao-mcp-hub connects to remote MCP servers per tool call without connection pooling or HTTP keepalive. Each tool invocation pays a fresh TLS handshake + connection setup (50-150ms) on top of the actual tool latency. At scale, this creates connection churn against MCP servers (which may rate-limit or refuse excessive new connections) and adds latency to every agent turn that uses MCP tools.

Required Fix

Add connection pooling and keepalive to the MCP hub: (1) Maintain a pool of warm HTTP/2 connections per (mcpServer, space) keyed in the hub DO's in-memory state, reused across tool calls within the connection's lifetime. (2) Use HTTP keepalive (Connection: keep-alive) so the underlying CF fetch reuses connections within the isolate. (3) For stateful MCP sessions (SSE transport, G-AD31), maintain the session across multiple tool calls rather than re-initializing. (4) Implement a circuit breaker per MCP server (G-AD30) so a dead server is not hammered with new connection attempts. (5) Pre-warm connections to frequently-used MCP servers on agent session start.

G-AD30 HIGH §mcp — MCP health and failover

No MCP Server Health Checks, Circuit Breaker, or Failover — A Down MCP Server Hangs Every Agent Turn That Uses It

The Gap

When a remote MCP server is slow or down, the spec's only protection is a 30-second timeout. Every agent turn that tries to use a tool from that server waits the full timeout before failing, burning the user's time and the space's credits, and potentially blocking the agent loop. There is no health checking, no circuit breaker to fast-fail when a server is known-down, and no failover to an alternative server or graceful degradation.

Required Fix

Add MCP server resilience: (1) Health checks: periodically ping each connected MCP server (lightweight tools/list call); track health in the hub. (2) Circuit breaker per server: after N consecutive failures, open the circuit and fast-fail tool calls (return a tool error immediately) without waiting for the timeout; periodically half-open to test recovery. (3) When a server's circuit is open, inform the LLM via the tool result ("the X integration is temporarily unavailable") so it can adapt rather than hang. (4) For critical tools, support a fallback server in the manifest. (5) Surface MCP server health in the builder dashboard so builders see which integrations are degraded.

G-AD31 MEDIUM §mcp — MCP transports

MCP Hub Supports Only HTTP Proxy — No stdio or SSE Transport, and Tool Results Cannot Stream Past the 30s Worker Limit

The Gap

The MCP specification defines multiple transports: stdio (local subprocess), SSE (server-sent events for streaming), and Streamable HTTP. The naelao-mcp-hub implements only synchronous HTTP request/response. This means: (a) MCP servers that use SSE for streaming results are unsupported, (b) long-running MCP tools that exceed the 30-second Worker limit cannot return results, and (c) stdio-based MCP servers (which need a process host) cannot run at all.

Required Fix

Extend the MCP hub with multi-transport support: (1) Streamable HTTP + SSE: for streaming MCP servers, hold the SSE connection in a DO (which can outlive a Worker request) and stream chunks to the agent via the existing WebSocket. (2) Long-running tools: use the async pattern — the hub returns a pending handle, the DO polls or holds the SSE stream, and delivers the result via a follow-up message when ready (decoupling from the 30s Worker limit). (3) stdio MCP servers: run them inside a CF Container (sandbox) with the hub speaking stdio to the subprocess over the container bridge. (4) Declare the transport per MCP server in its registry entry so the hub selects the right adapter.

G-AD32 CRITICAL §ops — DO migration runner

No Live-Fleet Schema Migration Runner — Millions of Hibernating DOs Wake With Stale Schemas

The Gap

DO SQLite schemas are initialized with CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS at DO startup. When a schema change ships (new column, new table, new index), already-existing DOs do not get it: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is a no-op on an existing table, so ALTER TABLE changes never apply. A hibernating DO that wakes weeks after a deploy runs on an old schema, and queries referencing new columns crash. There is no versioned migration runner that applies pending migrations to each DO as it wakes.

Required Fix

Implement a versioned migration runner per DO: (1) Track schema version with PRAGMA user_version. (2) Define migrations as an ordered array: [{ version: 1, up: sql }, { version: 2, up: sql }, ...]. (3) In the DO constructor, inside blockConcurrencyWhile, read the current user_version and apply all migrations with version > current in order, then set user_version to the latest. This runs lazily as each DO wakes — no need to touch all DOs at once. (4) Migrations must be forward-only and idempotent. (5) Log migration application to Analytics Engine (do_id, from_version, to_version) so the fleet's migration progress is observable. (6) Test the hibernate→deploy→wake path explicitly (per G-W34).

G-AD33 HIGH §ops — migration rollback

DO Migrations Have No Failure Handling or Rollback — A Bad Migration Bricks Every DO That Applies It

The Gap

If a migration in the runner (G-AD32) throws partway (bad SQL, constraint violation on existing data), the DO is left in an inconsistent state — some statements applied, user_version not advanced — and every subsequent wake re-attempts and re-fails, permanently bricking that DO and locking out its space. There is no per-migration transaction, no rollback, and no quarantine for DOs that fail to migrate.

Required Fix

Make migrations safe to fail: (1) Wrap each migration in a transaction so a failure rolls back that migration's partial changes (note DO SQLite transaction limitations — use savepoints or careful single-statement migrations). (2) On migration failure, do NOT advance user_version; instead set a degraded flag in DO state, log the failure with full error detail, and return a maintenance response for that space rather than crash-looping. (3) Alert the ops team with the do_id and failing migration. (4) Provide an admin tool to inspect and manually remediate a quarantined DO. (5) Test every migration against a snapshot of real production data shapes in CI before deploy, catching constraint violations pre-ship.

G-AD34 HIGH §api — idempotency-key standard

Public API POST Endpoints Have No Idempotency-Key Standard — Network Retries Create Duplicate Resources and Charges

The Gap

Internal flows (Stripe webhooks, notifications) have ad-hoc idempotency, but the public builder-facing API has no idempotency-key standard. When a client's POST (create space, create agent, purchase credits, start a run) times out and is retried — a routine occurrence on mobile/flaky networks — the operation may execute twice, creating duplicate resources or double-charging. Every serious API (Stripe, GitHub) supports an Idempotency-Key header; Naelao's does not.

Required Fix

Adopt a platform-wide Idempotency-Key standard: (1) Every non-GET public API endpoint accepts an Idempotency-Key header (client-generated UUID). (2) An idempotency middleware stores key → { response, status, created_at } in KV/DO with a 24h TTL. (3) On a repeat key: if the original is still processing, return 409 (retry later); if complete, return the stored response verbatim (same status, same body) without re-executing. (4) Scope keys per (api_key, endpoint) to prevent cross-tenant collisions. (5) Document the header in the API reference and bake it into the generated SDK (G-AD49) so retries are idempotent by default.

G-AD35 MEDIUM §ops — structured logging standard

No Structured Logging Standard — Logs Are Free-Form and Cannot Be Correlated or Queried Across Workers

The Gap

Each of the 22 Workers logs in its own ad-hoc format. There is no shared structured-logging schema, no mandated correlation ID field, and no consistent field ordering. This makes cross-Worker debugging nearly impossible: an operator investigating an incident cannot grep a single request's journey across naelao-router → naelao-auth → naelao-agents → DOs → billing because the logs share no common key. The positional Analytics Engine schema also silently corrupts when fields are added in the wrong order.

Required Fix

Define and enforce a structured logging standard: (1) A shared logger utility emitting JSON with mandatory fields: { ts, level, worker, trace_id, space_id, user_id, event, ...payload }. (2) trace_id is the W3C trace ID (G-AD36), present on every log line, enabling single-request reconstruction. (3) A registry maps Analytics Engine positional blob/double slots to named fields, versioned, so additions never shift existing slots. (4) A Tail Worker ingests all logs, indexes by trace_id, and ships to a log aggregator (Axiom/Baselime). (5) Lint in CI: reject console.log calls that bypass the structured logger.

G-AD36 HIGH §ops — trace context wiring

W3C Trace Context Is Designed But Not Wired Through All Workers, Queues, and DO Hops

The Gap

A trace-context design exists (traceparent propagation) but is not actually wired into the request path: Service Binding calls, Queue message payloads, DO stub calls, and the WebSocket path do not propagate or generate trace IDs. The result is that the documented capability does not exist in practice — each Worker's logs remain isolated islands, and a single agent turn spanning 7+ hops cannot be reconstructed causally. This blocks all production debugging at scale.

Required Fix

Wire trace context end-to-end: (1) naelao-router generates a trace_id (and root span) at ingress; if an inbound traceparent header exists, continue it. (2) Propagate trace_id on every hop: as a header on Service Binding fetch calls, as a field in every Queue message body, as an argument/header on DO stub calls, and in the WebSocket session context. (3) Each hop creates a child span (parent = caller's span). (4) Emit spans to a tracing backend (the Tail Worker → Axiom/Honeycomb/Baselime). (5) Include trace_id in every structured log line (G-AD35) and every Analytics Engine event so logs, traces, and metrics all correlate by the same ID. (6) Expose the trace in the builder debug trace viewer (G-AB11).

G-AD37 HIGH §api — API versioning lifecycle

API Versioning Has a /v1/ Prefix But No Lifecycle, Deprecation Policy, or Breaking-Change Detection

The Gap

Endpoints carry a /v1/ prefix but there is no actual versioning strategy: no defined criteria for what constitutes a breaking change, no path to introduce /v2/ without breaking all callers, no Deprecation/Sunset HTTP headers, no migration window, and no CI check that detects accidental breaking changes to the public API. As the platform evolves, breaking changes will be shipped silently and break builder integrations without warning.

Required Fix

Establish an API versioning lifecycle: (1) Define breaking vs non-breaking change rules (removing/renaming a field or changing its type/semantics is breaking; adding optional fields is not). (2) Maintain an OpenAPI 3.1 spec as the source of truth; run an API diff tool (oasdiff) in CI that fails the build on an undeclared breaking change to /v1. (3) Introduce new behavior additively within /v1; reserve /v2 for genuine breaking redesigns, supported in parallel with /v1 for a documented window (e.g., 12 months). (4) Emit Deprecation and Sunset headers on endpoints scheduled for removal, and notify affected builders by email based on observed usage. (5) Generate the SDK (G-AD49) from the OpenAPI spec so clients track versions.

G-AD38 CRITICAL §webhooks — outbound delivery

No Outbound Webhook Delivery System — Agent Results Cannot Reliably Reach Builder Backend Systems

The Gap

Naelao documents inbound webhooks (external events triggering agents) but has no outbound webhook system to deliver agent results back to a builder's own infrastructure. This is the critical integration point for real products: a real-estate agent that generates a listing must POST it to the builder's CRM; a support agent must push resolved tickets to the builder's helpdesk. Without reliable outbound delivery (retries, signing, ordering, dead-lettering), builders must poll or write fragile glue code, and results are silently lost on failure.

Required Fix

Build an outbound webhook delivery system: (1) Builders register endpoints per product/event-type: { url, secret, events: ["run.completed", ...] }. (2) On a triggering event, enqueue a delivery to a CF Queue (durable, at-least-once). (3) The delivery consumer POSTs the payload with an HMAC-SHA256 signature header (signed with the builder's secret) and a unique delivery ID for idempotency. (4) Retry with exponential backoff + jitter (e.g., 6 attempts over 24h). (5) After max retries, move to a DLQ and alert the builder; expose failed deliveries for manual replay. (6) Guarantee per-resource ordering where required via a per-key serialized queue. (7) Provide a delivery log (status, attempts, response codes) in the builder dashboard.

G-AD39 MEDIUM §webhooks — endpoint verification

Outbound Webhook Endpoints Are Not Verified — Misconfigured or Malicious URLs Receive Data or Enable SSRF

The Gap

When a builder registers a webhook endpoint, the spec does not verify that the builder controls the URL and that it is a legitimate external endpoint. An unverified endpoint can be a typo (data silently lost), an SSRF target (an internal Naelao URL or cloud metadata endpoint), or someone else's server (data leak). Webhook registration without verification is both a reliability and a security hole.

Required Fix

Verify webhook endpoints before activation: (1) On registration, send a verification challenge: POST a random challenge token to the URL; the endpoint must echo it back (or expose it at a well-known path) within a timeout. (2) Validate the URL: must be HTTPS, must resolve to a public IP (reject RFC-1918, link-local, cloud metadata ranges — SSRF guard), and must not be a Naelao-internal domain. (3) Only after successful verification is the endpoint marked active for delivery. (4) Periodically re-verify; auto-disable endpoints that fail health checks for an extended period and notify the builder. (5) Sign all deliveries (G-AD38) so the receiver can verify authenticity.

G-AD40 HIGH §voice — concurrency at scale

Voice Pipeline Has No Concurrency Model or Call Admission — Simultaneous Calls Are Unbounded and Unbudgeted

The Gap

The voice feature handles a call but the spec does not define how concurrent voice calls scale. There is no per-space concurrent-call limit, no admission control when capacity is exhausted, no audio-stream backpressure handling, and no cost model for many simultaneous calls (each consuming STT + LLM + TTS continuously). A product that gets 1000 simultaneous callers has undefined behavior: calls may all degrade, the third-party voice provider quota may be exhausted, or costs may spike uncontrollably.

Required Fix

Define a voice concurrency model: (1) Per-plan concurrent-call limits (free = 1, pro = 25, enterprise = configurable), enforced by a VoiceAdmissionDO per space. (2) When at capacity, new callers get a graceful "all agents busy" message or a callback-queue option, not a hard failure. (3) Each call reserves credits up front (estimated duration × per-minute cost) and settles on completion (per G-AC36 reservation pattern). (4) Apply audio backpressure: if STT/LLM/TTS can't keep up, buffer with a bounded queue and signal the caller rather than dropping audio. (5) Track concurrent-call metrics and provider quota headroom; alert before the provider limit is hit.

G-AD41 MEDIUM §voice — barge-in turn-taking

Voice Turn-Taking Uses a Hardcoded End-of-Turn Threshold With No Barge-In / Interruption Handling

The Gap

The voice pipeline detects end-of-turn with a fixed silence threshold and does not handle barge-in: when a user starts speaking while the agent's TTS is still playing, the agent should stop talking and listen. Without barge-in, the agent talks over the user, the user must wait for long agent responses to finish before speaking, and overlapping speech corrupts the STT input. The hardcoded threshold also fails across languages and speaking styles (fast vs. deliberate speakers).

Required Fix

Implement natural turn-taking: (1) Barge-in: continuously run VAD (voice activity detection) during TTS playback; when user speech is detected, immediately stop/duck TTS and switch to listening, discarding the interrupted agent utterance from context or marking it interrupted. (2) Adaptive end-of-turn: adjust the silence threshold based on detected language, recent turn patterns, and whether the utterance seems syntactically complete (use endpointing models rather than a fixed timeout). (3) Handle overlapping speech by prioritizing the user. (4) Make endpointing parameters configurable per space and per language. Consider a voice-orchestration platform (Vapi/LiveKit/Pipecat, per G-AA20) which provides barge-in out of the box.

G-AD42 HIGH §bootstrap — space provisioning state machine

Space Creation Marks Spaces "Ready" Before Provisioning Completes — Users Hit a Half-Built Space

The Gap

Space creation involves multiple async steps: DO creation, SQLite schema init, Vectorize index creation, default-data seeding, billing setup, and (for Turso topology) external DB provisioning. The spec marks a space "ready" without a state machine ensuring all steps completed. A user (or the builder) can access a space whose knowledge index doesn't exist yet or whose schema is half-applied, causing confusing errors during the most important first-run moment.

Required Fix

Implement a space provisioning state machine driven by a CF Workflow: states { provisioning → seeding → ready | failed }. (1) Space creation returns immediately with status: "provisioning" and a poll endpoint. (2) The provisioning Workflow runs each step idempotently (DO init, index creation, Turso DB provisioning, default-data seed, billing setup), advancing status only after each confirms. (3) The space is queryable for status but blocks normal operations until ready. (4) On any step failure, set status: "failed" with a reason, run compensating cleanup (delete partial resources), and surface a retry. (5) Expose GET /spaces/{id}/status returning the current step and progress for a first-run loading experience.

G-AD43 MEDIUM §bootstrap — default data seeding

No Default Data Seeding or First-Run Experience — New Spaces Are Empty With No Guidance

The Gap

When a space is created from a Space Type/template, the spec does not seed default content: example agents, sample knowledge, starter workflows, or an onboarding checklist. The builder lands in an empty space with no examples to learn from and no clear next step. Empty-state onboarding is a major driver of activation; an empty space with no guidance leads to abandonment.

Required Fix

Add a seeding phase to provisioning (G-AD42): (1) Each Space Type/template declares seed_data: example agents, starter knowledge documents, sample workflows, and a getting-started checklist. (2) The seeding step populates these into the new space (agents created, knowledge ingested + indexed, workflows installed). (3) Seeded items are clearly labeled "example" and easily deletable. (4) Provide an onboarding checklist resource (GET /spaces/{id}/onboarding) tracking first-run milestones (created first agent, sent first message, connected a channel) that the UI renders as a progress guide. (5) Make seeding optional via a manifest flag for builders who want a blank space.

G-AD44 HIGH §notifications — write-before-deliver

Notification Idempotency Key Is Written After Delivery — A Crash Mid-Send Causes Duplicate or Lost Notifications

The Gap

The notification system writes its idempotency/dedup key after attempting delivery. If the worker crashes between sending and recording the key, a retry re-sends (duplicate notification) — or, with a different ordering, the key is recorded but delivery never happened (lost notification). For critical notifications (billing alerts, approval timeouts, security alerts), both failure modes are damaging.

Required Fix

Switch to write-before-deliver with status tracking: (1) Before any channel attempt, atomically write notification_log(idempotency_key, status="processing", created_at). If the key already exists, skip (dedup). (2) Attempt delivery. (3) On success, update status="delivered"; on failure, status="failed" with the error, and schedule a retry. (4) A recovery sweeper finds rows stuck in "processing" past a timeout (crashed mid-send) and retries them with the same idempotency key, so the downstream channel dedups if the original actually went out. (5) Give the idempotency key a TTL aligned to the notification's relevance window (not infinite — per the G-G21 fix) so legitimate periodic notifications aren't permanently blocked.

G-AD45 MEDIUM §notifications — channel circuit breaker

No Per-Channel Circuit Breaker or Escalation Chain — A Failing Channel Silently Drops Critical Notifications

The Gap

The notification dispatcher attempts each configured channel (push, email, Slack, SMS) but has no per-channel circuit breaker: if FCM is persistently failing, every notification still tries (and waits on) FCM, wasting time and quota. Critically, there is no escalation chain: if a high-priority notification (billing failure, approval needed, security alert) fails on its primary channel, it is not escalated to a backup channel, so the user simply never finds out.

Required Fix

Add channel resilience and escalation: (1) Per-channel circuit breaker (a ChannelHealthDO tracking failure rates); when open, fast-fail that channel and skip to the next. (2) Define per-notification-priority escalation chains: e.g., critical → [push, then email if push fails, then SMS if email fails, then in-app dashboard pin]. (3) For critical notifications, require delivery confirmation; if none within a timeout, escalate to the next channel in the chain. (4) Track read receipts where the channel supports it; re-escalate unread critical notifications. (5) Surface channel health in the builder dashboard so misconfigured integrations (expired APNs key, revoked Slack token) are visible.

G-AD46 MEDIUM §memory — decay job not implemented

Memory Decay Fields Exist in the Schema But No Job Ever Applies Decay — Stale Facts Accumulate Equal Priority

The Gap

The agent memory schema defines decay_rate and last_used columns intended to down-weight stale facts over time, but no scheduled job or query ever applies the decay. As a result, a fact learned six months ago and never used again has the same relevance score as a fact confirmed yesterday. Over a long-lived agent, stale and possibly-outdated facts crowd the memory injection, degrading response quality and wasting context budget.

Required Fix

Implement memory decay: (1) A scheduled DO alarm (hourly or daily) recomputes effective relevance: effective_score = base_relevance × (decay_rate ^ days_since_last_used). (2) Memory retrieval ranks by effective_score so recently-used facts surface first. (3) When a fact is referenced/confirmed, bump last_used and optionally reinforce base_relevance (spaced-repetition style). (4) Garbage-collect facts whose effective_score falls below a floor and that have zero references for > 90 days, with a tombstone for auditability. (5) Cap total facts per agent; when over cap, evict the lowest effective_score facts. Consider a managed memory layer (mem0/Zep, per G-AA22) which implements decay and consolidation.

G-AD47 MEDIUM §collaboration — presence persistence

Real-Time Presence Is Held in an In-Memory Map and Is Lost on DO Hibernation

The Gap

Collaborative presence ("who is here," cursor positions, active editors) is stored in an in-memory Map inside the DO. When the DO hibernates or is evicted, this Map is wiped, so presence silently breaks: connected users disappear from the "who's online" list even though their WebSocket may still be alive, and presence does not recover on DO wake. This makes the collaboration feature unreliable precisely when it matters (multiple users working together).

Required Fix

Persist presence durably: (1) Store presence in a SQLite table presence(connection_id, user_id, cursor, last_heartbeat) rather than an in-memory Map, so it survives hibernation. (2) Clients send a heartbeat every ~15s updating last_heartbeat. (3) On DO wake, rebuild the presence view from the table (filtering out stale entries past the heartbeat TTL). (4) On WebSocket close, remove the presence row and broadcast a leave event. (5) A periodic alarm prunes stale presence rows (heartbeat older than 45s) and broadcasts the corrected roster. (6) Re-broadcast the full presence roster on DO wake so reconnecting clients resync. For rich collaboration, layer a CRDT (Yjs/Liveblocks, per G-AA21) over this presence substrate.

G-AD48 HIGH §sdk — public client SDK

No Public Client SDK or OpenAPI Spec — Builders Must Reverse-Engineer the REST API With No Typed Contract

The Gap

Builders embedding Naelao into their own applications (web, mobile, backend) have no official client SDK and no published OpenAPI specification. They must reverse-engineer endpoints, hand-roll auth and retry logic, manually parse streaming responses, and re-implement webhook signature verification. This dramatically raises integration cost and is a major adoption barrier for a platform whose entire premise is enabling builders to ship products fast.

Required Fix

Ship a public SDK and API contract: (1) Maintain an OpenAPI 3.1 spec as the source of truth for all public endpoints (also the basis for versioning, G-AD37). (2) Generate typed client SDKs for TypeScript/JS, Python, and Go from the OpenAPI spec, covering auth (token refresh built-in), CRUD operations, streaming responses (SSE/WebSocket helpers), idempotency keys (G-AD34), and webhook signature verification. (3) Publish a browser/React SDK with hooks (useAgentChat, useAgent, useVoiceAgent) for embedding the assistant UI. (4) Version SDKs in lockstep with the API. (5) Provide a sandbox/test mode and example apps. Auto-publish SDK updates from CI when the OpenAPI spec changes.

G-AD49 HIGH §ops — cross-store referential integrity

No Cross-Store Referential Integrity Reconciliation — SQLite, R2, and Vectorize Drift Out of Sync Over Time

The Gap

A single logical entity (a knowledge document) spans three stores: a SQLite metadata row, R2 object(s) for content, and Vectorize vectors for embeddings. There is no foreign-key relationship across stores and no reconciliation job. Over time, partial failures cause drift: SQLite rows pointing to deleted R2 objects, R2 objects with no SQLite row (orphans consuming storage/cost), Vectorize vectors for documents that no longer exist (returning ghost results), and documents missing their vectors (silently absent from RAG). At scale this drift is continuous and invisible.

Required Fix

Run a periodic cross-store reconciliation Workflow per space (e.g., weekly): (1) For each SQLite document row, verify the R2 object exists and the expected Vectorize vectors exist; flag/repair mismatches (re-embed missing vectors, mark broken rows). (2) List R2 objects and Vectorize vectors and find any with no backing SQLite row (orphans); delete them after a grace period. (3) Emit a drift report (counts of orphans, missing vectors, broken refs) to the ops dashboard. (4) Make each write path transactional-ish via an outbox pattern: record intended cross-store mutations in an outbox table, process them with retries, so partial failures self-heal rather than accumulate. (5) Alert when drift exceeds a threshold, indicating a systemic write-path bug.

G-AD50 HIGH §ops — graceful capability degradation

No Graceful Degradation Map — A Single Dependency Outage (Vectorize/Analytics/Stripe) Fails Entire Agent Turns

The Gap

The platform depends on many subsystems (Vectorize for RAG, Analytics Engine for metering, Stripe for billing, MCP servers for tools, the embedding API, the LLM gateway). The spec has fallback for the LLM gateway (model fallback chain) but no systematic degradation map for the others. When Vectorize is down, does the agent fail the whole turn or proceed without RAG? When Analytics Engine is down, are turns blocked or do they proceed with deferred billing? Without a defined degradation policy, any single dependency outage causes total turn failures instead of degraded-but-functional service.

Required Fix

Define a per-dependency degradation policy: (1) Vectorize down → proceed without RAG, inform the agent context "knowledge base temporarily unavailable," do not fail the turn. (2) Analytics Engine down → proceed (billing is durable via WalletDO + Queue, per G-AC30); defer the analytics write. (3) Embedding API down → queue ingestion for later; serve chat from existing index. (4) MCP server down → fast-fail that tool with a circuit breaker (G-AD30), let the agent adapt. (5) Stripe down → allow service to continue on existing balance; queue billing operations. (6) Encode each policy as { dependency, onFailure: "fail" | "degrade" | "defer", userMessage }. Surface current degradation state on the status page (G-AA43) and the builder dashboard so degraded mode is visible, not silent.

Appendix AE — Twenty-Third Pass

Frontend & Widget · Channel Integrations · Orchestration Internals · Marketplace Discovery · Multi-Region & Deployment · System Completeness

G-AE01 CRITICAL §frontend — builder dashboard

Builder Dashboard Has No Architecture — Framework, State Management, and Real-Time Updates Are Undefined

The Gap

The spec references dashboard.naelao.app extensively (builders configure agents, branding, billing, team) but never specifies how the dashboard is actually built: the framework, the state-management approach, how it reflects real-time backend changes (agent run status, credit balance, deployment progress), or how it talks to the 22 Workers. Without this, the entire builder-facing surface — the product's primary interface — is undefined and unbuildable.

Required Fix

Define the dashboard architecture: a Next.js 14 (App Router) application deployed on Cloudflare Pages. Use a typed data layer from the generated client SDK (G-AD48). State: React Query (TanStack Query) for server state with optimistic updates; Zustand for local UI state. Real-time: a single multiplexed WebSocket to naelao-ws-gateway (G-AC37) feeding live updates (run status, credits, deploy progress) into the query cache. Auth: short-lived access token in memory + refresh flow (G-AD01). Document the route map, the component hierarchy, and the data-fetching pattern (server components for initial load, client hooks for live data).

G-AE02 CRITICAL §frontend — no-code config UI

The No-Code Configuration UI Is Not Specified — Builders Have No Visual Way to Toggle Capabilities

The Gap

The platform's core premise is that builders configure products by selecting features, not writing code. Yet the spec defines the manifest schema and the constraint engine (Appendix Y/AC) but never specifies the UI that renders those choices: how capability toggles, parameter inputs (e.g., assistants-per-user slider), and tenancy selection are presented; how the constraint engine's conflicts are surfaced live as the builder toggles; or how the form is generated from the manifest schema. The no-code promise has no no-code UI.

Required Fix

Build a schema-driven configuration UI: (1) Render the config form automatically from the Space Type manifest Zod schema + field metadata (minRole G-AC02, suitableFor, help text) — a JSON-schema-to-form generator. (2) On every toggle, call validateManifest (G-AC10) live and surface constraint violations inline ("Enabling per-seat billing requires team tenancy"). (3) Disable/grey options that conflictsWith current selections. (4) Show a live preview of the resulting product. (5) Gate fields by the viewer's role. This keeps the UI automatically in sync with the manifest schema — new capabilities appear in the UI with no UI code change.

G-AE03 HIGH §frontend — embeddable widget

Embeddable Space-Assistant Widget Has No Embed Spec — Script Tag, iframe, CSP, and Isolation Undefined

The Gap

A core distribution channel is embedding the assistant into a builder's own website. The spec mentions an "embeddable widget" but provides no embed mechanism: no script-tag snippet, no iframe sandbox model, no Content-Security-Policy guidance for host sites, no isolation of the widget's storage/cookies from the host page, and no load-performance strategy. End-user products cannot integrate the assistant.

Required Fix

Specify the widget embed: (1) A lightweight loader script (<script src="https://cdn.naelao.com/widget.js" data-product-id="...">) that injects a sandboxed iframe (sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin allow-forms") pointing at the product portal. (2) The iframe isolates the widget's storage, cookies, and JS from the host page (no host DOM access). (3) Communication via postMessage with strict origin checks (G-AE04). (4) Publish CSP guidance for host sites (frame-src, connect-src). (5) The loader is <15KB, lazy-loads the full widget on open, and exposes a JS API (window.Naelao.open(), .identify(user), .setContext()).

G-AE04 MEDIUM §frontend — widget postMessage protocol

Widget ↔ Host postMessage Protocol Is Unspecified — Cross-Origin Identity and Event Bridging Have No Contract

The Gap

An embedded widget must communicate with its host page: pass the host's authenticated user identity into the widget (so the assistant knows who the user is), receive context (current page, cart contents), and emit events back (conversation started, goal completed, handoff requested). The spec defines no postMessage protocol, no origin-verification model, and no identity-passing mechanism, so host integration is impossible and any naive implementation is an XSS/identity-spoofing hole.

Required Fix

Define a versioned postMessage protocol: (1) Host → widget: { type: "naelao:identify", payload: { userJwt } } where userJwt is a short-lived token signed by the builder's backend (verified by Naelao against the builder's configured JWKS, G-AD05) — never trust raw user IDs from the page. (2) Host → widget: "naelao:context" for page/cart context. (3) Widget → host: "naelao:event" (conversation_started, goal_completed, handoff). (4) Both sides verify event.origin against an allowlist configured per product. (5) Document the protocol and ship helpers in the client SDK.

G-AE05 HIGH §frontend — client streaming

Client-Side Streaming Has No Reconnect, Mid-Stream Token Refresh, or Backpressure Handling

The Gap

The server supports WebSocket hibernation and a token replay buffer, but the spec never defines the client side of streaming: how the browser reconnects after a drop and resumes from the last received token (without duplicating or losing content), how an access token that expires mid-stream is refreshed without tearing down the connection, and how a slow client handles backpressure. Without this, streamed agent responses are unreliable in real network conditions.

Required Fix

Specify the client streaming contract: (1) Each streamed token carries a monotonic seq; the client tracks lastSeq and on reconnect sends resumeFrom: lastSeq so the server replays only the gap from its buffer (pairs with G-AC39/G-AC41). (2) Mid-stream token refresh: when the access token nears expiry, the client refreshes (G-AD01) and sends the new token over the existing WebSocket via a "reauth" frame — no reconnect. (3) Backpressure: the client acks batches; if it falls behind, the server coalesces deltas. (4) Render incrementally with a bounded buffer. Ship all of this in the client SDK so builders get reliable streaming for free.

G-AE06 HIGH §frontend — white-label theming

White-Label Theming Has No Design-Token System — Builders Cannot Apply Custom Branding to Their Product

The Gap

The spec mentions white-label portals and "set brand color / upload logo" but defines no theming system: no design-token schema, no mechanism to inject a builder's theme into the product portal and widget, no storage/retrieval of brand assets, and no preview. A white-label product cannot actually look like the builder's brand — it remains Naelao-branded.

Required Fix

Implement a design-token theming system: (1) A theme manifest per product: { logoUrl, faviconUrl, colors: { primary, surface, text, ... }, font, radius, customCss? }. (2) Store brand assets in R2/CF Images; store tokens in the product config. (3) The portal/widget loads the theme at runtime and applies it via CSS custom properties (--color-primary, etc.) — no rebuild needed. (4) A constrained customCss escape hatch (sanitized, scoped) for advanced builders. (5) Live theme preview in the dashboard. (6) Enforce contrast/accessibility checks (WCAG, per G-AA45) on chosen colors. (7) "Remove Naelao branding" is a plan-gated entitlement.

G-AE07 MEDIUM §frontend — build & deploy pipeline

Frontend Build/Deploy Pipeline Is Undefined — No CF Pages Config, Env Injection, or Preview Deploys

The Gap

The spec names "Next.js on CF Pages" but specifies no frontend build/deploy pipeline: no build configuration, no per-environment variable injection (API base URL, product ID, feature flags), no preview deployments for PRs, no asset versioning/cache-busting, and no rollback. The frontend deployment story is undefined, making the UI unshippable and unmaintainable.

Required Fix

Define the frontend pipeline: (1) CF Pages projects per app (dashboard, product-portal, marketplace, admin) built via the monorepo (Turborepo) so shared packages are versioned together. (2) Environment config injected at build via CF Pages environment variables (staging vs production), with public runtime config served from a /config endpoint for values that must vary per product/tenant. (3) Preview deployments on every PR (CF Pages preview URLs) for review. (4) Immutable hashed asset filenames + long cache TTL for cache-busting. (5) Instant rollback via CF Pages deployment history. (6) Source maps uploaded to Sentry (G-AA10) on each deploy.

G-AE08 MEDIUM §frontend — client error handling

No Client-Side Error Boundaries, Retry Strategy, or Frontend Error Reporting

The Gap

The spec defines server-side resilience but nothing client-side: no React error boundaries (a single component crash white-screens the app), no client retry policy with backoff for failed API calls, no offline/degraded UI states, and no frontend error reporting so the team learns about client crashes. Production users will hit blank screens with no telemetry reaching the team.

Required Fix

Add a client resilience layer: (1) Error boundaries at the route and major-section level with graceful fallback UIs and a "reload" action. (2) A shared API client (in the SDK) with retry + exponential backoff + jitter (G-AD50) for idempotent calls, surfacing user-friendly errors for the rest. (3) Explicit UI states for loading / empty / error / offline. (4) Frontend error + performance monitoring via Sentry browser SDK (capturing stack traces with uploaded source maps, breadcrumbs, and the trace_id so client errors link to backend traces, G-AD36). (5) A global toast/notification system for transient failures.

G-AE09 MEDIUM §frontend — mobile & PWA

No Responsive/Mobile Strategy or PWA Offline Support for End-User Products

The Gap

A large share of end-users access products on mobile, but the spec defers mobile ("React Native unchanged") and specifies no responsive design system, no PWA installability, and no offline support. Products built on Naelao would be desktop-web only, and any network blip loses in-progress messages with no client-side queue.

Required Fix

Define the mobile/PWA strategy: (1) The product portal and widget are mobile-first responsive (the UI kit ships responsive components and touch targets meeting accessibility guidance). (2) Ship a PWA manifest + service worker for installability and basic offline: cache the app shell, queue outbound messages in IndexedDB when offline, and flush via Background Sync on reconnect (idempotent via client message IDs, G-AD34). (3) Show clear offline/reconnecting indicators. (4) For native apps, provide a thin React Native wrapper around the client SDK + a WebView for the product portal, sharing the same streaming/auth logic.

G-AE10 MEDIUM §frontend — optimistic state sync

No Client/Server State Sync Model — Optimistic Updates and DO State Reconciliation Are Undefined

The Gap

The dashboard and product UI display state that lives in DOs (agent config, conversation, credits). The spec does not define how the client reconciles its local view with authoritative DO state: whether updates are optimistic (instant UI, reconcile on server confirm) or pessimistic (wait for round-trip), how conflicts are resolved when the server rejects an optimistic change, and how the delta-patch broadcasts (G-AC41) are applied client-side.

Required Fix

Define the state-sync model: (1) Mutations are optimistic — apply locally immediately, mark "pending," and reconcile against the server response; on rejection, roll back the optimistic change and surface the error. (2) Live state arrives as JSON-Patch deltas (G-AC41) over the WebSocket, applied to the query cache keyed by a version/seq so out-of-order or duplicate patches are handled. (3) On reconnect, request a full snapshot if the seq gap is too large. (4) Implement this once in the client SDK (a useNaelaoResource hook) so every builder UI gets consistent optimistic + live behavior.

G-AE11 HIGH §channels — formatting layer

No Channel Formatting Layer — Rich Output Cannot Render as Slack Blocks, Discord Embeds, or WhatsApp Templates

The Gap

Agents produce rich output (headings, lists, buttons, cards, images) but each channel renders differently: Slack uses Block Kit, Discord uses embeds, WhatsApp uses approved HSM templates with interactive buttons, web chat uses Markdown/HTML. The spec sends plain text to channels with no formatting-translation layer, so output is either lowest-common-denominator plain text or broken per-channel markup.

Required Fix

Add a channel formatting layer: (1) Agents emit output in a canonical rich format (a small block model: text, list, button, card, image, quick_replies). (2) Per-channel renderers translate the canonical blocks to the channel's native format (Block Kit, Discord embeds, WhatsApp template params, Markdown for web). (3) Unsupported elements degrade gracefully (buttons → numbered text options on SMS). (4) For WhatsApp, map to pre-approved templates and validate parameter counts before send. (5) Renderers are part of the channel-adapter package so a new channel implements one renderer interface.

G-AE12 HIGH §channels — cross-channel identity

No Cross-Channel Identity Resolution — The Same Person on Slack, Email, and Web Is Treated as Three Strangers

The Gap

A single end-user may reach a product via multiple channels (Slack, then email, then the web widget). The spec keys sessions by channel-native IDs with no identity-resolution layer, so the same human is treated as separate users with separate memory and conversation history. The agent cannot recognize "this is the same person who emailed yesterday," fragmenting context and breaking continuity.

Required Fix

Add an identity-resolution layer: (1) A canonical end-user record per product with linked channel identities: identities(user_id, channel, external_id, verified). (2) Auto-link when a strong signal matches (same verified email across channels, an explicit login, or a magic-link confirmation). (3) Never auto-merge on weak signals (display name) — require verification to avoid cross-account leakage. (4) Conversation history and memory are keyed by the canonical user_id, so context follows the person across channels. (5) Expose a merge/unmerge admin action and an audit trail of identity links.

G-AE13 HIGH §channels — per-channel rate limits

Channel-Specific API Rate Limits Are Not Modeled — Outbound Sends Hit Slack/Discord/WhatsApp Limits and Get Dropped

The Gap

Each messaging platform enforces its own API limits (Slack ~1 msg/sec per channel + tier limits, Discord per-route buckets, WhatsApp daily HSM caps and per-number throughput, SMS carrier throughput). The spec dispatches channel replies with no awareness of these limits, so at volume the platform gets 429s, messages are dropped or delayed, and the integration's API access can be throttled or revoked.

Required Fix

Implement per-channel rate-limit-aware dispatch: (1) A ChannelDispatchDO per (product, channel) enforcing the channel's known limits with a token bucket. (2) Respect 429 Retry-After and platform rate-limit headers (Discord X-RateLimit-*), backing off per route/bucket. (3) Queue and pace outbound messages rather than dropping; surface queue depth. (4) For WhatsApp, track daily HSM quota and warn before exhaustion. (5) Per-recipient throttling to avoid spamming a single user. (6) Encode each channel's limits in the channel-adapter so they are enforced uniformly.

G-AE14 MEDIUM §channels — token lifecycle

Channel Bot Tokens Have No Refresh, Rotation, or Revocation Handling — Integrations Silently Die

The Gap

Channel integrations store bot/OAuth tokens (Slack, Discord, Telegram, WhatsApp). The spec stores them but does not handle their lifecycle: tokens that expire or are rotated by the platform are not refreshed, and when a workspace admin revokes the integration, the agent keeps trying to use a dead token, producing silent failures with no builder notification.

Required Fix

Manage channel token lifecycle: (1) Store token_expires_at and refresh_token where the platform supports refresh (Slack token rotation, etc.); proactively refresh before expiry. (2) On a 401/invalid_auth from a channel, mark the integration degraded, stop retrying, and notify the builder to reconnect. (3) Detect revocation events (Slack app_uninstalled, etc.) via the channel's event APIs and immediately disable the integration. (4) Surface integration health (connected / expiring / revoked) in the dashboard. (5) Encrypt tokens with the space DEK and rotate per the credential policy (G-AD17).

G-AE15 MEDIUM §channels — message ordering

No Per-Conversation Message Ordering Guarantee Across Channel Delivery

The Gap

Inbound and outbound channel messages flow through queues and async handlers with no ordering guarantee per conversation. Two rapid user messages can be processed out of order, or two agent replies can arrive reversed, producing confusing conversations ("answer before question"). The spec acknowledges interleaving for internal threads but not for channel delivery.

Required Fix

Guarantee per-conversation ordering: (1) Route all messages for a given conversation through a single ordered processor (the conversation's DO, which is single-threaded) so inbound handling and outbound dispatch are serialized per conversation. (2) Assign a per-conversation monotonic sequence to outbound messages; the channel dispatcher sends in sequence and does not send message N+1 until N is accepted (or after a bounded timeout, with reordering protection). (3) For channels without native ordering, include a visible/threaded reference. (4) Drop or merge duplicate inbound deliveries (channels deliver at-least-once) using channel message IDs.

G-AE16 MEDIUM §channels — media normalization

Inbound/Outbound Media and Attachments Are Not Normalized Across Channels

The Gap

Users send images, audio, documents, and video through channels; agents produce files and images to send back. Each channel handles media differently (Slack file API, Discord attachments, WhatsApp media IDs with download tokens, email attachments). The spec has no media normalization, so inbound media may be ignored and outbound media may fail or be sent in an unsupported way per channel.

Required Fix

Add a media normalization layer: (1) Inbound: download channel media (handling channel-specific auth/expiry for media URLs), store in R2, virus/type scan, and present to the agent as canonical attachments with metadata. (2) Outbound: accept canonical attachments from the agent and upload/format per channel (Slack files.upload, WhatsApp media upload → media ID, email MIME attachment). (3) Enforce per-channel size/type limits and transcode where needed (e.g., audio formats). (4) Strip EXIF/metadata for privacy. (5) Implement in the channel-adapter so each new channel provides upload/download functions.

G-AE17 HIGH §channels — adapter abstraction

No Channel Adapter Interface — Adding a New Channel Requires Hand-Coding a Bespoke Handler From Scratch

The Gap

Each channel (Slack, Discord, Telegram, email) is implemented as a separate bespoke handler with duplicated logic for verification, normalization, identity, formatting, and dispatch. Adding WhatsApp, Microsoft Teams, Instagram DM, or a new channel means rewriting all of this with inconsistent behavior and repeated bugs. There is no adapter abstraction.

Required Fix

Define a ChannelAdapter interface that every channel implements: { verifyInbound(req), normalizeInbound(payload): InboxMessage, resolveIdentity(payload), render(blocks): nativePayload, dispatch(message), refreshToken(), healthCheck() }. The core message pipeline (auth → normalize → identity-resolve → route to agent → render → rate-limited dispatch) is channel-agnostic and consumes adapters. New channels implement one interface and register in a channel registry. Ship adapters for Slack, Discord, Telegram, WhatsApp, email, SMS (Twilio), and the web widget. This makes the channel layer extensible and uniformly correct.

G-AE18 MEDIUM §channels — web widget persistence

Web Chat Widget Conversations Are Not Persisted or Resumable Across Sessions/Devices

The Gap

The web widget conversation is tied to a browser session. The spec does not define how an anonymous visitor's conversation persists across page reloads, how it resumes if they return later, or how it merges into their identified account once they log in. Visitors lose their conversation on refresh and start over, and there is no continuity when an anonymous visitor becomes a known user.

Required Fix

Persist widget conversations: (1) On first load, assign a stable anonymous visitor ID stored in the widget's isolated storage (within the sandboxed iframe). (2) Conversation history is persisted server-side keyed by visitor ID and restored on return. (3) When the visitor identifies/logs in (G-AE04), link the anonymous visitor ID to the canonical user (G-AE12) and migrate the conversation + any learned context. (4) Support resume across devices once identified. (5) Respect retention/consent: anonymous conversations expire per policy; provide a "clear conversation" control and honor cookie/consent settings (G-AA48).

G-AE19 CRITICAL §orchestration — DAG partial failure

Multi-Agent DAG Has No Partial-Failure Handling — One Failed Sub-Agent Has Undefined Effect on the Whole Plan

The Gap

When the DynamicOrchestrator runs a DAG of sub-agents, the spec does not define what happens when one node fails: are downstream nodes that depend on it skipped, is the whole orchestration aborted, are successful siblings' results preserved, and is there any compensation for side effects already performed (emails sent, payments made) by completed nodes? Partial failure in a multi-agent plan is the common case and is entirely unspecified.

Required Fix

Define DAG failure semantics: (1) Each node declares onFailure: "abort" | "skip-downstream" | "continue" | "retry(n)" and whether it has compensatable side effects. (2) On node failure, the orchestrator: retries per policy, then for non-recoverable failures marks downstream-dependent nodes skipped while letting independent branches complete. (3) Successful nodes' results are always preserved and returned (partial success is a valid outcome). (4) Nodes with side effects register compensation handlers (saga pattern); on abort, compensations run in reverse order. (5) The final result reports per-node status (succeeded/failed/skipped/compensated) so the agent and builder see exactly what completed.

G-AE20 HIGH §orchestration — result aggregation

Concurrent Sub-Agent Result Aggregation Is Unspecified — Merged Context Is Lossy or Incorrect

The Gap

When multiple sub-agents run in parallel and return results, the spec polls for completion but never specifies how the results are merged back into a coherent context for the parent: ordering, deduplication, conflict resolution when two sub-agents return contradictory findings, and handling of oversized results (which exceed the 128KB queue/message limits). Naive concatenation produces incoherent or truncated context.

Required Fix

Specify result aggregation: (1) Results are written to a results store (DO SQLite or R2 for large payloads) keyed by node ID, not passed through size-limited queues (avoids the 128KB drop). (2) The aggregator assembles results in a deterministic order (DAG topological order) with clear provenance labels per sub-agent. (3) For large results, summarize each before merging into the parent context (map-reduce pattern) to fit the context window. (4) Conflicting findings are presented as such ("Agent A found X; Agent B found Y") rather than silently picking one. (5) The aggregation strategy (concat / summarize / reduce / vote) is declared per orchestration.

G-AE21 HIGH §orchestration — human-in-the-loop

Human-in-the-Loop Approval Mid-Orchestration Has No Pause/Resume Semantics for the Whole DAG

The Gap

Some orchestration steps require human approval (send customer email, execute payment, publish content). The spec has per-action approval flags but does not define how approval works inside a running multi-agent DAG: does the entire orchestration pause or only the blocked node, what happens to in-flight parallel branches, how long does it wait, and how does it durably resume after approval that may come hours or days later?

Required Fix

Define HITL-in-DAG semantics: (1) An approval gate pauses only the gated node; independent parallel branches continue. (2) The gated node's state is durably checkpointed (the CF Workflow step suspends via step.waitForEvent or an alarm-polled approval flag) so it survives DO eviction and waits indefinitely without consuming compute. (3) An approval request is delivered to the approver (notification + dashboard task) with a deadline; on timeout, apply the node's onApprovalTimeout policy (auto-approve / auto-reject / escalate). (4) On approval, the node resumes from its checkpoint. (5) The orchestration status shows which nodes are awaiting approval and from whom.

G-AE22 HIGH §orchestration — cascading cancellation

Cancelling an Orchestration Does Not Cascade to Spawned Sub-Agents — Orphaned Runs Keep Burning Credits

The Gap

A POST /cancel marks a single agent run cancelled, but the spec does not define cascading cancellation across an agent tree. Cancelling a parent orchestration leaves its spawned sub-agents (and their sub-agents) running — orphaned, consuming credits and possibly producing side effects, with no parent to receive their results. There is also no graceful-vs-forceful cancellation distinction.

Required Fix

Implement cascading cancellation: (1) Maintain the parent→child spawn tree (each sub-agent records its parent orchestration ID and the CF Workflow instance ID, fixing the "instance ID never stored" gap). (2) Cancellation propagates depth-first: signal each descendant to cancel. (3) Graceful cancel lets a node finish its current atomic step and run compensations (G-AE19) before stopping; forceful cancel terminates immediately. (4) On cancel, release reserved credits (G-AC36) and admission slots (G-AC44). (5) Mark the whole subtree cancelled with reasons, and ensure no orphaned Workflow instances remain (sweeper reconciles tree state against active instances).

G-AE23 MEDIUM §orchestration — pause & resume

Orchestrations Cannot Be Paused and Resumed — Long Plans Have No Suspend State

The Gap

Beyond cancellation, there is no way to pause a running orchestration (e.g., the builder wants to inspect intermediate results, the space hit a budget cap, or a dependency is temporarily down) and resume it later. The spec has no suspend state, no checkpoint of the full DAG execution position, and no resume entrypoint, so a long-running plan is all-or-nothing.

Required Fix

Add pause/resume: (1) POST /orchestrations/{id}/pause sets the orchestration to paused — running nodes finish their current atomic step and then halt; queued nodes do not start. (2) The full DAG execution state (completed nodes, results, pending nodes, in-flight checkpoints) is durably persisted. (3) POST /orchestrations/{id}/resume continues from the saved position. (4) Auto-pause triggers: budget cap reached (resume after top-up), dependency circuit open (resume on recovery). (5) Paused orchestrations consume no compute (Workflow steps suspended). Surface paused state and remaining work in the dashboard.

G-AE24 HIGH §orchestration — long-running continuation

Tasks Exceeding the 1000-Step Workflow Limit Have No Transparent Continuation Chaining

The Gap

CF Workflows cap at 1000 steps per instance. A long-running agent (multi-day research, a monitoring loop, a months-long automation) exceeds this and is silently terminated. The spec notes the limit but does not specify how the orchestration layer transparently chains continuation instances so a logically long-running task survives across the step ceiling without the agent author having to manage it.

Required Fix

Implement transparent continuation chaining: (1) The Workflow runtime tracks step count; approaching the limit (e.g., step 900), it serializes the orchestration's durable state to R2/DO and spawns a continuation Workflow instance that resumes from that state, linking continuation IDs into the tree (G-AE22). (2) Continuations are invisible to the agent author — logically one task. (3) For idle waits (polling, scheduled checks), use step.sleep/alarms so waiting consumes no steps. (4) Cap total continuations and total wall-clock per plan tier to bound runaway tasks. (5) Persist a stable task ID across continuations so status, cancellation, and results address the logical task, not a single instance.

G-AE25 MEDIUM §orchestration — cost preview

No Pre-Execution Cost/Resource Estimate for a Proposed DAG — Builders and Users Approve Blindly

The Gap

When the DynamicOrchestrator proposes a plan (a DAG of N sub-agents, each with tool calls), there is no cost or resource estimate before execution. The user/builder approves a plan with no idea whether it will cost 100 credits or 100,000, or whether it fits within remaining budget. Expensive runaway plans are only discovered after the credits are spent.

Required Fix

Add a cost/resource preview: (1) Before executing, estimate the plan's cost from per-node heuristics (expected LLM calls × avg tokens × model price + expected tool/API costs + sub-agent fan-out). (2) Check the estimate against the space's remaining budget; if it would exceed, require explicit confirmation or block. (3) Present the estimate (credits, est. duration, sub-agent count, external calls) for approval on high-cost plans (over a threshold). (4) Enforce a hard budget cap during execution (auto-pause at the cap, G-AE23). (5) After execution, compare actual vs estimated cost and feed the delta back to improve future estimates.

G-AE26 HIGH §marketplace — search infrastructure

Marketplace Has No Search Infrastructure — Users Cannot Find Agents, Templates, Skills, or Containers

The Gap

The marketplace lists publishable assets (agents, templates, skills, containers, MCP apps) but the spec defines no search infrastructure: no full-text search, no semantic search, no faceted filtering (by category, capability, price, rating, tenancy fit), and no pagination strategy at scale. With thousands of listings, users cannot discover anything, killing the marketplace flywheel that is core to the monopoly strategy.

Required Fix

Build marketplace search: (1) Index every listing (title, description, tags, capabilities, category) in both a full-text index (SQLite FTS5 / Turso) and a vector index (Vectorize) for semantic queries. (2) Hybrid search with RRF (per G-AD09) over both. (3) Faceted filters: category, price model, rating, tenancy compatibility, required capabilities, last-updated. (4) Cursor-based pagination + result caching. (5) Rank by a relevance + quality score (G-AE27). (6) A dedicated search Worker backed by the indexes, with sub-100ms p95. Re-index on listing publish/update via a queue.

G-AE27 MEDIUM §marketplace — ranking & recommendations

No Ranking or Recommendation Algorithm — Listing Order Is Arbitrary and There Are No "You Might Like" Surfaces

The Gap

Beyond raw search matching, the marketplace has no ranking signal (what makes one agent rank above another?) and no recommendation engine (similar listings, "builders who installed X also installed Y," personalized suggestions). Discovery is flat and arbitrary, so quality listings are not surfaced and the catalog does not drive installs.

Required Fix

Add ranking and recommendations: (1) A composite ranking score per listing: install count (time-decayed), rating (provenance-weighted per G-AB24), retention of installs (do users keep it?), recency, and editorial boost. (2) "Similar listings" via vector similarity on the listing embedding. (3) Collaborative-filtering "also installed" from co-install patterns (privacy-preserving, aggregated). (4) Personalized recommendations from the builder's space type and installed capabilities. (5) Cold-start: new high-quality listings get a temporary boost to gather signal. (6) Expose ranking inputs to publishers so they understand how to improve placement.

G-AE28 HIGH §marketplace — install dependency resolution

Installing a Template or Agent Has No Dependency Resolution — Missing Capabilities/Skills Cause Broken Installs

The Gap

A marketplace asset often depends on other things: a template requires certain capabilities enabled, an agent requires specific skills or MCP integrations, a skill requires a capability version. The spec's install flow does not resolve these dependencies, so installing an asset into a space that lacks its prerequisites produces a silently broken install (the agent references a skill that isn't there).

Required Fix

Implement install dependency resolution: (1) Each listing declares dependencies: { requiresCapabilities: [...], requiresSkills: [{name, version}], requiresMcp: [...], minSpaceTypeVersion }. (2) On install, resolve against the target space: enable missing capabilities (subject to constraint engine G-AC01 and plan limits), install required skills at compatible versions (G-AB05), and prompt to connect required MCP integrations. (3) If a dependency cannot be satisfied (plan-gated capability, conflicting config), block the install with a clear explanation and remediation. (4) Record the resolved dependency set so uninstall can clean up what it added. (5) Detect version conflicts and surface them before install.

G-AE29 MEDIUM §marketplace — install/uninstall lifecycle

Install/Uninstall Lifecycle Is Undefined — No Clean Uninstall, Update, or Rollback of Marketplace Assets

The Gap

The spec mentions installing assets but does not define the full lifecycle: how an installed asset is updated when the publisher ships a new version, how it is cleanly uninstalled (removing what it added without breaking unrelated config), and how a bad update is rolled back. Installed assets accrete and orphan state over time.

Required Fix

Define the asset lifecycle: (1) Install records an installation manifest (what was added: agents, skills, capabilities, config, dependencies G-AE28). (2) Update: notify on new versions; updates go through the same dependency resolution and a preview/diff of changes; support pinned versions and opt-in upgrades (per G-AB50). (3) Uninstall: reverse the installation manifest, removing only what the install added and warning about data that would be orphaned (per G-AC06 impact analysis). (4) Rollback: restore the previously-installed version from history. (5) Track installed-version per space so publishers see version adoption.

G-AE30 MEDIUM §marketplace — public SEO pages

No Public, SEO-Indexable Marketplace Listing Pages — Zero Organic Discovery

The Gap

The marketplace appears to live behind authentication, with no public, crawlable, SEO-optimized listing pages. This forfeits organic discovery: a search for "AI invoice agent" should surface a Naelao marketplace listing. Without public pages with proper metadata, structured data, and fast SSR, the marketplace cannot drive top-of-funnel growth — critical for the network-effect strategy.

Required Fix

Ship public marketplace pages: (1) Server-rendered (Next.js SSR/SSG on CF Pages) public listing pages at naelao.com/marketplace/{slug} with full descriptions, screenshots, ratings, and "install" CTAs. (2) SEO: per-listing meta tags, OpenGraph/Twitter cards, JSON-LD structured data (SoftwareApplication), canonical URLs, and a generated sitemap.xml updated on publish. (3) Category and search landing pages for long-tail queries. (4) Fast TTFB via edge SSR + caching. (5) Public pages expose only public listings (never space-private assets, guarding the G-AB? cross-tenant leak). (6) Track organic → install conversion.

G-AE31 LOW §marketplace — curation & featuring

No Editorial Curation, Featuring, or Collections Mechanism for the Marketplace

The Gap

The spec has no way for the Naelao team to curate the marketplace: feature high-quality listings, create themed collections ("Best agents for e-commerce"), highlight new/trending assets, or editorially promote during launches. Curation is a key trust and discovery lever; without it, the marketplace is an undifferentiated list.

Required Fix

Add a curation system: (1) Editorial fields per listing: featured flag, badges (verified, staff pick, trending), and collection membership. (2) Curated collections (ordered lists of listings) managed via the admin UI, rendered on the marketplace home and category pages. (3) Automated "trending" computed from install velocity. (4) A submission → review → feature pipeline for publishers to request featuring. (5) Time-boxed promotions (launch spotlights). (6) Editorial placement is clearly distinguished from organic ranking for transparency.

G-AE32 MEDIUM §marketplace — publisher analytics

Publishers Have No Listing Analytics — Impressions, Installs, Conversion, and Churn Are Invisible

The Gap

Builders who publish to the marketplace get no analytics on their listings: how many people viewed it, the view→install conversion rate, how many installs are retained vs uninstalled, ratings over time, or search terms that surfaced it. Without this, publishers cannot improve their listings or understand their funnel — reducing the incentive to publish quality assets.

Required Fix

Provide publisher analytics: (1) Track listing events (impression, detail-view, install, uninstall, rating) to Analytics Engine keyed by listing ID. (2) Expose GET /publisher/listings/{id}/analytics: impressions, views, install conversion, install retention curve, rating trend, and top search terms that led to the listing. (3) Revenue analytics for paid listings (gross, payouts, refunds — ties to G-AC35). (4) Cohort retention of installs. (5) Alerts on anomalies (sudden uninstall spike, rating drop). This closes the loop so publishers iterate on quality.

G-AE33 HIGH §scale — multi-region read replicas

No Multi-Region Read-Replica Strategy — Global Reads Pay Full Cross-Region Latency to a Single-Region DO

The Gap

A DO and its SQLite live in one region. Read-heavy global access (dashboards, conversation history, marketplace, knowledge lookups) from distant users pays full cross-region latency on every read. The spec addresses DO placement (Smart Placement, locationHint) but not read replication — there is no read-replica or edge-cache layer so a Tokyo user reading a US-pinned space's data waits 200ms+ per read.

Required Fix

Add a multi-region read path: (1) For cacheable reads (space config, published content, marketplace, knowledge metadata), serve from a regional cache (KV with short TTL, or CF Cache API) populated from the canonical DO — reads hit the edge, not the cross-region DO. (2) For per-user data where staleness is tolerable, use regional read replicas (Turso embedded replicas, which replicate to edge regions automatically, fit this well per the Turso topology G-AC21). (3) Writes always go to the canonical primary; reads prefer the nearest replica with read-your-writes consistency for the writer (route the writer's reads to the primary briefly after a write). (4) Document the per-resource consistency model (strong vs eventual).

G-AE34 HIGH §deploy — monorepo deploy ordering

No Deploy-Order/Dependency-Graph Management for 22 Interdependent Workers

The Gap

The Workers depend on each other via Service Bindings (router → everything; agents → spaces/auth/billing/...). Deploying them in the wrong order, or deploying a worker that calls a not-yet-deployed binding target, breaks the mesh. The spec lists a deploy order in prose but provides no automated dependency-graph-driven deployment, so deploys are fragile and manual.

Required Fix

Automate dependency-ordered deploys: (1) Declare each worker's Service Binding dependencies in its config; build a dependency graph. (2) The deploy pipeline (Turborepo + a deploy orchestrator) topologically sorts and deploys in order, leaf dependencies first. (3) Deploy each worker with gradual rollout (G-AB10) and health-gate (G-AB13) before proceeding to dependents. (4) Handle binding bootstrapping (a new binding target must exist before its caller references it). (5) On any worker's deploy failure, halt the cascade and report. (6) Support per-worker independent deploys when no binding contract changed (detected via the OpenAPI/contract diff).

G-AE35 MEDIUM §deploy — environment promotion

No Environment Promotion or Config-Drift Detection Between Staging and Production

The Gap

The spec mentions staging and production environments but defines no promotion process (how a validated staging build is promoted to prod with identical artifacts) and no config-drift detection (staging and prod silently diverge in bindings, env vars, resource configs, and secrets, causing "works in staging, breaks in prod" incidents).

Required Fix

Define environment promotion + drift control: (1) Build immutable artifacts once; promote the exact same artifact from staging to production (no rebuild). (2) Manage per-environment configuration declaratively (wrangler environments + a config repo) so differences are explicit and reviewed. (3) A drift-detection check compares deployed config (bindings, vars, resource IDs, cron schedules) against the declared config and fails CI on undeclared drift. (4) Secrets are managed per environment via a secrets manager (G-AA13) with the same key set enforced across environments. (5) A pre-prod smoke test (synthetic journey) gates promotion.

G-AE36 HIGH §ops — maintenance mode

No Platform-Wide Maintenance Mode or Graceful Degradation Switch

The Gap

There is an emergency agent kill switch, but no platform-wide maintenance mode: a controlled way to put the platform (or a single space, or a subsystem) into read-only/maintenance state during migrations, incidents, or upstream outages, with a user-facing message instead of raw errors. Operators have no graceful big-red-button between "fully up" and "hard down."

Required Fix

Implement maintenance mode: (1) A MaintenanceConfigDO (or a strongly-consistent flag) with scopes: global, per-subsystem, per-space. (2) Modes: read-only (mutations rejected with a clear 503 + message), maintenance (a branded maintenance page/response), and degraded (specific features disabled per the degradation map G-AD50). (3) The router checks maintenance state (cached, fast) and short-circuits with a friendly message + Retry-After. (4) In-flight operations are allowed to drain (configurable grace). (5) Scheduled maintenance windows publish to the status page (G-AA43) in advance. (6) Per-space maintenance lets one tenant be paused (e.g., during their migration) without affecting others.

G-AE37 MEDIUM §deploy — worker bundle size

No Worker Bundle Size Budget Management — Workers Will Hit the Size Limit as Features Accrete

The Gap

Cloudflare Workers have a compressed bundle size limit (1MB free / 10MB paid). As workers (especially naelao-agents and naelao-router) accumulate dependencies, tool definitions, and shared code, they will approach this limit and deploys will start failing. The spec has no bundle-size budgeting, monitoring, or code-splitting strategy.

Required Fix

Manage bundle size: (1) Track each worker's compressed bundle size in CI; fail the build if it exceeds a budget (e.g., 80% of the limit) with a report of the largest modules. (2) Externalize large/rarely-used code: move heavy tool implementations behind dynamic imports or into separate workers called via Service Binding. (3) Avoid bundling large dependencies into hot-path workers; prefer lightweight alternatives (Web Crypto over crypto libs, as the spec already mandates). (4) Share common code via packages without duplicating it into every bundle. (5) Monitor bundle-size trend over time and alert on regressions.

G-AE38 HIGH §security — secret rotation fleet

No Coordinated Secret Rotation Across 22 Workers — Rotating a Shared Secret Requires Risky Manual Coordination

The Gap

Many secrets are shared across workers (the internal service token, signing keys, provider API keys, encryption keys). The spec has no coordinated rotation: rotating a shared secret means updating it in many workers near-simultaneously, and any window where some workers have the old value and others the new breaks inter-service calls. There is no overlap-window rotation mechanism.

Required Fix

Implement coordinated secret rotation: (1) Source all shared secrets from a central secrets manager (G-AA13: Doppler/Infisical/Vault or CF Secrets Store), not per-worker copies. (2) Support dual-secret (current + previous) validation during rotation windows so a secret can be rotated with both values accepted until all workers pick up the new one (applies to the internal service token → per-caller JWTs, signing keys G-AD04, webhook secrets). (3) A rotation runbook + automation rotates, verifies propagation across all workers (via a /_secretversion health field), then retires the old value. (4) Alert on secrets nearing expiry. (5) Audit every rotation.

G-AE39 MEDIUM §deploy — infrastructure as code

CF Resources (KV, R2, Queues, Vectorize, DOs) Are Not Provisioned via Infrastructure-as-Code

The Gap

The platform uses many CF resources (multiple KV namespaces, R2 buckets, Queues with DLQs, a Vectorize index, Analytics Engine datasets, DO namespaces). The spec does not define how these are provisioned reproducibly.
