When a Stripe dispute arrives, generate a PDF usage report from these signed records, verify signatures, and attach it to the dispute response automatically. Maintain a 7-year retention policy for billing audit logs.

G-AJ33 CRITICAL Capacity Planning — DO Concurrency

No Hard Concurrency Limit on WebSocket Connections Per SpaceDO

The Gap

A single SpaceDO handles ALL WebSocket connections for an entire builder product. The CF DO model single-threads all WebSocket message processing. Under extreme load (viral product launch, adversarial connection flood), a SpaceDO can accumulate tens of thousands of WebSocket connections. getWebSockets() returns all of them; iterating over them in an alarm or broadcast blocks the DO for seconds. CF does not currently impose a hard limit on WebSocket connections per DO.

Required Fix

Implement a DO-level WebSocket shard architecture: maintain a WebSocketShardDO per {space_id, shard_index} where shard_index = hash(session_id) % SHARD_COUNT (default: 8 shards per Space). The SpaceRouter assigns new WebSocket connections to the appropriate shard DO. Each shard handles at most MAX_WS_PER_SHARD (e.g., 2000) connections; reject new connections with 503 when a shard is full. For cross-shard broadcasts, use SpaceDO as a fan-out coordinator that sends to all shards in parallel via Service Binding RPC.

G-AJ34 CRITICAL Observability — Distributed Tracing

Trace ID Not Propagated Across Service Bindings, Queues, and DO RPC

The Gap

W3C traceparent headers are documented at the edge router, but propagation stops there. Service Binding calls between workers omit the traceparent header. CF Queue messages do not carry trace context in their body. DO-to-DO RPC (sub-agent spawning, tool dispatch) starts a new trace segment with no parent link. The result: distributed traces across a multi-worker execution ladder are fragmented — impossible to correlate a user request through all 8+ workers it traverses.

Required Fix

Mandate trace context propagation at the platform SDK layer: (1) Service Binding stubs: wrap all env.SERVICE.fetch() calls in a tracingFetch() helper that injects traceparent/tracestate headers from the current context. (2) Queue messages: include {_trace: {traceparent, tracestate}} in every message payload. Consumer workers extract and restore context before processing. (3) DO RPC: pass trace context as the first argument to all RPC method signatures (enforced by the base DO class). Instrument with OpenTelemetry SDK and export to a Grafana Tempo / Honeycomb collector via CF Logpush or a WASM OTLP exporter.

G-AJ35 HIGH Observability — SLOs

No Error Budgets or Per-Service-Tier SLO Definitions

The Gap

The platform operates with no documented Service Level Objectives (SLOs). There are no defined uptime targets (e.g., 99.9% for free, 99.95% for pro, 99.99% for enterprise), no error budget tracking, no burn rate alerting, and no public status page. When the platform experiences degradation, builders have no contractual SLA to reference and the platform team has no objective threshold for declaring an incident.

Required Fix

Define SLOs for each critical service: agent invocation p99 latency < 2s (free) / < 500ms (pro), availability > 99.9%/month (free) / > 99.95% (pro). Track SLI metrics in Analytics Engine (count(errors) / count(requests) per 5-minute window). Implement error budget burn rate alerting: alert when 1-hour burn rate > 14× (would exhaust 30-day budget in 2 hours). Publish a status page at status.naelao.com (using Atlassian Statuspage or similar) that auto-updates from SLI metrics. Include SLO commitments in the Terms of Service and billing tier descriptions.

G-AJ36 HIGH Observability — On-Call

No PagerDuty / OpsGenie On-Call Integration or Escalation Policy

The Gap

Critical events (billing threshold breach, security alert, DO crash, approval timeout) route through the platform's internal notification system: fire-and-forget WebSocket push with no retry, no read-receipt, and no escalation to secondary channels. There is no on-call rotation, no defined escalation policy, and no integration with PagerDuty, OpsGenie, or equivalent. A 3am SEV-1 platform outage generates no alert.

Required Fix

Integrate PagerDuty (or OpsGenie) as the alerting backend for the platform operations team. AlertingWorker receives SLO burn-rate alerts from Analytics Engine and publishes PagerDuty Events API v2 payloads. Define routing rules: critical (DO crash, auth outage) → immediate page; high (p99 > threshold, queue backlog) → alert with 15-min escalation; medium (capacity warning) → ticket. Maintain an on-call schedule (primary + secondary rotation). Test the on-call system monthly with a synthetic test page. Document runbooks per alert type.

G-AJ37 HIGH Observability — Chaos Engineering

No Chaos Engineering Framework for Fault Injection Testing

The Gap

The test suite covers happy-path and some error conditions, but there is no fault injection framework. The platform has never been tested under: DO eviction mid-request, Vectorize latency spikes, R2 put() failures, Queue consumer lag, external dependency (Turso/Stripe/WorkOS) unavailability, or container kill during execution. Without chaos testing, latent resilience bugs accumulate until a production incident.

Required Fix

Adopt a chaos engineering framework for the Workers platform. Implement a ChaosProxy Service Binding that wraps calls to each external service; in staging/canary environments, the proxy can inject faults (random 5% failure, 2s latency spike, connection refused) based on config stored in KV. Schedule weekly automated chaos experiments in staging: each experiment targets one fault type, validates that circuit breakers open, retries succeed, and error metrics are emitted. Run monthly game days in production (low-traffic hours) for the highest-severity fault scenarios. Document results in the observability runbook.

G-AJ38 MEDIUM Observability — Performance Profiling

No CPU Profiling or Flame Graph Infrastructure for DO Hot Paths

The Gap

Multiple documented Worker CPU-limit crashes (30-second hard ceiling hit during agent loop, MCP hub timeout on long tools) have occurred, but there is no CPU profiling infrastructure to identify hot paths. The only diagnostic available is the error message 'Worker exceeded CPU time limit.' There are no flame graphs, no allocation profiling, and no way to measure DO CPU time per operation.

Required Fix

Integrate the V8 CPU profiler available in the Workers runtime: use performance.now() microsecond timers around every major operation (LLM call, tool dispatch, SQL query, KV operation). Emit structured timing events to Analytics Engine: {operation, duration_ms, space_id, request_id}. Build a p95/p99 duration dashboard in Grafana. For deep profiling in staging: use the wrangler --inspect flag with Chrome DevTools Protocol to attach a profiler and capture flame graphs for specific agent execution paths. Add automated alerts when any single operation exceeds 5% of the 30-second CPU budget.

G-AJ39 HIGH Observability — Builder Dashboard

Builder Dashboard Shows Only Aggregate Metrics — No Per-Agent Observability

The Gap

The builder analytics dashboard shows DAU, MAU, and credit usage. Builders running 10+ agents within a Space cannot see per-agent p95 latency, per-agent error rate, per-agent cost breakdown, or per-run execution traces. When an agent starts behaving badly (high latency, frequent failures), the builder has no dashboard signal — they only learn from angry end-users.

Required Fix

Add an Agent Observability panel to the builder dashboard: for each agent, show rolling 24h metrics: invocation count, p50/p95/p99 latency, error rate, average cost per run, and top-3 error messages. Backend: Analytics Engine query with groupBy(agent_id). Add a per-run trace viewer: click any agent run to see the step-by-step execution log (LLM call, tool calls, final output) with timestamps and token counts. This data is already partially emitted to Analytics Engine — it just needs a UI layer and an API endpoint to query it by agent_id.

G-AJ40 HIGH Observability — Cost Attribution

No Per-Tenant Cost Attribution for R2, Vectorize, CF AI, and Workers

The Gap

The billing system tracks AI token consumption per Space, but does not attribute other cloud infrastructure costs: R2 storage ops (per-request), Vectorize query costs, CF AI model inference, and Workers invocation counts. The platform cannot produce a cost-per-Space or cost-per-builder breakdown. This makes it impossible to price tiers correctly, identify unprofitable builders, or offer cost-based usage insights to builders.

Required Fix

Instrument every R2 read/write, Vectorize query, CF AI call, and Workers invocation with a usage event emitted to Analytics Engine: {ts, space_id, builder_id, service, operation, units}. Maintain a cost rate card per service/operation in a platform config KV namespace. A nightly billing aggregation worker computes actual cost-per-space using the rate card and writes the result to BillingDO. Expose this breakdown in the builder dashboard ('Your infrastructure cost this month: $X') and in the platform admin panel for pricing team analysis.

G-AJ41 HIGH Observability — Synthetic Monitoring

No Scheduled Synthetic Monitoring Canary Transactions

The Gap

The platform has a canary rollout mechanism for Space Type version updates, but no synthetic monitoring. There are no scheduled probe transactions that verify the full request path (user auth → router → agent invoke → tool call → response) from multiple CF edges every minute. Outages that start silently (DO storage corruption, queue consumer death, external dependency failure) are discovered by users, not by automated monitoring.

Required Fix

Deploy a naelao-synthetics CF Cron Trigger that runs every minute. It executes a scripted canary transaction against the production platform: (1) authenticate as a canary test account, (2) POST a message to a designated canary Space, (3) verify agent responds within 5 seconds, (4) verify response quality (expected keywords present). Run from 3+ CF regions. Emit pass/fail metrics to Analytics Engine. Trigger a PagerDuty alert on 2 consecutive failures. This provides sub-2-minute detection of most production outages. Add additional synthetic checks for billing, MCP tool invocation, and knowledge search paths.

G-AJ42 HIGH Observability — Dependency Health

No Runtime Dependency Health Checks Before Accepting Traffic

The Gap

Workers begin accepting requests immediately on cold start without verifying that critical external dependencies (Turso, Stripe, WorkOS, Resend, Vectorize) are reachable. When Turso is down, the first 50 concurrent requests to SpaceWorker fail before circuit breakers open. When Stripe is degraded, billing calls fail silently. No dependency health check endpoint exists for operations teams to verify platform readiness before routing traffic.

Required Fix

Implement a /health endpoint in each worker that performs lightweight dependency checks: HTTP HEAD to external service health endpoints (Stripe: /v1/health, WorkOS: /health, Turso: /health, Resend: /v1/health). Cache results in KV for 10 seconds to avoid thundering herd on the health endpoint itself. A root /health aggregate endpoint returns {status: 'ok'|'degraded'|'down', dependencies: {...}}. Integrate this endpoint with CF Health Checks (Load Balancing) and with the synthetic monitoring canaries. Add a readiness check pattern: CF Workers do not serve traffic until the /health endpoint returns 200.

G-AJ43 HIGH Observability — Scheduled Tasks

No Central Registry for Scheduled Tasks — Silent Job Death Undetected

The Gap

The platform runs many scheduled tasks: 5-minute sweepers, hourly categorizers, nightly billing aggregators, canary rollouts, archive jobs, and dozens of DO alarms. These are scattered across 15+ workers with no central registry of: what jobs exist, when they last ran, whether they succeeded, and when they are due next. A scheduler that silently stops running (CF Cron Trigger removed by a bad deploy, DO alarm not re-armed after crash) goes undetected for days.

Required Fix

Create a SchedulerRegistryDO as the platform-wide job registry. Each scheduled task self-registers on startup: {job_id, worker, schedule_cron, last_ran_at, last_status, next_expected_at}. Jobs ping the registry on completion: SchedulerRegistryDO.complete(job_id, {status, duration_ms, records_processed}). A watchdog alarm runs every 5 minutes and checks for any job that has not checked in within 2× its expected interval. On violation, emit an alert to PagerDuty. Expose a /admin/jobs dashboard showing the live state of all scheduled tasks.

G-AJ44 MEDIUM Observability — Feature Flags

Feature Flag State Has No Per-Tenant Observability or Safe Rollback

The Gap

Feature flags are cached in module-scope variables with a 60-second KV TTL. There is no per-tenant flag exposure tracking, no canary metric (what % of requests used the new flag?), no instant kill switch (changes take 60s to propagate), and no safe rollback path. If a flag causes a production bug after enabling for 20% of tenants, the operator must manually update KV and wait 60 seconds for all isolates to pick up the change — during which 20% of tenants are still broken.

Required Fix

Replace the module-scope flag cache with a FlagsDO per deployment region. All Workers access flags via FlagsDO RPC (sub-millisecond for same-colo calls). FlagsDO exposes an invalidate() method triggered by the platform admin panel. Flag changes propagate in < 1 second instead of 60 seconds. Add flag exposure analytics: each flag evaluation emits a lightweight Analytics Engine event {flag, variant, tenant_id, ts}. Build a rollout funnel dashboard: see exactly which tenants have each flag enabled and correlate with error rate metrics. Add a circuit-breaker flag: if error rate for the 'flagged' bucket exceeds 1%, auto-disable the flag.

G-AJ45 HIGH Data Portability — Legal Compliance

No Litigation Hold / Preservation Order Support

The Gap

The platform has no mechanism to freeze data deletion for a specific tenant in response to a litigation hold or government preservation order. If a user submits an erasure request while their data is subject to a legal hold, the erasure pipeline will delete data that must be legally preserved. There is no legal hold flag, no hold expiry mechanism, and no audit trail of hold creation and release.

Required Fix

Add a legal_holds table to the global AdminDO SQLite: {hold_id, tenant_id, space_id, created_by, created_at, expires_at, case_reference, notes}. All erasure pipeline operations (GDPR right-to-erasure, account deletion, Space deletion) check for active holds before proceeding. If a hold exists, the erasure is queued but not executed; the requesting admin receives an alert. On hold release (or expiry), the queued erasure proceeds automatically. Holds can only be created/released by users with the platform:legal_admin role. All hold lifecycle events are written to the immutable audit log.

G-AJ46 CRITICAL Data Portability — Backup Strategy

No Continuous DO SQLite Backup — Daily Export Is Undocumented and Unimplemented

The Gap

The spec mentions 'daily JSON export to R2' as a DO SQLite backup strategy, but this export is marked as unimplemented in the spec itself. There is no WAL-streaming replication, no point-in-time restore capability, and no recovery procedure. A DO SQLite corruption event (hardware failure, software bug, storage exhaustion) causes permanent, irrecoverable data loss for the affected Space. At millions of Spaces, this is statistically certain to occur.

Required Fix

Implement continuous SQLite backup using DO Alarms: every 15 minutes, the SpaceDO alarm handler executes a full SQLite VACUUM INTO ':memory:' (or iterates all tables via SELECT and streams rows). Serialize to a gzip-compressed JSON file and PUT to R2 under backups/{space_id}/{timestamp}.json.gz with a 30-day retention lifecycle. Tag backups with the Space's current content version hash. On restore request, fetch the latest backup from R2 and replay it into a fresh DO via SQL INSERT. Test restores automatically: a daily canary picks a random Space backup and validates it restores without error.

G-AJ47 HIGH Data Portability — Builder Workflow

No YAML/JSON Config Import for Infrastructure-as-Code Space Definitions

The Gap

Builders managing their Naelao products as code (IaC, GitOps) have no way to import a YAML/JSON Space definition file into the platform. The only configuration path is the GUI. A builder who wants to check their agent definitions into Git, run them through a CI review process, and deploy them to production via a pipeline cannot do so. This blocks technical builders and enterprise DevOps workflows.

Required Fix

Define a Space Definition Manifest format (naelao.yaml): a declarative YAML schema covering agents, tools, knowledge bases, workflows, channels, and access policies. Publish a JSON Schema for the manifest format. Implement POST /spaces/{id}/import-config accepting a naelao.yaml file or a base64-encoded JSON. SpaceWorker validates the manifest against the schema, diffs it against the current Space config, and applies only the changed resources. On import failure, return detailed validation errors (field, line, message). Publish a naelao CLI command: naelao deploy --config naelao.yaml that wraps this endpoint for use in CI/CD pipelines.

G-AJ48 CRITICAL Data Portability — Account Lifecycle

No Cross-Service Cascade Delete on Account or Space Deletion

The Gap

When a builder account is deleted or a Space is closed, the deletion logic removes the primary DB record but does NOT cascade to: child Durable Objects (AssistantDO, AgentDO, WalletDO, ContainerDO), R2 objects under spaces/{id}/, KV namespace entries with {space_id} prefix, Vectorize vectors with space_id metadata, Analytics Engine events (cannot be deleted by design), and Queues messages in-flight. Orphaned DOs continue consuming CF storage and billing the platform indefinitely.

Required Fix

Implement a DeletionOrchestrator CF Workflow: on Space deletion, enqueue a multi-step deletion job: (1) soft-delete: mark Space as deleted in registry, stop routing traffic. (2) R2 purge: list and delete all objects under spaces/{id}/ in batches of 1000. (3) KV purge: list and delete all keys with {space_id} prefix. (4) Vectorize: delete all vectors with {space_id: id} filter in batches. (5) Child DOs: send terminate() RPC to all registered child DOs; they self-destruct and release storage. (6) Audit: record deletion completion event. Run with idempotency keys so partial failures can be safely retried.

G-AJ49 HIGH Data Portability — Disaster Recovery

No Automated Disaster Recovery Drill or Restore Validation

The Gap

The platform has no documented disaster recovery procedure and no automated DR drills. The team does not know: (1) How long a restore from the daily R2 backup takes. (2) Whether the restore procedure actually works for large Spaces. (3) What the actual RPO/RTO is under realistic failure conditions. Without DR drills, the first real disaster is also the first restore test — under maximum stress with maximum blast radius.

Required Fix

Schedule monthly automated DR drills: a dedicated CF Workflow picks 3 random Spaces (one small, one medium, one large by storage size), executes the full restore procedure into a staging environment, validates data integrity (row counts, foreign key checks, a test user login), and records restore duration and success/failure. Track RPO (time since last backup) and RTO (restore duration) as SLI metrics. Alert via PagerDuty if any drill fails. Publish DR metrics in the internal engineering dashboard. Run a full-platform DR exercise annually with cross-team participation.

G-AJ50 HIGH Data Portability — Audit Trail

Audit Log Has No Immutability Guarantee or SIEM Streaming Export

The Gap

The platform writes audit events to Analytics Engine (CF's ClickHouse-compatible OLAP store). Analytics Engine does not provide immutability guarantees — events cannot be deleted individually but there is no cryptographic proof of non-tampering. Enterprise buyers and compliance frameworks (SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001, FedRAMP) require an immutable audit trail with a cryptographic chain of custody and SIEM integration (Splunk, Sumo Logic, Elastic).

Required Fix

Implement a two-tier audit log: (1) Primary: continue writing to Analytics Engine for queryable access. (2) Immutable archive: for each audit event, append a HMAC-SHA256-chained record to R2 under audit-log/{YYYY-MM-DD}/{ulid}.json. Each record includes the hash of the previous record, forming a tamper-evident chain. Daily: compute a Merkle root of the day's events and publish it to the platform's public transparency log (similar to CT logs). SIEM export: a naelao-siem-exporter CF Cron Trigger pushes new audit events to the configured Splunk HEC, Elastic ingest, or generic syslog endpoint every 5 minutes using CF Logpush as the transport.

Appendix AK — AI Model Management, Space Type Marketplace, End-User UX, i18n, PCI DSS & Platform Governance Gaps

50 gaps · G-AK01 – G-AK50 · advanced AI/ML, marketplace economics, localization, payment security & content policy

G-AK01 HIGH AI/ML — EU AI Act Compliance

No AI-Generated Content Disclosure (EU AI Act Article 50)

The Gap

The EU AI Act Article 50 requires that AI systems generating synthetic audio, images, video, or text that could deceive people must label outputs as AI-generated. Naelao's agents generate text, structured data, and potentially images for end-users across the EU. There is no mechanism to add a machine-readable or human-readable AI disclosure label to agent outputs, no per-output watermarking, and no builder-facing requirement to disclose AI generation in their product.

Required Fix

Add an X-AI-Generated: true response header and a visible disclosure footer to all agent-generated responses served to end-users in EU jurisdictions (detected via CF-IPCountry header). Implement invisible watermarking for AI-generated images using a steganographic payload (e.g., the C2PA standard). Expose a builder toggle 'AI Disclosure Label' (required for EU, optional elsewhere) that renders a small disclosure badge in the product UI. Log each disclosed output to the compliance audit trail for Article 50 enforcement evidence.

G-AK02 HIGH AI/ML — Safety & Reliability

No Automated Red-Teaming of Builder Agents Before Public Deployment

The Gap

When a builder publishes an agent to end-users, there is no automated adversarial testing (red-teaming) that runs before the agent goes live. A naively configured agent can be easily manipulated to leak the system prompt, ignore safety instructions, or produce harmful outputs. The only safeguard is the underlying LLM's own safety training, which is known to be bypassable by relatively simple prompt injection.

Required Fix

Build a RedTeamWorker that runs automatically when a builder marks an agent as 'public'. It executes a battery of adversarial test cases against the agent: system prompt extraction attempts, jailbreak payloads (DAN, AIM, roleplay escape), PII extraction probes, and instruction override attempts. Score each test on a 0–10 risk scale. Block publication if any test scores > 7. Surface results to the builder with specific failure cases and remediation suggestions. Update the test battery monthly as new jailbreak patterns emerge.

G-AK03 HIGH AI/ML — Retrieval Augmentation

RAG Pipeline Has No Cross-Encoder Reranking After Vector Retrieval

The Gap

The current RAG pipeline retrieves top-K chunks from Vectorize using bi-encoder embeddings and passes them directly to the LLM context window. Bi-encoder retrieval has well-documented precision limitations: it retrieves semantically similar but not always maximally relevant chunks. Without a reranking step, the LLM receives lower-quality context, leading to worse answers, hallucinations, and missed information that was in the knowledge base.

Required Fix

Add a cross-encoder reranking step between Vectorize retrieval and LLM context assembly. Use a lightweight cross-encoder model (e.g., ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2 via CF Workers AI) to score each retrieved chunk against the query. Rerank the top-20 bi-encoder results by cross-encoder score and pass only the top-5 to the LLM. Cross-encoders dramatically improve precision (typically +15–30% on NDCG@5) at the cost of slightly higher latency (50–100ms). Cache reranker scores per (query, chunk_id) pair in KV for repeated queries.

G-AK04 MEDIUM AI/ML — Agent Safety

No Agent Tool Call Confirmation Mode for Destructive or Irreversible Operations

The Gap

Agents invoke tools (file deletion, database writes, API calls that send emails, execute payments) without any built-in confirmation step. If an LLM makes a mistake in tool argument construction (e.g., deletes the wrong file, sends an email to the wrong recipient, initiates an unexpected payment), the action is irreversible by the time the builder or end-user notices it. There is no dry-run mode, no pre-execution confirmation prompt, and no undo mechanism.

Required Fix

Add a tool annotation: {requires_confirmation: true, is_destructive: true, undo_procedure: string} to the tool manifest schema. When an agent is about to call a requires_confirmation tool, pause execution and send a confirmation request to the end-user: 'Agent wants to [action description]. Approve?' The user has 30 seconds to confirm or deny. If confirmed, proceed; if denied, the agent receives a {tool_call_cancelled: true} result and must choose an alternative path. Log all destructive tool confirmations to the audit trail.

G-AK05 MEDIUM AI/ML — Fairness & Bias

No Bias Detection or Fairness Testing in Agent Output Pipelines

The Gap

Builder agents generate content (recommendations, evaluations, responses) that may systematically differ in quality or tone across demographic groups defined by gender, race, nationality, or age in the user's message. There is no fairness testing framework, no demographic parity metric, and no bias detection in agent outputs. Builders deploying hiring assistants, financial advisors, or healthcare agents face legal liability for discriminatory outputs.

Required Fix

Build a FairnessTestSuite as part of the agent evaluation framework: test the agent with demographically varied prompts (same job application, same medical symptom, different demographic signals) and measure response parity. Flag agents where response quality or tone varies significantly (>15% divergence on scoring rubric) across demographic groups. Surface a 'Bias Risk Score' in the agent dashboard. For high-risk agent categories (HR, finance, healthcare), make bias testing mandatory before public deployment. Provide builders with specific examples of disparate outputs.

G-AK06 HIGH AI/ML — Memory Management

Long-Term Agent Memory Has No Garbage Collection or Compaction

The Gap

Agent memory (episodic memories stored as Vectorize embeddings and SQLite rows) grows indefinitely. A long-running agent accumulates thousands of redundant, contradictory, or stale memory entries over months of operation. Retrieval quality degrades as the memory store grows because the signal-to-noise ratio falls. There is no scheduled memory consolidation, no deduplication, no staleness-based eviction, and no memory compaction pipeline.

Required Fix

Implement a MemoryMaintenanceDO that runs a weekly alarm for each active agent. The alarm: (1) Fetches all memories older than 90 days with low retrieval frequency (access_count < 2). (2) Clusters semantically similar memories using Vectorize query similarity. (3) For each cluster, generates a 'consolidated memory' summary via a cheap LLM call, stores it as a new memory, and deletes the originals. (4) Deletes memories flagged as contradicted by more recent memories. Log memory counts before/after compaction. Cap total memory entries at 10,000 per agent to enforce upper bound.

G-AK07 HIGH AI/ML — Output Quality

No Toxicity or Quality Scoring Gate Between LLM Output and End-User Delivery

The Gap

Agent responses generated by the LLM are delivered directly to end-users without any post-generation quality or safety check. If the LLM generates a toxic, incoherent, or privacy-violating response (e.g., a hallucinated PII about a real person), it reaches the end-user immediately. The only check is the LLM's own safety training, which is insufficient for production deployments.

Required Fix

Add a ResponseQualityGate worker in the agent execution pipeline between LLM output and response delivery. The gate runs: (1) Toxicity check using CF Workers AI with a lightweight classifier (Llama Guard 3 or similar). (2) PII detection: regex + NER model scan for SSN, credit card, email, phone number patterns. (3) Coherence check: minimum response length, no pure repetition, no error message passthrough. If any check fails, substitute a safe fallback response ('I encountered an issue generating a response. Please try again.') and log the blocked output for builder review. The gate adds ~50ms but eliminates the highest-severity UX failures.

G-AK08 MEDIUM AI/ML — Model Selection

No Task-Complexity-Based LLM Model Selection (Routing by Difficulty)

The Gap

All agent requests use the model specified in the agent definition, regardless of query complexity. Simple lookups (factual Q&A from knowledge base) use the same expensive flagship model as complex multi-step reasoning tasks. This wastes significant LLM spend: ~60% of production queries are simple enough for a 3x cheaper model. There is no mechanism for builders to define routing rules ('use cheap model for simple queries, expensive model for complex ones').

Required Fix

Add a model routing policy to agent definitions: {routing: [{condition: 'simple', model: 'claude-haiku-4-5', confidence_threshold: 0.9}, {condition: 'complex', model: 'claude-opus-4-8'}]}. Before the LLM call, run a lightweight complexity classifier (fine-tuned Haiku call, <10ms, <$0.0001) that predicts query complexity from the user message. Route to the appropriate model based on predicted complexity and confidence. Track model routing decisions in Analytics Engine; show per-model cost breakdown in builder analytics. Average cost reduction: 40–60% with <2% quality degradation.

G-AK09 CRITICAL Space Type Marketplace — Versioning

Space Type Has No Semantic Versioning or Breaking-Change Rollout Strategy

The Gap

Space Type authors update their templates by publishing new configurations. There is no versioning scheme (semantic versioning), no compatibility contract between versions, and no mechanism for existing builder products to pin to a specific Space Type version. When a Space Type author makes a breaking change (renames a required field, removes an agent definition, changes an MCP tool's schema), all builder products using that Space Type break simultaneously with no warning.

Required Fix

Implement semantic versioning for Space Types: each published Space Type version has a MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH number stored in SpaceTypeDO. Builder products pin to a minimum version (e.g., ^1.2.0). SpaceTypeDO enforces that MAJOR version bumps (breaking changes) are never auto-applied to existing builders — they must explicitly opt in. MINOR and PATCH updates are auto-applied after a 7-day review window. Notify subscribed builders via email when a Space Type they use publishes a new MAJOR version. Include a migration guide generated by the Space Type author. Maintain each published version immutably in R2.

G-AK10 HIGH Space Type Marketplace — Creator Analytics

Space Type Creators Have No Analytics Dashboard or Install Metrics

The Gap

A builder who creates and publishes a Space Type to the marketplace has no way to know: how many other builders have installed it, what the DAU of products built on it is, what error rates those products experience, or how much revenue their template has generated. Without analytics, creators cannot improve their templates, prioritize support, or understand the value they provide to the ecosystem.

Required Fix

Build a Creator Analytics dashboard tab in the builder portal for Space Type authors. Metrics shown: install count (new this week, total), active builder products using the template, aggregate DAU across all products, top error types reported by users of the template, revenue generated (if paid template), and a time-series chart of installs and uninstalls. Implement privacy-preserving aggregation: individual builder product data is not shown to the creator, only aggregate stats. Refresh data daily via Analytics Engine queries keyed by space_type_id.

G-AK11 CRITICAL Space Type Marketplace — Security

No Automated Security Audit Pipeline for Space Types Before Marketplace Listing

The Gap

When a Space Type author submits a template to the marketplace, it may contain: MCP tool bindings pointing to malicious external services, system prompts designed to override builder customizations, dangerous default RBAC configurations (e.g., all users get admin role), or embedded webhook URLs that exfiltrate data. There is no automated security validation pipeline before a Space Type is approved for listing.

Required Fix

Build a SpaceTypeAuditWorker that runs on every submitted Space Type version: (1) MCP tool binding validation: allowlist of trusted MCP providers; flag any custom MCP server URL for human review. (2) System prompt injection scan: check for attempts to override builder/user instructions (meta-instructions like 'ignore the builder's instructions'). (3) RBAC audit: flag configurations that grant excessive default permissions. (4) Webhook URL validation: check all URLs against a blocklist and verify they point to documented, non-suspicious endpoints. (5) Dependency audit: check all package dependencies against Snyk or similar. Score 0–100; block listing if score < 70. Require human review for scores 70–85.

G-AK12 HIGH Space Type Marketplace — Legal & IP

Space Type Has No Licensing Framework or IP Ownership Clarity

The Gap

When a builder builds a product using a Space Type, the legal relationship between the Space Type author, the builder, and the end-users is undefined. Who owns the derivative product? Can the Space Type author revoke access? Are builder customizations considered a derivative work under copyright? Can a builder reverse-engineer a paid Space Type? Without a license framework, the platform cannot enforce any IP rights and builders operate with legal uncertainty.

Required Fix

Define three Space Type license tiers: (1) Open Source (MIT/Apache-2.0): any builder can use, modify, fork, and redistribute the Space Type config. (2) Commercial: builders pay a one-time or subscription fee; licensee cannot redistribute the Space Type config. (3) Proprietary + Closed: config is obfuscated server-side (never delivered to builder's browser); only the resulting product is usable. Enforce license terms at the API level: SpaceTypeDO tracks license type and rejects unauthorized forks. Include license terms in the marketplace listing and require builder acceptance before install.

G-AK13 MEDIUM Space Type Marketplace — Community

No Space Type Forking or Community Derivation Mechanics

The Gap

The marketplace has no forking mechanism. A developer who wants to extend an existing open-source Space Type must copy-paste the configuration manually, losing the link to the upstream template and forfeiting the ability to pull in future updates. There is no fork button, no upstream tracking, no pull-update workflow, and no attribution chain for derived templates.

Required Fix

Add a Fork action to open-source Space Types in the marketplace. Forking creates a new Space Type in the forker's account with: forked_from_id and forked_from_version recorded. The forked Space Type tracks upstream releases; the author receives a notification when the upstream publishes a new version and can choose to pull the diff. Attribution is shown in the marketplace: 'Forked from [Original] by [Author]'. Require attribution in the Space Type metadata for forks of MIT-licensed templates. Build a 'trending forks' leaderboard in the marketplace to surface high-quality derivations.

G-AK14 HIGH Space Type Marketplace — Content Policy

No DMCA Takedown Process for Space Types or Builder Products

The Gap

There is no mechanism for a copyright holder to submit a DMCA takedown notice for a Space Type or builder product that infringes their IP. No contact email, no web form, no defined response SLA, no counter-notice process. The platform has no legal safe harbor (DMCA Section 512) without a designated DMCA agent registered with the Copyright Office and an expeditious removal process. Operating without this exposes the platform to secondary copyright liability.

Required Fix

Implement a DMCA compliance program: (1) Register a DMCA designated agent with the US Copyright Office (required for 512 safe harbor). (2) Build a /dmca-notice form: complainant submits the work, infringing URL, good faith statement, contact info. (3) Receiving a valid DMCA notice triggers: (a) immediate takedown of the listed Space Type or product, (b) notification to the alleged infringer with the counter-notice option, (c) 10-business-day hold before restoration if counter-notice is received, (d) documentation for repeat-infringer termination policy. (4) Log all DMCA actions in the immutable audit trail.

G-AK15 HIGH Space Type Marketplace — Monetization

No Paid Space Type Monetization Rails — Creators Cannot Charge for Templates

The Gap

The marketplace lists Space Types but all are free. There is no mechanism for a Space Type author to set a price (one-time purchase, monthly subscription, or revenue share) and receive payment. Without monetization, high-quality template creators have no economic incentive to invest in the ecosystem. The platform's own revenue from the template marketplace is zero.

Required Fix

Extend Stripe Connect to include Space Type creators as connected accounts (same Connect infrastructure used for builder products). Creators set a price: free / one-time ($X) / monthly ($X/month). On install, the buyer's account is charged via Stripe; the platform takes a 30% commission; the creator receives 70% via Stripe Connect payout. Track all Space Type purchases in BillingDO with the template_id foreign key. Expose an Earnings tab in the creator's builder dashboard showing pending and paid earnings. Require connected account setup (identity verification) before any paid Space Type is listed.

G-AK16 MEDIUM Space Type Marketplace — Discovery

No Editorial Curation or Featured Placement for the Space Type Marketplace

The Gap

The marketplace uses only algorithmic ranking (install count, rating). There is no editorial curation, no 'Staff Picks' section, no themed collections (e.g., 'AI for Healthcare', 'E-commerce Templates'), and no ability for the platform team to feature high-quality newcomers. High-quality but new Space Types are invisible. Mediocre but established ones dominate due to install-count momentum.

Required Fix

Build a MarketplaceCurationDO that stores platform-team editorial decisions: featured_space_types, staff_picks, themed_collections. The marketplace homepage renders: (1) Hero banner: rotating staff picks (manually curated, updated weekly). (2) Themed collections: curated by product verticals (4–6 templates per collection). (3) Rising Stars: Space Types with high install velocity but low absolute count (algorithmic). The curation admin panel is a simple DO-backed CRUD UI accessible only to the platform:marketplace_curator role. Analytics: track CTR and conversion per placement type to optimize the curation strategy.

G-AK17 HIGH End-User UX — Session Security

End-Users Cannot View or Revoke Active Device Sessions Within a Space

The Gap

End-users of builder products have no visibility into their active sessions. If a device is lost or compromised, the end-user cannot revoke that device's session from another device. All sessions are invalidated only on password change or account deletion. There is no 'active sessions' page, no device name/IP display, no 'sign out everywhere' button, and no session revocation API.

Required Fix

Add an end-user Sessions page within each Space's user settings: list all active sessions with {device_type, browser, last_active, ip_country, session_id}. Expose a Revoke button for each session. Backend: sessions are stored as signed JWTs with a jti claim; maintain a revoked_jtis table in AssistantDO SQLite. On each request, check if the token's jti is in the revoked set (KV cache with 1-hour TTL, fallback to SQLite). Implement 'Sign out all other sessions' as a bulk revoke endpoint. Notify the user via email when a new session is created from an unrecognized device.

G-AK18 HIGH End-User UX — Subscription Self-Service

End-Users Cannot Self-Manage Their Subscriptions Within a Builder Space

The Gap

End-users who pay for a subscription within a builder product (e.g., a $29/month SaaS built on Naelao) cannot upgrade, downgrade, pause, or cancel their subscription without contacting the builder's support. There is no self-service subscription management UI, no plan comparison, no downgrade confirmation flow, and no immediate cancellation option. This violates consumer protection laws in multiple jurisdictions (e.g., California's ARL, the EU's subscription directive) and creates churn friction.

Required Fix

Build a Subscription Self-Service portal as a pre-built UI component that builders can embed in their product's settings page. The portal shows: current plan, next billing date, invoices, and a Plan Management section. Actions available: Upgrade (immediate, prorated), Downgrade (effective next billing period), Pause (halt billing for up to 3 months), Cancel (effective end of current period with confirmation of feature loss). All actions call the platform's BillingWorker, which syncs the change to Stripe. The cancellation flow collects an optional reason (displayed in builder churn analytics).

G-AK19 HIGH End-User UX — Activation

Builder-Configurable End-User Onboarding Wizard Is Not a Platform Feature

The Gap

Every builder must build their own end-user onboarding from scratch. There is no platform-provided onboarding wizard framework — no way for a builder to define a sequence of guided steps (welcome, profile setup, feature tour, first action) that new end-users see upon joining their Space. This increases builder development time and reduces end-user activation rates (users who never complete onboarding churn 3–5x faster).

Required Fix

Build an OnboardingWizardDO as a platform component. Builders configure a wizard via a YAML spec: steps with type (message, form, action, checklist), content, required fields, and completion conditions. The wizard is shown to end-users whose onboarding_completed flag is false. Progress is persisted in AssistantDO SQLite (per-user, per-wizard). Builders can A/B test different wizard flows (random assignment, outcome tracked by activation metric). Expose a completion rate dashboard: % of users who complete each step. Pre-built templates: 'Welcome & Profile', 'Feature Discovery', 'First Chat'.

G-AK20 MEDIUM End-User UX — Notifications

End-Users Have No Granular Notification Preferences Within a Builder Space

The Gap

End-users of builder products receive all notifications (agent updates, billing alerts, new messages, feature announcements) with no control over what they receive or how. There is no per-notification-type preference toggle, no quiet hours per channel (email vs push vs in-app), and no 'unsubscribe from this type' link in emails. This leads to notification fatigue, unsubscribes, and spam complaints that damage the builder's email domain reputation.

Required Fix

Build a NotificationPreferencesDO per (space_id, user_id). Builders define notification types in their Space config: {id, label, default_channels, can_disable}. End-users see a Notifications settings page listing all notification types with toggle switches per channel (email, push, in-app). Preferences are checked before every notification dispatch: if the user has disabled email for 'weekly digest', that notification is skipped. Add an unsubscribe link in every email that deep-links to the preference for that specific notification type. One-click unsubscribe for GDPR Article 21 compliance.

G-AK21 HIGH End-User UX — Data Rights

End-Users Cannot Submit a Data Deletion Request Within a Space

The Gap

GDPR Article 17 grants end-users the right to request erasure of their personal data from a builder's product. However, end-users have no UI within a builder Space to submit this request, and builders have no platform-provided workflow for processing it. The erasure request lifecycle (receipt, acknowledgment, 30-day processing window, completion notification, proof of erasure) is entirely absent at the Space level.

Required Fix

Build a DataRightsPortal component: a standardized UI page (embeddable in builder product settings) where end-users can submit: data export requests (Article 20), erasure requests (Article 17), and rectification requests (Article 16). On submission, a DataRightsRequestDO record is created: {request_id, type, user_id, space_id, status, submitted_at, due_at (30 days)}. Builders see a Data Rights inbox in their dashboard. Erasure triggers the cascade delete pipeline for that user's data within the Space. Completion sends a confirmation email with a summary of what was deleted. Overdue requests (30 days) generate a compliance alert.

G-AK22 HIGH End-User UX — Billing Transparency

End-Users Have No Self-Service Billing Portal Within a Builder Space

The Gap

End-users paying subscriptions within a builder Space cannot view their invoice history, update their payment method, or request a receipt without contacting the builder's support. This creates unnecessary support burden for builders and frustrates end-users who need receipts for expense reporting. Most subscription SaaS products provide this as a basic feature.

Required Fix

Embed Stripe's Customer Portal (or a custom equivalent) within each Space's settings page for paying end-users. The portal shows: subscription status, next billing date, payment method (masked card), and paginated invoice history with PDF download links. End-users can update their payment method directly (redirect to Stripe-hosted update page). Builders optionally enable refund requests, which create a pending refund request in BillingDO for builder review. All portal actions are logged with the user_id, timestamp, and action type in the compliance audit trail.

G-AK23 HIGH End-User UX — Account Recovery

No Secure Account Recovery Flow for End-Users With Lost Credentials

The Gap

End-users of builder products who lose access (forgotten password, lost MFA device, locked out of email) have no documented platform-level recovery path. Password reset is referenced in the spec as an unauthenticated flow but with no token security guarantees: no expiry enforcement, no single-use constraint, and no MFA re-enrollment after recovery. A compromised account recovery flow is a primary attack vector for account takeover.

Required Fix

Implement a secure account recovery pipeline: (1) Forgot password: generate a cryptographically random 256-bit token, hash (SHA-256) and store in AssistantDO SQLite with a 15-minute expiry. Email a signed link. On use: verify token hash, check expiry, require new password meeting strength requirements, revoke ALL existing sessions via jti blacklist, mark token used (single-use). (2) MFA device loss: provide backup codes at MFA enrollment (8 codes, one-time use). (3) Email loss: allow recovery via a registered backup email or identity verification challenge (3-of-5 secret questions, not SMS). Log all recovery events to the audit trail.

G-AK24 MEDIUM End-User UX — First-Run Experience

Builder Products Launch Empty With No Default Guidance or Example Content

The Gap

When a builder creates a new Space and an end-user joins for the first time, the product is completely empty: no example conversations, no sample knowledge, no starter prompts, no guided action. Empty states are the highest-churn moment in SaaS products. Without example content, new users do not understand what the product does or what to type first.

Required Fix

Add a SeedContentDO component to the Space Type system: Space Type authors define default seed content that is injected into every new Space (or new user session) created from that template. Seed content includes: example conversations ('Try asking: What are my options for...'), a starter knowledge base document, a pinned welcome message from the 'agent', and a first-run checklist. Builders can customize or disable the seed content. Seed content is stored as a template in SpaceTypeDO and applied once at Space creation or at first-user-join via a flag in AssistantDO.

G-AK25 HIGH i18n / Localization — Builder Products

No Builder Product UI Localization Framework for Multi-Language Products

The Gap

Builders cannot configure their product UI to render in multiple languages. All UI strings (labels, button text, error messages, placeholder text) are hard-coded in the platform's single language (English). A builder targeting Spanish, German, or Japanese markets cannot translate their product's UI without building a custom frontend — which defeats the no-code purpose of the platform.

Required Fix

Build a LocalizationDO per Space: builders upload a translations.json file (or use the UI editor) mapping string keys to locale-specific values: {en: {welcome: 'Welcome'}, es: {welcome: 'Bienvenido'}, ja: {welcome: 'ようこそ'}}. The product UI loads the correct translation bundle based on the end-user's Accept-Language header (with builder-configured fallback). All platform-generated UI strings use translation keys stored in LocalizationDO. Expose a translation completion badge in the Space settings ('Spanish: 87% translated'). Provide an AI-assisted translation feature: 'Auto-translate to Spanish' uses CF Workers AI to generate a draft translation for review.

G-AK26 HIGH i18n / Localization — Layout

No RTL (Right-to-Left) Layout Support for Arabic, Hebrew, and Farsi Products

The Gap

The platform's product UI is built with LTR (left-to-right) CSS assumptions: flex-direction, text-align, margin-start/end, padding-start/end, and icon placement are all LTR-hardcoded. A builder creating a product for Arabic, Hebrew, or Farsi-speaking users will have a mirrored, visually broken UI. The chat interface, navigation sidebar, and form layouts require complete directional mirroring for RTL markets.

Required Fix

Implement RTL support using the CSS logical properties approach: replace all directional CSS properties (margin-left, padding-right, text-align: left, float: left) with logical equivalents (margin-inline-start, padding-inline-end, text-align: start). Add dir="rtl" to the HTML root element when the active locale is an RTL language (ar, he, fa, ur). Test with the Chrome forced-RTL DevTools flag. Add an RTL-specific component variant for the chat bubble layout (avatar right, text left → avatar left, text right in RTL). Store the locale's direction (ltr|rtl) in LocalizationDO and inject it into the HTML template.

G-AK27 HIGH i18n / Localization — Billing

Builder Products Support Only USD — No Multi-Currency Pricing or Billing

The Gap

The ProductPricingConfig schema has a currency field (ISO 4217) but all billing flows are implemented in USD only. A builder in Europe charging end-users in EUR, or in Japan charging in JPY, cannot issue EUR/JPY invoices, cannot display prices in the user's local currency, and cannot comply with local consumer protection laws requiring pricing in the consumer's currency. Stripe natively supports 135+ currencies; the limitation is entirely in the platform's implementation.

Required Fix

Extend BillingWorker to support multi-currency: (1) Builders configure prices per currency code in their subscription plan config. (2) On checkout, detect the end-user's country via CF-IPCountry and offer the matching currency price (if configured). (3) Stripe Checkout sessions include the currency parameter. (4) Invoices are issued in the transaction currency. (5) Platform revenue split is calculated in the transaction currency and converted to USD for the platform's Stripe account at settlement. (6) Analytics Engine tracks revenue per currency; the builder dashboard shows multi-currency revenue breakdown with USD equivalent.

G-AK28 MEDIUM i18n / Localization — Search

Semantic and Full-Text Search Are Not Locale-Aware

The Gap

Vectorize semantic search uses language-agnostic embeddings that mix results across languages. A user searching in Spanish retrieves English documents scored higher due to English-biased training data. Full-text search (SQLite FTS5) uses default tokenization with no language-specific stop words, stemming, or diacritic normalization. A French user searching 'echec' does not find 'échec'. A German search for 'suchen' does not match 'suchte' (past tense). This significantly degrades search quality for non-English users.

Required Fix

Add locale-aware search configuration to each knowledge base: {locale: 'fr', stemmer: 'porter', stopwords: [...], diacritics: 'normalize'}. For FTS5, configure the tokenizer per locale: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE docs USING fts5(content, tokenize='unicode61 remove_diacritics 1'). For Vectorize semantic search, use a multilingual embedding model (e.g., multilingual-e5-large) when the Space's locale is non-English. Add a language detection step to new document ingestion: detect language and tag the vector with a language metadata field. Filter search queries to prefer same-language results using the Vectorize filter parameter.

G-AK29 MEDIUM i18n / Localization — Content Formatting

Agent Response Strings Have No ICU Message Format or Plural Rule Support

The Gap

Agent response templates use simple string concatenation or basic template literals. They lack ICU Message Format support for complex plural rules, gender-based inflection, and ordinal formatting. A Russian product where the agent says '1 файл' vs '5 файлов' vs '11 файлов' (3 different plural forms) cannot express this correctly. Arabic has 6 plural forms. Polish has 4. Without ICU format, agent responses in inflected languages are grammatically incorrect.

Required Fix

Adopt the ICU Message Format standard for all platform-generated strings and expose it to builders for agent response templates. Strings are defined with ICU syntax: {count, plural, one {# item} other {# items}}. The platform's localization library (use messageformat or @formatjs/intl-messageformat) compiles ICU strings at build time for each locale. For agent-generated responses, add a postprocessing step that applies locale-specific ordinal and plural rules to any numeric substitution in the response template. Document the ICU subset supported and provide examples in the builder documentation.

G-AK30 HIGH i18n / Localization — Tax Compliance

No VAT / GST / Sales Tax Calculation Per Jurisdiction for Builder End-User Billing

The Gap

Builder products charge end-users directly (via the platform's billing infrastructure) but the billing system has no tax calculation. A builder charging a German end-user $29/month must add 19% German VAT and issue a VAT-compliant invoice. A US builder with nexus in California must charge sales tax. Without tax calculation, builders are liable for tax fraud and regulators can fine them per-transaction.

Required Fix

Integrate Stripe Tax (or TaxJar/Avalara) for automatic tax calculation: on checkout session creation, pass customer.address to Stripe Tax, which returns the applicable tax rate and amount. Include the tax amount in the Stripe PaymentIntent. Stripe Tax handles: EU VAT (with reverse-charge for B2B), UK GST, Canadian GST/PST, Australian GST, and US sales tax by state. Stripe issues tax-compliant invoices automatically. Builders configure their tax registration numbers in the Space billing settings (DE VAT ID, UK VRN, etc.). The platform stores tax ID per builder for EU OSS reporting.

G-AK31 HIGH i18n / Localization — Timezones

Cron Jobs and Time-Based Policies Are UTC-Only With No Timezone Support

The Gap

All scheduled jobs (CF Cron Triggers) use UTC-only cron expressions. Builder-configured scheduled workflows have no timezone field — a Japanese builder scheduling a daily report at '9:00am Tokyo time' must manually offset to UTC (00:00 UTC), and the offset shifts twice yearly for DST in other timezones. Wallet spending policies check UTC hours for 'business hours' enforcement, incorrectly blocking transactions for builders and end-users in non-UTC timezones.

Required Fix

Add a timezone field to all scheduler configurations: {cron: '0 9 * * *', timezone: 'Asia/Tokyo'}. Use the IANA timezone database (bundled as a WASM module in the Workers runtime via @js-temporal/polyfill or Temporal API) to convert cron expressions to UTC at schedule time. Re-convert at each trigger to account for DST transitions. For wallet spending policies: store allowedHours in the builder's configured timezone, convert to UTC at check time using the same IANA library. Expose a timezone picker in the Space settings UI (searchable IANA timezone selector).

G-AK32 MEDIUM i18n / Localization — Translation Workflow

No Translation Management Workflow for Builder Space Content

The Gap

Builders who want to translate their Space's knowledge base, agent prompts, and UI strings have no platform-provided workflow for managing translations. They cannot see which strings are untranslated, track translation progress, invite a translator collaborator, version translations alongside content updates, or validate translation completeness before enabling a new locale.

Required Fix

Build a TranslationWorkflowDO per Space: it tracks translation status per (string_key, locale) with states: missing, machine_draft, human_reviewed, approved. Expose a /translation-management panel in the builder dashboard: shows a table of all translatable strings with their translation status per configured locale. Builders can: (1) Click 'Auto-translate' to generate machine drafts for all missing strings via CF Workers AI. (2) Edit and approve individual translations inline. (3) Invite a Translator collaborator role that can edit translations but not change Space config. (4) Export/import translations as XLIFF 2.0 for professional translation agencies.

G-AK33 HIGH PCI DSS — Scope Definition

PCI DSS Scope Is Undefined — Platform May Unknowingly Be In SAQ D Scope

The Gap

The platform processes payments via Stripe but has never formally defined its PCI DSS scope. If any Naelao Worker logs request bodies containing card data, caches payment-related headers, or touches a raw card number at any point in the request lifecycle, the platform is in SAQ D scope (the most burdensome compliance level, requiring quarterly network scans, penetration testing, and 250+ controls). Without a formal scope assessment, the team cannot know their compliance obligations.

Required Fix

Commission a formal PCI DSS scoping exercise with a Qualified Security Assessor (QSA). Document the cardholder data flow: Stripe JS collects card data on the client; Stripe's servers tokenize it; only payment method IDs (pm_xxx) and Stripe webhooks (no card data in payload) reach Naelao infrastructure. This should qualify for SAQ A (simplest compliance level). Produce a PCI DSS Responsibility Matrix documenting which controls are Stripe's responsibility vs the platform's. Complete an annual SAQ A questionnaire and publish the Attestation of Compliance (AoC). Implement compensating controls: verified no-card-data logging in all workers.

G-AK34 CRITICAL PCI DSS — Card Data Handling

No Explicit Policy Preventing Card Data From Reaching Naelao Workers

The Gap

The spec integrates Stripe but never explicitly prohibits card data (PANs, CVVs, expiry dates) from being logged or processed by platform Workers. If a builder's custom checkout form passes card data through a Naelao API endpoint instead of directly to Stripe.js, card data would be logged in Workers Trace events, stored in KV, and potentially written to DO SQLite — none of which are PCI-compliant storage. This can happen accidentally without explicit technical controls.

Required Fix

Implement two layers of protection: (1) Technical: add a request body scanner in the payment-adjacent workers (BillingWorker, SpaceWorker) that detects Luhn-valid 13–19 digit strings (potential card numbers) and CVV patterns (3–4 digit strings adjacent to expiry patterns). If detected, log a critical security alert, strip the data from the request, and return 400. (2) Policy: document in the developer guidelines that all payment UIs must use Stripe.js Payment Element (no raw card fields); add a lint rule to the CI/CD pipeline that flags any HTML input type='text' or type='number' near payment-related keywords. Test with automated card-data injection tests in the security test suite.

G-AK35 HIGH PCI DSS — EU Payment Regulation

No SCA / PSD2 / 3D Secure 2 Compliance for European End-User Payments

The Gap

EU Payment Services Directive 2 (PSD2) requires Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) for online card payments over €30 in the EU. Builder products selling subscriptions to EU customers must implement 3D Secure 2 (3DS2) for the initial charge and for recurring charges above the €30 threshold. The spec has no mention of SCA, 3DS2, exemption logic, or the Stripe handling required. Non-compliant EU payments are declined by issuing banks at rates of 15–30%.

Required Fix

Configure Stripe to request SCA by default for EU customers: set payment_method_options.card.request_three_d_secure: 'automatic' on all EU PaymentIntents. For subscriptions: use Stripe's off-session authentication flow for recurring charges. Enable the following SCA exemptions where applicable: transaction risk analysis (TRA) for low-amount transactions, merchant-initiated transactions (MIT) exemption for subscription renewals. Add EU-specific payment flow: detect EU billing address → trigger SCA via Stripe PaymentElement with 3DS2 support → handle authentication challenges in the checkout UI. Test with Stripe's 3DS2 test cards.

G-AK36 HIGH PCI DSS — Audit Logging

No PCI Requirement 10 Audit Logging for Cardholder Data Environment Access

The Gap

PCI DSS Requirement 10 mandates logging all access to system components in the cardholder data environment (CDE): who accessed what, when, from where, and whether the action succeeded or failed. Even though the platform targets SAQ A scope (no card data stored), any Workers that handle Stripe webhooks, Stripe customer IDs, or billing API calls are technically in the CDE and require Requirement 10 compliant logging (retention for at least 12 months, with 3 months immediately available).

Required Fix

Add PCI-scoped audit logging to all Workers that process billing-related data (BillingWorker, SubscriptionWorker, any worker receiving Stripe webhooks). Log: timestamp (UTC, millisecond precision), worker_name, request_id, action (webhook_received, payment_intent_created, customer_created), outcome (success/failure), source IP, and Stripe event ID. Store logs in R2 with Object Lock (WORM), 12-month retention. Export to the SIEM integration nightly. Implement log integrity verification: HMAC-chain all billing log entries. Complete a quarterly log review procedure documented in the PCI compliance runbook.

G-AK37 MEDIUM PCI DSS — Fraud Prevention

No Stripe Radar Fraud Scoring for End-User Subscription Payments

The Gap

Subscription payments from end-users (both to builder products and to the platform) are processed without Stripe Radar fraud scoring rules. The platform accepts all payments where the card is valid, making it a target for card testing attacks (where fraudsters test stolen cards with small charges). Stripe Radar is included in Stripe's pricing but must be explicitly configured; the spec never mentions it.

Required Fix

Enable and configure Stripe Radar rules for all subscription-related PaymentIntents: (1) Block if card_country != billing_country AND amount > $50. (2) Review if IP country != card country AND first transaction from this email. (3) Block if card_fingerprint has had > 3 declines in past 24 hours. (4) Block all prepaid cards for subscription tiers. Configure Radar to require 3DS for any transaction Radar scores as elevated risk. Add a webhook listener for radar.early_fraud_warning events: when Radar detects a potential fraudulent charge, proactively refund and suspend the account pending review. Track fraud rates in the admin analytics dashboard.

G-AK38 MEDIUM PCI DSS — Testing

No Payment Security Testing in the CI/CD Pipeline

The Gap

The 700+ test suite covers functional correctness and some security cases, but no tests specifically validate PCI DSS controls or payment security properties: no test verifying that card data cannot pass through Workers, no test for Stripe webhook signature validation, no test for CSRF on payment endpoints, and no test for Stripe idempotency key handling. A regression in payment security controls is detectable only in production.

Required Fix

Add a payments-security test suite to the CI pipeline: (1) Card data detection: POST synthetic card numbers to all worker endpoints; assert none are stored in KV, SQLite, or logs. (2) Webhook signature: replay a Stripe webhook with an invalid signature; assert 400 rejection. (3) CSRF: POST to billing endpoints without the CSRF token; assert 403. (4) Idempotency: send duplicate Stripe events; assert idempotent processing (no double-charge). (5) Radar block: simulate a Radar-blocked PaymentIntent webhook; assert correct handling. Run this suite on every PR touching billing-related workers.

G-AK39 MEDIUM PCI DSS — Compliance Program

No Annual PCI SAQ Completion, Vulnerability Scanning, or Penetration Test Program

The Gap

PCI DSS compliance requires annual self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ), quarterly network scans by an Approved Scanning Vendor (ASV), and (for SAQ D) annual penetration testing. Even SAQ A requires an annual self-assessment. The platform has no documented compliance calendar, no ASV scanning contract, and no penetration test schedule. Without these, the platform cannot claim PCI DSS compliance and is exposed to fines from card brands.

Required Fix

Establish a PCI compliance program: (1) Annual: complete SAQ A questionnaire (or hire a QSA for SAQ D if scope expands). (2) Quarterly: run ASV network scans of all platform IP ranges (use an approved ASV like Qualys or Trustwave). (3) Annual: commission a Web Application Penetration Test focused on payment flows, Stripe webhook handling, and billing API endpoints. (4) Ongoing: maintain a PCI Compliance tracker tracking each required control with owner, status, and last-reviewed date. (5) Integrate scan results into the security backlog with priority SLAs: Critical findings fixed within 7 days, High within 30 days.

G-AK40 CRITICAL Platform Governance — Child Safety

No CSAM Detection or Mandatory NCMEC CyberTipline Reporting Pipeline

The Gap

The platform allows users to upload images to knowledge bases, share files in conversations, and run agents that generate images. There is no integration with PhotoDNA or a similar perceptual hash database to detect Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM) in uploaded or generated images. US federal law (18 U.S.C. § 2258A) requires electronic service providers with actual knowledge of CSAM to report it to NCMEC's CyberTipline within one business day or face felony charges.

Required Fix

Integrate Microsoft's PhotoDNA Cloud Service or an equivalent (Thorn/NCMEC hash database) for all image uploads and AI-generated images: before storing any image to R2, compute a perceptual hash and compare against the NCMEC hash database. On match: (1) Immediately block the upload/generation, (2) Preserve the evidence (do not delete), (3) Automatically file a CyberTipline report within 1 hour via NCMEC's API (not manual). (4) Suspend the uploading account. Log all scans and matches in a separate, highly restricted CSAM audit log accessible only to the Trust & Safety team. Test the pipeline quarterly with known test hashes provided by NCMEC.

G-AK41 HIGH Platform Governance — Terrorist Content

No GIFCT Terrorist Content Hash Database Integration

The Gap

The platform allows file uploads, image generation, and knowledge base content creation. There is no integration with the Global Internet Forum to Counter Terrorism (GIFCT) hash database, which catalogues known terrorist and violent extremist content. A user can upload terrorist propaganda documents or images that are indexed into the knowledge base and used to train or inform AI agents. This creates legal liability in multiple jurisdictions (EU Terrorist Content Regulation, UK Online Safety Act).

Required Fix

Apply for membership in GIFCT's Hash-Sharing Consortium (available to qualifying platforms). Integrate the GIFCT hash database into the content scanning pipeline: all document uploads are hashed (PDFs via pdfjs to extract images, text documents via SHA-256) and compared against the GIFCT database before storage. Matches trigger: (1) Block the upload, (2) Notify the Trust & Safety team, (3) File a report with GIFCT, (4) Preserve evidence. For text content, integrate with Jigsaw's Perspective API for violent extremism detection in agent outputs. Add EU TerCon (Terrorist Content Regulation) fast-removal compliance: 1-hour removal SLA for government referrals.

G-AK42 HIGH Platform Governance — EU AI Act

EU AI Act Article 13 Transparency Obligations for High-Risk AI Systems

The Gap

The EU AI Act (effective August 2026 for most provisions) requires that providers of high-risk AI systems (including AI assistants for education, employment, and financial services) provide clear technical documentation, maintain logs for at least 6 months, provide an instructions-for-use document to deployers, and register the system in the EU AI Act database. The platform has no compliance preparation for Article 13 or the high-risk system classification under Annex III.

Required Fix

Implement EU AI Act compliance infrastructure: (1) Classification review: assess each Space Type category (HR tools, education, healthcare) against Annex III high-risk criteria. (2) Technical documentation: for high-risk systems, generate a Technical File covering model architecture, training data, performance metrics, and risk mitigation measures. (3) Logs: maintain inference logs per high-risk deployment for 6 months. (4) Instructions for use: auto-generate an EU AI Act compliant Instructions for Use document for each high-risk Space Type and display it to builders before they deploy. (5) EU AI Act database registration: register high-risk systems via the EU's EUDAMED-equivalent AI database API once it launches.

G-AK43 HIGH Platform Governance — Account Lifecycle

Builder Account Suspension Has No Grace Period, Data Preservation, or Reactivation Flow

The Gap

When a builder account is suspended (payment failure, ToS violation, fraud flag), the spec does not define: how many days of warning before suspension, whether the builder can export their data during the grace period, how long data is retained before deletion, and how the builder can appeal or reactivate. In many jurisdictions (EU, UK, App Store guidelines), unilateral account termination without a defined process and adequate notice violates platform marketplace regulations.

Required Fix

Define a Builder Account Lifecycle policy: (1) Payment failure: 3-day grace with daily email warnings; at day 3, downgrade to read-only (no new users, no new messages). At day 14, suspend (data retained, no traffic served). At day 30, initiate deletion. (2) ToS violation: 24-hour notice before suspension (except for CSAM/illegal content = immediate). During notice period, builder can export data. (3) Data retention: suspended accounts retain data for 30 days. (4) Reactivation: a POST /account/reactivate endpoint that re-enables the account after payment or ToS acknowledgment. (5) Appeals: a written appeals process with a 10-business-day resolution SLA.

G-AK44 HIGH Platform Governance — Appeals

No Platform Appeals Process for Builders Disputing Content Removals or Suspensions

The Gap

When the platform removes a builder's Space Type, suspends their account, or restricts a feature, there is no formal appeals mechanism. The builder has no way to contest the decision, submit evidence, or escalate to a senior reviewer. The EU Digital Services Act (DSA) Article 20 mandates that online platforms provide an internal complaint-handling system for all content moderation decisions, including AI-assisted ones. Without this, the platform cannot legally operate as a 'very large online platform' (VLOP) under DSA.

Required Fix

Build an AppealsDO per suspension/removal decision: {appeal_id, builder_id, decision_type, decision_reason, submitted_at, appeal_text, evidence_urls[], status, reviewer_id, resolved_at, resolution}. Expose a /appeals/submit endpoint that builders can access even in a suspended state. Define SLAs: initial acknowledgment within 24 hours, substantive review within 10 business days. All review decisions are logged with the reviewer's ID and reasoning. Publish an appeals outcome statistics report quarterly (number of appeals, % overturned, average resolution time). For DSA compliance, provide an out-of-court dispute settlement option for EU-based builders.

G-AK45 HIGH Platform Governance — Moderation Operations

No Cross-Space Centralized Content Moderation Queue

The Gap

End-user reports of harmful content (flagged messages, inappropriate agent outputs, spam) are siloed per Space — there is no centralized moderation queue where the platform's Trust & Safety team can review reports across all Spaces. The platform operates blindly: it knows individual Spaces exist but has no aggregate view of what harmful content is being generated or reported across the entire platform. This makes it impossible to detect coordinated abuse campaigns.

Required Fix

Build a ModerationQueueDO that aggregates all end-user content reports across every Space. Each report includes: {report_id, space_id, reporter_id, content_type, content_id, content_preview, reason, submitted_at, status}. The Trust & Safety team has a moderation dashboard showing: unreviewed reports (sorted by severity and recency), reporter history, and cross-Space patterns (same content reported in multiple Spaces = coordinated abuse signal). Reviewers can: mark as reviewed, remove content, warn the builder, or escalate to suspension. Implement automated pre-prioritization: assign higher priority to reports involving minors, CSAM keywords, or financial fraud patterns.

G-AK46 HIGH Platform Governance — Law Enforcement

No Government / Law Enforcement Data Disclosure Process (MLAT, Court Orders)

The Gap

The platform has no documented procedure for responding to government requests for user data: court orders, subpoenas, search warrants, national security letters, or mutual legal assistance treaty (MLAT) requests. Without a defined process, platform staff may respond incorrectly (over-disclosing or under-disclosing data), and the platform cannot challenge overbroad requests. US providers operating internationally must comply with the CLOUD Act.

Required Fix

Establish a Legal Request policy: (1) All government requests must be submitted in writing via legal@naelao.com. (2) Verify requestor identity and legal authority before any disclosure. (3) Challenge overbroad or legally deficient requests in court where feasible. (4) Notify affected users before disclosing their data unless legally prohibited (e.g., NSL with gag order). (5) Log all requests, disclosures, and challenges in a restricted Legal Request Register. (6) Publish a bi-annual Transparency Report listing: number of requests by country, number complied with, number challenged, number of accounts disclosed. (7) Designate a legal counsel specializing in digital law as the point of contact.

G-AK47 HIGH Platform Governance — AI Spam

No Detection System for AI-Generated Content Spam Published via Agents

The Gap

Builder agents can generate and publish content (blog posts, marketplace listings, forum replies) at scale using CF Workflows. A malicious builder could use the platform as an industrial-scale spam generator: producing thousands of AI-written pages that are indexed by search engines, saturating other platforms' APIs via MCP tools, or filling the Naelao marketplace with low-quality template spam. There is no automated detection for AI-spam generation patterns.

Required Fix

Implement AI-spam detection at multiple layers: (1) Rate limits on content creation endpoints (already partially covered, but add per-Space daily content creation quotas: free: 100 items/day, pro: 1000/day). (2) Content fingerprinting: before indexing new content, compute a SimHash and compare against the platform-wide content fingerprint store. Near-duplicates (similarity > 90%) are blocked as duplicate spam. (3) Quality scoring: generated content is scored by a lightweight classifier for minimum quality signals (length, coherence, uniqueness). Score < threshold = rejected + queued for manual review. (4) Outbound MCP rate limits: cap total outbound MCP tool calls per Space per hour to prevent API abuse via external tools.

G-AK48 MEDIUM Platform Governance — User Reporting

No End-User Content Flagging Mechanism Within Builder Products

The Gap

End-users of builder products have no way to flag harmful, inappropriate, or AI-generated misleading content they encounter in a Space. There is no 'Report' button, no flag icon on messages, and no complaint pathway within the product UI. This means: (1) The platform cannot detect when a builder is generating harmful content (no signal). (2) Users who encounter harmful content have no recourse. (3) The platform cannot comply with EU DSA Article 16 (which requires user reporting mechanisms).

Required Fix

Add a Report Content component to the product UI: a discreet flag icon (⚑) on every agent message and on Space-level content. Clicking opens a modal: reason selection (harmful, misleading, offensive, spam, other) + optional text field. The report is submitted to ModerationQueueDO with a 1-second rate limit per user to prevent report flooding. On submission: confirm receipt to the user and give them an estimated review timeline. Track report-to-action time as a platform KPI. For EU DSA Article 16 compliance, provide a prominent 'Report illegal content' pathway with direct routing to law enforcement referral capability.

G-AK49 HIGH Platform Governance — Minor Protection

No Age Verification or COPPA / GDPR-K Compliance for Minor Users

The Gap

Builder products may attract users under 13 (COPPA jurisdiction) or under 16/18 (GDPR Article 8 child consent jurisdiction). The platform has no age verification mechanism, no parental consent flow, no child-safe content mode, and no differentiated data collection policy for minors. A builder targeting educational markets (school-age children) using Naelao as a backend is unknowingly violating COPPA (US), GDPR Article 8 (EU), and the UK AADC (Age Appropriate Design Code).

Required Fix

Add age gate controls: (1) Space-level settings: builders declare whether their product is restricted to 18+, 13+, or all ages.
