(2) For all-ages Spaces: during onboarding, collect date-of-birth (not just year — month+day required). Users under 13 (US) or under the GDPR consent age for their country are blocked from creating accounts and shown a parent/guardian consent flow. (3) For minor accounts: disable analytics tracking, disable cross-Space data sharing, apply enhanced content filtering. (4) COPPA compliance: no targeted advertising, no persistent identifiers, parental access right to view/delete child data. (5) GDPR-K: treat under-16 user data with heightened protection per Article 8.

G-AK50 MEDIUM Platform Governance — Transparency

No Platform Transparency Report or Public Content Policy Documentation

The Gap

The platform has no public-facing transparency report and no documented content policy. Users and builders do not know: what content is prohibited, how decisions are made, how many accounts were suspended, what government requests were received, or how AI moderation affects content. The EU Digital Services Act (Article 15) requires large platforms to publish annual transparency reports. Without these documents, the platform cannot be trusted by enterprise buyers or regulators.

Required Fix

Publish the following governance documents: (1) Community Standards / Acceptable Use Policy: what is and is not allowed on the platform, with specific examples. (2) Content Moderation Policy: how decisions are made, what human review looks like, what automated signals are used. (3) Privacy Policy: compliant with GDPR, CCPA, PIPEDA. (4) Law Enforcement Guidelines: what data the platform has, the process for requesting it, what the platform challenges. (5) Semi-annual Transparency Report: content removal counts, account suspensions, government requests, appeal outcomes, AI moderation metrics. Publish at trust.naelao.com. Build the Transparency Report as a data export from ModerationQueueDO and the Legal Request Register.

Appendix AL — Network Security, Container Supply Chain, Developer Portal, Analytics Pipeline, IaC/DevOps & Database Scaling Gaps

50 gaps · G-AL01 – G-AL50 · zero-trust network, container runtime, DX infrastructure, analytics depth & SQLite scaling

G-AL01 HIGH Network Security — CF Access

CF Access JWT Is Not Session-Bound — Stolen Token Valid Across Any Context

The Gap

The naelao-admin Worker gates routes using the Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion header. CF Access JWTs are validated for expiry and signature but are not bound to the original device fingerprint, source IP, or WebSocket session. A JWT stolen from one context (e.g., intercepted from a compromised machine) can be replayed from any other context until it expires. There is no secondary session binding or device attestation check.

Required Fix

Add CF Access service token + application token binding: require a device-pinned client certificate (CF Access mTLS) for admin Worker access. Generate short-lived Access tokens (15-minute expiry) instead of the default 24-hour tokens. Implement session binding in the admin Worker: on first use of a JWT, record the source CF-Connecting-IP; subsequent requests with the same JWT from a different IP get challenged with a Turnstile re-authentication. Add anomaly detection: alert if the same JWT is used from 2+ distinct IP prefixes within a 5-minute window.

G-AL02 MEDIUM Network Security — Service Bindings

Service Binding Internal Calls Have No Mutual TLS or Listener Hostname Verification

The Gap

Cloudflare Service Bindings transmit requests over CF's internal fabric with automatic TLS. However, the receiving Worker has no way to verify that the caller is the expected upstream Worker (only CF guarantees this at the infrastructure level). There is no application-layer authentication between workers, no per-caller service token (the spec notes NAELAO_INTERNAL_TOKEN is a single static shared secret), and no request signing that would prevent a compromised Worker from impersonating another.

Required Fix

Replace the static NAELAO_INTERNAL_TOKEN with per-caller short-lived service JWTs: each Worker possesses its own ECDSA private key (stored as a Worker Secret). Before calling a downstream Worker via Service Binding, it signs a JWT: {iss: 'naelao-agents', aud: 'naelao-billing', iat, exp: now+60, jti}. The downstream Worker verifies the JWT's issuer matches the expected caller, the audience matches its own identity, and the jti has not been replayed (KV-backed nonce store, TTL = exp). This provides cryptographic caller authentication at the application layer, independent of CF's infrastructure guarantees.

G-AL03 CRITICAL Network Security — WebSocket Security

WebSocket Origin Validation Uses Weak Allowlist Logic — Subdomain Spoofing Bypass

The Gap

WebSocket upgrade requests are validated against an origin allowlist. The check uses string matching that is inconsistent between the router and the DO implementations: one uses .includes() on the full origin string; another uses .endsWith() on the hostname. An attacker can craft origins like https://evil.naelao.com (passes endsWith check for 'naelao.com') or https://naelao.com.evil.com (passes includes check for 'naelao.com') depending on which code path handles the request. This enables WebSocket hijacking and auth token theft.

Required Fix

Standardize origin validation across ALL workers using a single shared utility function: validateOrigin(origin: string, allowedHosts: string[]): boolean. The function: (1) Parses the origin URL using the URL constructor (never string manipulation). (2) Extracts the hostname. (3) Compares hostname === allowedHost (exact match only) OR hostname.endsWith('.'+allowedHost) (subdomain, with leading dot to prevent bypass). (4) Verifies the protocol is https (never http). Add a unit test matrix covering all known bypass patterns: evil.naelao.com, naelao.com.evil.com, naelao.com@evil.com. Run this test on every PR.

G-AL04 HIGH Network Security — Admin Access

No Cloudflare Tunnel for Admin Worker — Internal Admin Endpoints May Be Internet-Exposed

The Gap

The naelao-admin Worker is deployed as a public CF Worker accessible at its worker.dev subdomain or a custom domain. Admin endpoints (user suspension, billing overrides, content moderation actions) are protected only by CF Access JWT validation. A misconfiguration of CF Access rules (which has happened on real platforms) would expose the admin panel to the public internet. There is no secondary network-layer protection (private routing, VPN requirement, IP allowlist).

Required Fix

Move admin Worker behind CF Access with additional network controls: (1) Deploy the admin Worker to a private CF Zone with IP allowlist restricted to the ops team's known IP ranges and VPN exit nodes. (2) Use CF Access policies requiring both: a valid Access JWT AND an mTLS client certificate (issued to ops team members via CF Access certificate authority). (3) Consider deploying a CF Tunnel to route admin traffic exclusively over the CF Tunnel network, making the admin origin unreachable from the public internet even if CF Access is misconfigured. (4) Add a CF WAF rule: block all requests to /admin/* that do not have the CF-Access-Authenticated-User-Email header set.

G-AL05 HIGH Network Security — WebSocket Security

No DNS Rebinding Attack Prevention on WebSocket Upgrade Requests

The Gap

WebSocket connections from browser clients are vulnerable to DNS rebinding if the WebSocket server validates only the Origin header and not the Host header. An attacker who controls a domain with a short-lived DNS TTL can rebind DNS to point to the SpaceDO's IP, then use a victim's browser to establish WebSocket connections that bypass the same-origin policy. The spec validates Origin but does not cross-check Origin against the Host header.

Required Fix

Add Host header validation to the WebSocket upgrade handler in SpaceWorker and all DO WebSocket accept paths: assert that request.headers.get('Host') matches the platform's allowed hostname list (same list as the origin allowlist). Additionally: set X-Frame-Options: DENY and Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin to prevent framing attacks that enable DNS rebinding exploitation. Add a Connection: Upgrade, Keep-Alive header validation that rejects requests where Connection does not explicitly include 'Upgrade'. These are low-cost defensive headers that eliminate the DNS rebinding surface.

G-AL06 HIGH Network Security — HTTP Security

HTTP Request Smuggling via Proxy Path Normalization Between CF Edge and Workers

The Gap

The CF edge normalizes HTTP/1.1 request headers before forwarding to Workers. If a Worker parses the raw request path or headers independently (e.g., for authentication decisions) without relying solely on CF's normalized representation, path normalization discrepancies can lead to request smuggling: authentication checks pass on the normalized path while the downstream Worker processes the original unnormalized path. This class of vulnerability has been found in CF Workers deployments.

Required Fix

Audit all Workers for any code that directly accesses request.url or request.headers without using the CF-provided normalized URL object. Replace any raw header parsing with: const url = new URL(request.url); and use url.pathname (CF-normalized) for routing and auth decisions. Add a CI lint rule: flag any direct string operations on request.url that bypass URL parsing. Test with path normalization attack vectors: double-slashes (//admin), encoded slashes (%2F), null bytes (%00), and Unicode normalization variants. Add a CF WAF Managed Rule for HTTP Request Smuggling detection.

G-AL07 MEDIUM Network Security — Outbound Security

No Certificate Pinning for Outbound HTTPS from Workers to External APIs

The Gap

Workers make outbound HTTPS calls to Together AI, Stripe, WorkOS, Resend, Turso, and other external APIs. These calls rely entirely on the default TLS verification (certificate chain to trusted CA). A compromised or fraudulently-issued certificate (supply chain attack, CA compromise, BGP hijack) could allow an attacker to intercept API credentials and request/response bodies. Certificate Transparency (CT) logs provide passive detection but no active prevention.

Required Fix

Implement certificate transparency monitoring: subscribe to CT log notifications for the certificate domains of all critical external dependencies (stripe.com, workos.com, together.ai). Alert immediately if a new certificate for these domains is issued that was not expected. For the highest-risk calls (Stripe, credential providers): add a fetch wrapper that extracts the certificate's Subject Public Key Info (SPKI) hash from the TLS connection info (available via CF's TLS metadata) and compares it against a pinned expected hash. On mismatch: block the call and alert. Rotate the pinned hash as part of the scheduled certificate renewal process.

G-AL08 HIGH Network Security — Container Egress

Container Network Policy Declared in Manifest But Runtime Enforcement Is Undefined

The Gap

The Container marketplace manifest supports allowEgress and blockAll network policy fields. However, the spec never documents how these policies are enforced at runtime — whether CF Containers implements a network namespace filter, whether the policy is declarative-only (not enforced), or whether a container that ignores its manifest policy is blocked. Containers currently have access to internal CF infrastructure (169.254.x.x link-local, internal CF APIs) with no documented block.

Required Fix

Require explicit network policy in every container manifest: no egress allowed by default (zero-trust default-deny). Containers that need outbound network access must enumerate permitted hosts in the manifest's allowEgress list. CF Containers (or the SandboxManagerDO layer) enforces this list by intercepting network system calls via LD_PRELOAD or seccomp bpf hooks. Block all RFC-1918 (10.x, 172.16.x, 192.168.x) and link-local (169.254.x.x, fe80::) addresses at the container network namespace level regardless of manifest declarations. Add a network policy compliance test in the container review pipeline.

G-AL09 MEDIUM Network Security — Webhook Ingress

No Source IP Allowlisting for Inbound Webhooks From External Services

The Gap

Webhooks from Stripe, GitHub, and WorkOS are accepted from any IP address. The only validation is HMAC signature verification. If HMAC validation has a bug (timing attack, hash collision edge case, format mismatch) or a secret is leaked, an attacker can forge webhooks from any IP. Several external services (Stripe, GitHub) publish static IP ranges for their webhook sources; not validating source IP adds an unnecessary attack surface.

Required Fix

Add source IP allowlisting as a defense-in-depth layer for webhook ingress: (1) Maintain an IP allowlist for each webhook source in KV (refreshed daily from official published lists: Stripe publishes its webhook IPs, GitHub publishes its hook IPs via the meta API). (2) The webhook handler checks CF-Connecting-IP against the allowlist BEFORE computing the HMAC (fail fast, reduce attack surface). (3) For sources without published IP ranges (custom MCP webhooks), require HMAC-SHA256 validation with a 300-second timestamp skew tolerance. (4) Log all webhook deliveries with source IP for anomaly detection.

G-AL10 CRITICAL Container Security — Supply Chain

No Container Image Signing or Provenance Verification Before Execution

The Gap

Builder-submitted container images undergo a claimed review process before marketplace listing, but there is no cryptographic signing of approved images. After an image passes review and is listed, there is nothing preventing a compromised container registry, a rogue platform employee, or a supply chain attack from silently replacing the approved image with a malicious one. When a builder deploys a 'verified' container, the platform cannot verify it is the same image that was reviewed.

Required Fix

Implement container image signing using Cosign (part of the Sigstore project): (1) After a container image passes the review pipeline, the review worker signs the image manifest using the platform's Cosign private key and writes the signature to the OCI registry. (2) The SandboxManagerDO verifies the Cosign signature before starting any container: cosign verify --key platform-public-key.pem registry/image:digest. (3) Reject any container start whose signature verification fails. (4) Publish the platform's Cosign public key at /.well-known/cosign-public-key.json for transparency. This ensures a cryptographic chain of custody from review → deployment.

G-AL11 CRITICAL Container Security — Vulnerability Scanning

Container Marketplace Approval Claims Scanning But No Scanner Technology Is Specified

The Gap

The spec states that marketplace container images undergo 'image scanning' during the review process but never specifies: which scanner is used (Trivy, Grype, Snyk, Clair), which CVE database is referenced, what severity threshold blocks approval (all Critical CVEs? CVSS > 7?), how often images are re-scanned after initial approval (new CVEs are discovered after approval), and who reviews scanner output. The 'scanning' is likely a placeholder claim with no implementation.

Required Fix

Implement a concrete container scanning pipeline: (1) On submission: run Grype against the image (free, fast, SBOM-native) and Trivy for OS-level CVEs. (2) Block approval for any image with: CVSS 9.0+ CVEs (Critical), CVSS 7.0+ CVEs with public exploits available. (3) Generate an SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) using Syft in SPDX format and store it in R2 alongside the image manifest. (4) Re-scan all published images weekly against updated CVE databases. (5) On a new Critical CVE: notify the image author and give 14 days to publish a fixed version; after 14 days, automatically unlist the affected image. Track re-scan status in ContainerRegistryDO.

G-AL12 HIGH Container Security — Runtime Security

No seccomp or AppArmor Syscall Filtering for Container Runtime

The Gap

CF Containers run builder images with no documented syscall filtering. Containers have access to the full Linux syscall surface available in the CF Containers platform. Unnecessary syscalls (ptrace, mount, setuid, kexec_load, perf_event_open, iopl) significantly expand the kernel attack surface. A container escape exploit that requires one of these syscalls would succeed where a seccomp-filtered container would block it.

Required Fix

Apply a strict seccomp profile to all containers in the platform's default container start configuration. Use the Docker default seccomp profile as a baseline (blocks ~48 dangerous syscalls) and additionally block: ptrace (prevents container-to-container debugging), perf_event_open (side-channel attacks), kexec_load (kernel replacement), iopl/ioperm (direct hardware I/O). For AppArmor: apply the docker-default AppArmor profile. When CF Containers exposes seccomp configuration, set it via the container manifest. Until then, implement a seccomp-enforce wrapper inside the container entrypoint using libseccomp. Maintain the profile in version control and update it with each CF Containers platform upgrade.

G-AL13 HIGH Container Security — Privilege Management

Builder Containers Run as Root — No Rootless Execution Policy

The Gap

Container images submitted by builders run their processes as root (UID 0) by default unless the Dockerfile explicitly sets USER to a non-root user. A container running as root that achieves a container escape lands with root privileges on the host. The platform has no policy requiring non-root execution, no UID validation during the review process, and no runtime enforcement of non-privileged execution.

Required Fix

Enforce rootless execution in the container review pipeline: (1) Parse the submitted Dockerfile and reject any image that does not have a USER directive setting a non-root UID (e.g., USER 65534 or USER nobody). (2) In the container start configuration, set user: '65534:65534' (nobody:nogroup) to override any Dockerfile USER directive. (3) Mount the /workspace R2 directory with UID 65534 ownership so the container can still write. (4) Add a container review checklist item: 'Dockerfile USER directive sets non-root UID'. Publish builder documentation explaining why non-root execution is required and providing Dockerfile templates that comply.

G-AL14 HIGH Container Security — Network Isolation

No Enforced Container-to-Container Network Isolation

The Gap

Builder containers running in the same CF region can potentially reach each other via internal network paths if they share an IP subnet. The spec has no documentation of whether CF Containers provides network namespace isolation between different builders' containers. If network namespaces are shared or if containers can reach each other's bound ports, a compromised builder container could scan and attack neighbor containers — a cross-tenant data breach via network.

Required Fix

Document and verify CF Containers' multi-tenancy network isolation guarantees. Until CF publishes explicit network isolation SLAs for their container product: (1) Configure each container to listen only on localhost (127.0.0.1) for any internal services (Redis, PostgreSQL, local HTTP servers). The only externally reachable port is the one CF Containers routes inbound traffic through. (2) Add a network isolation test to the container review process: the reviewer starts the container and verifies it does not bind any ports that are externally reachable other than the declared port. (3) Document the expected CF Containers multi-tenant network isolation model in the platform security whitepaper.

G-AL15 HIGH Container Security — Filesystem Security

No Read-Only Root Filesystem Enforcement — Containers Can Write Anywhere

The Gap

Builder containers can write to any path on the container filesystem: system directories (/etc, /bin, /usr), shared library paths, and configuration files. A malicious container could overwrite system binaries to persist across container restarts, or write to paths that are inadvertently read by the container runtime. The only documented writable paths are /workspace (R2-mounted) and /tmp.

Required Fix

Add a read-only root filesystem requirement to the container manifest: readOnlyRootFilesystem: true. This is a standard container security option (equivalent to Docker --read-only flag) that mounts the container's root filesystem as read-only, allowing writes only to explicitly declared writable volumes. The only writable mounts should be: /workspace (R2 FUSE), /tmp (tmpfs, size-limited to 512MB), and any explicitly declared data directories. Containers that need writable config files should use /tmp during startup and copy files to /workspace for persistence. Add read-only filesystem enforcement as a mandatory requirement in the container review checklist.

G-AL16 HIGH Container Security — Resource Limits

No Container Image Size Limit — Unbounded Registry Storage Consumption

The Gap

The container registry accepts images of any size. A builder can push a 20GB+ container image (e.g., by including large model files, datasets, or unnecessary OS layers). This wastes registry storage (R2 costs), slows deployment (startup time scales with image size), and can be used to consume platform resources. There is no documented maximum image size, no layer deduplication accounting, and no size gate in the review pipeline.

Required Fix

Add image size limits enforced at the registry push API level: maximum total uncompressed image size = 2GB (adjustable per tier: pro: 5GB, enterprise: 20GB). Check the size during the OCI manifest submission: parse the layers from the manifest and sum Content-Length values. Reject pushes that exceed the limit with a clear error message. In the review pipeline, add a size check as the first gate (before running the vulnerability scanner) to fail fast on oversized images. Display current image size and a size history in the Container Marketplace creator dashboard. Encourage best practices: publish layer-optimization guidelines (multi-stage builds, minimal base images).

G-AL17 HIGH Container Security — Secrets Management

Secrets Injection Into Containers Exposes Credentials in Environment Variables

The Gap

The spec shows no documented mechanism for injecting API keys and credentials into running containers. The only option available is environment variables in the container manifest or the Workers secret store. Environment variables are visible in: the process list (/proc/PID/environ), child process inheritance, crash dumps, and any diagnostic output. If a container logs its environment (a common mistake), all secrets are exfiltrated.

Required Fix

Replace environment variable secret injection with a secrets-as-files pattern: (1) Store container secrets in the CF Secrets Store (or equivalent KV-based secrets namespace). (2) At container start, the SandboxManagerDO fetches the secrets via RPC, writes them to a tmpfs volume at /run/secrets/ (chmod 400, owned by container user). (3) Container processes read secrets from files (not env vars). (4) The tmpfs volume is destroyed when the container exits. Additionally: set HISTFILE=/dev/null in the container environment to prevent secrets from being written to shell history. Block the /proc/PID/environ read path via seccomp. Document this pattern in builder guidelines.

G-AL18 HIGH Container Security — Runtime Monitoring

No Container Escape or Breakout Monitoring — No eBPF or Kernel Tracing

The Gap

CF Containers provides process isolation but there is no platform-level monitoring for container escape attempts. Known container escape techniques (mounting the host filesystem, namespace unsharing, cgroups breakout, overlay filesystem exploits) generate distinctive kernel event patterns that eBPF-based tools (Falco, Tetragon) can detect. Without runtime monitoring, a successful container escape goes undetected until the attacker does something visible.

Required Fix

Integrate Falco (CNCF graduated project) or Tetragon with the CF Containers runtime layer: deploy Falco as a DaemonSet equivalent on the container host fleet. Configure Falco rules for the highest-priority escape signals: (1) Write to /etc, /bin, /sbin, /lib, /usr from a container process. (2) Execution of ptrace or /proc/*/mem access. (3) Namespace unsharing system calls. (4) Mount system calls from a container process. On rule trigger: terminate the container immediately, flag the builder account for review, emit a CRITICAL alert to PagerDuty, and preserve the container's filesystem snapshot for forensic analysis. Until Falco integration is available, add seccomp rules that block the most dangerous syscalls.

G-AL19 MEDIUM Developer Experience — API Documentation

No Interactive API Documentation — Builders Cannot Try API Calls from Docs

The Gap

The platform API is documented in prose format only. There is no interactive documentation interface (Swagger UI, Scalar, Redoc, or similar) where builders and developers can: browse all endpoints with parameter descriptions, execute test API calls with their own API key, see example request/response payloads, and understand authentication requirements with working examples. This significantly slows down developer onboarding and increases support volume.

Required Fix

Generate an OpenAPI 3.1 spec from the platform's existing routes (this work starts with G-AJ13 — OpenAPI schema generation). Publish an interactive documentation site at developers.naelao.com using Scalar (modern, open-source, supports OpenAPI 3.1). Enable authenticated API calls directly from the docs: builders enter their API key in the docs UI and can execute live calls against their own Spaces. Add 'code snippet' generation for each endpoint in TypeScript, Python, and cURL. Include webhook event schemas in the docs as well, using AsyncAPI 3.0 for event-driven documentation. Deploy the docs as a CF Pages site; auto-update on each API schema change via CI/CD.

G-AL20 HIGH Developer Experience — API Lifecycle

No API Deprecation Notice or Migration Warning System

The Gap

When the platform needs to deprecate an API endpoint (remove a field, change behavior, delete a route), there is no notification mechanism for builders who are actively using it. Breaking changes ship silently and builders discover them via runtime errors. The spec documents status fields (deprecated/suspended) but provides no way to proactively notify affected API consumers, no sunset date header, and no grace period policy.

Required Fix

Implement API deprecation governance: (1) All endpoint deprecations require a minimum 90-day notice period. (2) Add Deprecation and Sunset HTTP response headers to deprecated endpoints: Deprecation: Sat, 01 Nov 2026 00:00:00 GMT, Sunset: Sat, 01 Feb 2027 00:00:00 GMT (per RFC 8594). (3) Log all calls to deprecated endpoints in Analytics Engine; identify builders using deprecated endpoints. (4) 60 days before sunset: email all builders using the deprecated endpoint with the migration guide. (5) At sunset: return 410 Gone with a body explaining the replacement. (6) Maintain a public API deprecation schedule at developers.naelao.com/changelog/deprecations.

G-AL21 MEDIUM Developer Experience — SDK

No Automatic SDK Generation from OpenAPI Spec for TypeScript, Python, and Go

The Gap

The platform has a TypeScript SDK maintained manually. There are no Python or Go SDKs despite Python being the dominant language for AI tooling and Go being common for infrastructure automation. Manually maintained SDKs diverge from the actual API over time (missing new endpoints, incorrect types). There is no automated generation pipeline.

Required Fix

Add a SDK generation step to the CI/CD pipeline: on each API schema change, run openapi-typescript for the TypeScript SDK, openapi-generator (Python client template) for the Python SDK, and oapi-codegen for Go. Publish generated SDKs to npm (@naelao/sdk), PyPI (naelao), and pkg.go.dev (github.com/naelao/sdk-go) via an automated release pipeline triggered by version tags. The SDK packages include: fully typed request/response models, authentication helper, retry logic with exponential backoff, and streaming support. Maintain human-authored wrappers (high-level helpers) as a thin layer on top of the generated client — only the generated parts are auto-replaced on each API update.

G-AL22 HIGH Developer Experience — API Lifecycle

No Developer Changelog With Breaking Change Classification

The Gap

API changes ship with no structured changelog entry, no breaking vs non-breaking classification, no migration guide, and no version tag. Builders who track platform changes do so via trial and error or by watching GitHub commits. There is no email subscription for API changes and no RSS feed. Enterprise builders require a documented change history for compliance audits.

Required Fix

Build a developer changelog system: each PR that changes any Worker route, request/response schema, or auth behavior requires a CHANGELOG.md entry in a structured format: {date, type: 'breaking'|'feature'|'fix'|'deprecation', component, summary, migration_guide_url}. A CI check enforces this for all API-touching PRs. The changelog is published at developers.naelao.com/changelog with filtering by type and component. Email subscription: builders can subscribe to receive weekly digests of changes (all) or immediate alerts for breaking changes only. RSS/Atom feed available for integration with developer tools (Slack, Teams, Linear).

G-AL23 MEDIUM Developer Experience — Error Handling

API Error Responses Are Not Standardized — No RFC 7807 Problem Details

The Gap

API error responses vary in format across workers: some return {error: 'message'}, others return {success: false, message: 'text'}, others return plain text. There is no consistent error schema. Builders writing error handling code must handle multiple formats. Machine-readable error codes (beyond HTTP status codes) are absent, making it impossible to programmatically distinguish 'rate limit exceeded' from 'invalid parameter' within the same 400 status code.

Required Fix

Adopt RFC 7807 Problem Details (application/problem+json) as the universal error response format across all platform workers. Every error response returns: {type: 'https://developers.naelao.com/errors/rate-limit-exceeded', title: 'Rate Limit Exceeded', status: 429, detail: 'Exceeded 60 requests per minute for this Space', instance: '/spaces/abc123/agents/def456', extensions: {retry_after: 1234567890}}. Define a catalog of machine-readable error types at developers.naelao.com/errors (each type has a stable URL with documentation). Add a Content-Type: application/problem+json header to all error responses. Create a shared errorResponse() utility function used by all workers.

G-AL24 HIGH Developer Experience — Observability

No X-Request-ID Correlation Header Returned by Workers

The Gap

Workers do not return a consistent X-Request-ID or CF-Ray correlation header on all responses. When a builder's integration breaks and they contact support, neither party can correlate the failed request to a specific log entry without knowing the exact timestamp and endpoint. CF Workers automatically set CF-Ray, but this is not consistently surfaced in API responses, and there is no application-level request trace ID that ties together a multi-worker request chain.

Required Fix

Add X-Request-ID to all worker responses: on each request, generate or extract a request ID (use CF-Ray if available, else generate a ULID). Propagate this ID as X-Request-ID through all Service Binding calls (add it to every internal request header). Return it in every response (success and error). Include the request ID in all log entries and Analytics Engine events. Builder SDK: automatically capture and log X-Request-ID for every API call. Support team dashboard: allow searching logs by X-Request-ID to instantly reconstruct the full request chain. Add X-Request-ID to all error response bodies as the instance field in RFC 7807 Problem Details.

G-AL25 MEDIUM Developer Experience — Webhooks

No Webhook Test Delivery Tool in Builder Dashboard

The Gap

Builders configuring webhooks for their Space have no way to test whether their endpoint is reachable and correctly handling payloads without triggering a real event. Testing requires manually creating a real conversation, invoice, or agent trigger in production. This slows down webhook integration development and leads to misconfigured production webhooks that silently fail.

Required Fix

Add a Webhook Test Delivery feature to the builder dashboard: for each configured webhook endpoint, a 'Send Test' button dispatches a synthetic payload of the selected event type (e.g., conversation.started, agent.completed, invoice.paid) to the configured URL. The test request includes a Test-Delivery: true header and a randomly-generated event_id. The dashboard shows: HTTP response code, response body, response time, and any error. Store the last 50 test deliveries per webhook endpoint with replay capability. Add a webhook logs section showing all recent deliveries (test and real) with status, duration, and response preview. Builders can replay any failed delivery with a single click.

G-AL26 HIGH Developer Experience — Local Development

No Multi-Worker Local Development Emulator — Service Bindings Don't Resolve Locally

The Gap

wrangler dev runs a single Worker in isolation. Service Bindings between Workers (naelao-router → naelao-agents → naelao-billing, etc.) are not resolved locally: the binding stubs either error or fall back to the production Worker, making realistic local testing impossible without hitting production. A developer working on naelao-agents cannot test the full request path without deploying to a staging environment.

Required Fix

Build a local development orchestrator: a naelao-dev CLI command that reads the monorepo's worker dependency graph from the Turborepo config and starts all workers in the correct dependency order using wrangler dev with --local flag. Service Binding stubs between locally-running workers are resolved via localhost port mapping (worker A on :8787, worker B on :8788 — Service Binding from A to B rewrites to localhost:8788). Add a naelao dev proxy that routes requests to the correct local port based on the target worker name. Include a local KV, R2, and Queue emulator via wrangler's built-in miniflare. Document the complete local dev setup in a CONTRIBUTING.md guide.

G-AL27 HIGH Analytics — Conversion Tracking

No Funnel or Conversion Analysis for Builder Products

The Gap

The builder analytics dashboard shows DAU, MAU, and credit usage but has no funnel analysis capability. A builder who wants to understand 'What % of users who start a conversation complete a purchase?' or 'Where do users drop off in the onboarding flow?' has no tools to answer these questions. Funnel analysis is the most fundamental product analytics capability — its absence means builders cannot systematically improve their product's conversion.

Required Fix

Integrate a funnel analysis backend: extend the Analytics Engine event schema to support funnel steps. Builders define funnels in a YAML config: [{step: 1, event: 'session_started'}, {step: 2, event: 'message_sent'}, {step: 3, event: 'subscription_created'}]. The platform queries Analytics Engine for the user_id cohort at each step and computes drop-off rates. Render the funnel as a visual bar chart in the builder dashboard. For complex funnels requiring SQL JOINs across multiple event types, route the query to Turso (where the Space's SQLite is migrated) instead of Analytics Engine. Expose a /analytics/funnel API endpoint for builders who want to query funnel data programmatically.

G-AL28 HIGH Analytics — Retention

No Cohort or Retention Analysis — Builder Cannot See User Retention Over Time

The Gap

Builders have no way to see whether end-users return to their product week-over-week. There is no cohort analysis, no D7/D30 retention chart, no weekly active user retention heatmap, and no comparison of retention across signup cohorts. This is critical product data: without retention metrics, a builder cannot know if their product has product-market fit or if users are churning after first use.

Required Fix

Build a retention analysis module in the analytics pipeline: (1) Group users by signup week/month (cohort). (2) For each cohort, compute what % of users returned in week 1, week 2, week 3, etc. (3) Render as a retention heatmap table in the builder dashboard (rows = cohort, columns = week, cell = retention %). The calculation uses Analytics Engine event queries: for each (cohort, week_offset), count(distinct user_id where event='session_started'). Cap the query window at 12 weeks to avoid over-expensive Analytics Engine scans. Run the cohort computation as a nightly aggregation job (not real-time) and cache results in SpaceDO SQLite. Display alongside a simple D7/D30 retention summary number.

G-AL29 HIGH Analytics — Experimentation

No Builder-Facing A/B Testing Framework for Agent Configuration

The Gap

The spec has an internal canary rollout mechanism for Space Type versions, but builders have no framework for A/B testing their agent configurations. A builder who wants to test 'Does prompt variant A or prompt variant B lead to higher user satisfaction?' has no platform support. They would need to implement random assignment, variant tracking, and statistical analysis themselves — a significant engineering burden that few no-code builders can manage.

Required Fix

Build a builder-facing A/B testing framework: builders define an experiment in the dashboard: {name: 'Prompt Clarity Test', variants: [{name: 'control', agent_config_id: 'abc'}, {name: 'treatment', agent_config_id: 'def'}], split: 50}. On each new session, the platform randomly assigns the user to a variant (stored in AssistantDO SQLite per user). All agent invocations for that session use the assigned variant's agent config. Track per-variant metrics: session length, messages sent, task completion rate, subscription conversion. Dashboard shows: variant sample sizes, conversion rates, and a statistical significance indicator (p-value < 0.05 = winner detected). Allow builders to declare a winner and roll out 100% to the winning variant.

G-AL30 HIGH Analytics — Event Tracking

No Custom Event Tracking SDK for Builder-Defined Business Events

The Gap

The platform captures system events (session started, agent invoked, message sent, subscription created) automatically. But builders cannot instrument their own business events: 'User clicked the upgrade CTA', 'User completed the onboarding checklist', 'User exported their data'. Without custom events, builders cannot build funnel analyses based on their specific product flows.

Required Fix

Add a Custom Events API: POST /spaces/{id}/events with payload {event: 'user_completed_onboarding', user_id, properties: {duration_ms, steps_completed}}. Events are stored in Analytics Engine with the space_id, event name, user_id, and properties (up to 10 string properties). Expose a JavaScript SDK snippet builders can embed in their product UI: naelao.track('button_clicked', {button_id: 'upgrade-cta'}). Rate limit: 1000 custom events per minute per Space (free), 10k/min (pro). Custom events appear in the Analytics dashboard alongside system events. Builders can use custom events as funnel steps or A/B test outcome metrics. This makes the analytics platform as powerful as Mixpanel or Amplitude for builder products.

G-AL31 CRITICAL Analytics — Analytics Engine Limits

Analytics Engine index1-Only Indexed Field Causes Silent Dashboard Query Failures

The Gap

Cloudflare Analytics Engine only indexes the indexes[0] field (mapped to index1 in the schema). Multiple workers emit events with analytics data in indexes[1] and indexes[2] positions (e.g., space_type_id in index2, agent_id in index3). These fields are silently dropped or return empty query results when used as filters. Security event dashboards that query index2 return no results — operators believe there are no security events when in fact the query never matched.

Required Fix

Audit every Analytics Engine writeDataPoint() call in the codebase. Verify that all event fields intended for filtering or grouping are placed in indexes[0] (the only indexed field). For events that require filtering on multiple dimensions, encode a compound key in indexes[0]: e.g., '{space_id}|{event_type}' and use LIKE prefix matching. Move all non-filterable metadata fields to blobs[] positions. Add a unit test that verifies each event schema sends the intended data in indexes[0]. Add a Analytics Engine query validation step in CI: run test queries against the staging Analytics Engine and assert non-empty results for each event type. Document the indexes[0]-only limitation prominently in the developer analytics guide.

G-AL32 HIGH Analytics — Data Quality

No Event Schema Versioning — Analytics Schema Changes Break Historical Dashboards

The Gap

Analytics Engine events have no schema version field. When the platform changes the shape of an event (renames a field, adds a required dimension, changes a blob position), historical dashboard queries that relied on the old schema silently return wrong results. There is no migration path for historical data and no way to query across event schema versions.

Required Fix

Add a schema_version field (integer) to every Analytics Engine writeDataPoint() call, stored in blobs[19]. Dashboard queries include a WHERE schema_version IN (1, 2) clause to handle both old and new schemas. When an event schema changes: increment schema_version, add a migration note to the event schema registry (a KV-backed schema documentation store), and update dashboard queries to handle both versions during a 30-day transition window. After 30 days, drop support for the old version. Publish the event schema registry as a developer-facing reference at developers.naelao.com/analytics/events with field documentation per schema version.

G-AL33 MEDIUM Analytics — User Research

No Session Replay or User Journey Visualization for Builder Products

The Gap

Builders have quantitative analytics (counts, rates) but no qualitative analytics. They cannot watch a recording of how a specific user navigated their product, identify where users click repeatedly (rage clicks), or understand which UI interactions lead to abandonment. Session replay tools are the standard way product teams identify UX friction — without them, builders are flying blind on UX quality.

Required Fix

Offer an optional FullStory / PostHog session replay integration for builder products. Builders who enable session replay add a lightweight JS snippet (provided by the platform) to their product UI. Session recordings are stored in FullStory or PostHog (builder chooses); the platform provides a deep-link from the Analytics dashboard to the session recording for any specific session_id. Privacy controls: builders must add a 'Session Recording' disclosure in their product's privacy notice. PII masking: mask all input[type=password] and any input with data-pii=true attribute. GDPR compliance: session recordings are automatically deleted after 90 days.

G-AL34 HIGH Analytics — GDPR

Analytics Engine Events Cannot Be Deleted — GDPR Per-User Erasure Is Impossible

The Gap

Cloudflare Analytics Engine is a write-only append store — individual events cannot be deleted. When a user exercises GDPR Article 17 right to erasure, their Analytics Engine event data (which includes user_id in index1 or blobs) cannot be removed. The erasure pipeline handles SQLite (delete rows), R2 (delete objects), and Vectorize (delete vectors) but cannot delete Analytics Engine events. This is a permanent GDPR compliance gap as long as user_id or any PII is written to Analytics Engine.

Required Fix

Restructure Analytics Engine event data to avoid storing PII or GDPR-erasable identifiers: replace user_id with a pseudonymous, rotatable handle — a HMAC of user_id keyed by a per-Space erasure key. On GDPR erasure: delete the Space's erasure key from KV (this makes all existing Analytics Engine events for that user non-linkable, satisfying GDPR pseudonymization obligations). New events after erasure use a new erasure key. This approach is endorsed by regulators as a privacy-by-design pseudonymization technique. Document this design decision in the platform privacy whitepaper and add it to the GDPR controls catalogue.

G-AL35 HIGH IaC / DevOps — Infrastructure Provisioning

No Terraform or Pulumi IaC for Cloudflare Resource Provisioning

The Gap

KV namespaces, R2 buckets, Queues, Vectorize indexes, and Durable Object classes are created manually in the CF dashboard or via one-off wrangler CLI commands. There is no declarative IaC representing the full CF resource topology. This means: (1) No reproducible environment setup for staging or DR. (2) No change history for infrastructure (who created this KV? when? why?). (3) Environment drift (staging missing a Queue that production has). (4) No PR review for infrastructure changes.

Required Fix

Adopt the Cloudflare Terraform provider (cloudflare/cloudflare) or Pulumi CF provider (pulumi-cloudflare) to declare all CF resources as code. Commit the IaC to the monorepo under /infra/. Each environment (dev, staging, prod) has its own .tfvars file with account IDs and zone IDs. CI/CD: terraform plan runs on every PR touching /infra/; human approval required before terraform apply. Add a drift detection step: a daily scheduled job runs terraform plan -refresh-only and alerts if it detects changes not reflected in the IaC (manual dashboard changes). This is the foundation for reproducible staging and disaster recovery environments.

G-AL36 MEDIUM IaC / DevOps — Dependency Management

Wrangler Version Is Unpinned — Surprise Breaking Changes From Automatic Upgrades

The Gap

wrangler (the CF Workers CLI) is not pinned to a specific version in the project's package.json or CI configuration. CF frequently releases wrangler updates that change behavior (different toml parsing, new defaults, changed secret handling). An automatic npm upgrade on the CI server could silently change worker build behavior, causing a deploy that fails in non-obvious ways. The spec references a commented-out Hyperdrive binding issue that was caused by a wrangler parsing ambiguity.

Required Fix

Pin wrangler to a specific patch version in package.json: "wrangler": "3.XX.Y" (no caret prefix). Add a Renovate or Dependabot configuration that creates automated PRs for wrangler version upgrades (rather than auto-applying them). Each wrangler upgrade PR runs the full test suite and performs a staging deploy before the PR can be merged. Additionally: pin the Node.js version used in CI with .nvmrc and require the same version in package.json engines field. Document the wrangler upgrade process in the runbook: review the wrangler CHANGELOG for breaking changes, run staging deploy, verify all workers start correctly, then merge.

G-AL37 HIGH IaC / DevOps — Environment Management

No Environment-Specific Configuration Injection in the Deployment Pipeline

The Gap

All workers share a single wrangler.toml per worker with environment-specific values (staging vs production endpoints, feature flags, rate limit thresholds) hardcoded as string literals or absent. There is no systematic mechanism for injecting environment-specific values at deploy time. Developers accidentally deploy production-pointed code to staging, or staging code to production, because environment injection is manual and error-prone.

Required Fix

Implement environment-specific configuration using wrangler's [env] stanza and a centralized config injection step. Define three environments: dev, staging, prod. Each environment has its own wrangler.[env].toml overlay with environment-specific bindings (staging KV namespace IDs, staging Queue IDs, staging Vectorize indexes). The CI/CD pipeline selects the correct overlay based on the target branch (main → prod, staging/* → staging, dev/* → dev). Add a pre-deploy check: the deployment script reads the target environment from the branch name and validates it against the allowed environments for that branch. Prevent direct prod deploys from feature branches.

G-AL38 HIGH IaC / DevOps — Database Migrations

DO SQLite Schema Migrations Have No Rollback Strategy

The Gap

SpaceDO and other DOs apply SQL schema migrations using a migrations array of {sql, rollbackSql} objects. The rollbackSql field is declared but not required — most migration definitions omit it. If a migration fails midway (SQL syntax error, constraint violation, timeout), the DO is left in an inconsistent partial-migration state with no automated rollback. The migration version counter may advance past the failed migration, preventing retry.

Required Fix

Require rollbackSql for all migrations with schema changes (ALTER TABLE, CREATE TABLE, DROP COLUMN). Enforce this in the migration schema type definition (TypeScript: rollbackSql: string, not optional). Wrap each migration in a SQLite transaction (BEGIN → run SQL → COMMIT, or ROLLBACK on error). If the migration transaction fails, execute the rollbackSql before rethrowing the error, and decrement the migration version counter to allow retry. Add a migration dry-run mode: before applying migrations to a production DO, execute them in a test DO (created with a schema copy) to validate success. Test all migrations in the integration test suite against a realistic dataset.

G-AL39 HIGH IaC / DevOps — Deployment Strategy

No Blue-Green or Gradual Traffic Split Deployment for Cloudflare Workers

The Gap

CF Workers support instant deploys only: wrangler deploy immediately routes 100% of traffic to the new version. There is no native blue-green deployment or gradual traffic split (1% → 10% → 100%). A bad deploy that passes tests but fails in production immediately affects 100% of users. Rollback requires a re-deploy, which takes 30-60 seconds during which all users are on the broken version.

Required Fix

Implement application-level blue-green deployment using Durable Objects and KV: (1) Deploy the new Worker version with a new name suffix (naelao-agents-v2). (2) The naelao-router reads an active_version key from KV (updated atomically). (3) Route 1% of requests to naelao-agents-v2 via a random hash on session_id. (4) Monitor error rate for naelao-agents-v2 via Analytics Engine; if error rate > baseline by 1%: automatically revert active_version to v1. (5) Gradually increase the rollout: 1% → 5% → 20% → 100% with a 15-minute dwell time and error rate check at each step. This pattern adds ~5ms latency for the KV read but provides sub-minute rollback with zero traffic loss.

G-AL40 HIGH IaC / DevOps — API Contracts

No Cross-Worker API Contract Testing in CI Pipeline

The Gap

Workers communicate via Service Bindings with no versioned API contract. When Worker A changes its request format (adds a required field, renames a parameter, changes a response type), Worker B fails at runtime with no CI warning. There is no contract test that validates Service Binding compatibility before deploy. The first indication of a contract break is a runtime error in production.

Required Fix

Implement Pact contract testing between all Workers that communicate via Service Bindings. Each consumer Worker defines a Pact contract: 'When I call naelao-billing.chargeCredits({amount: number}), I expect {success: boolean, balance: number}'. Each provider Worker runs a Pact verifier in CI: it receives the recorded interactions from the consumer's contract and verifies its own responses match. Contract tests run before integration tests in CI. Failed contract tests block the deploy. Store Pact contracts in a PactBroker (or a Naelao-internal R2 bucket). This eliminates runtime API contract surprises and makes Service Binding interface changes a first-class PR review item.

G-AL41 MEDIUM IaC / DevOps — Drift Detection

No Infrastructure Drift Detection — Manual CF Dashboard Changes Silently Diverge From IaC

The Gap

Platform operators sometimes make emergency changes directly in the CF dashboard (add a KV namespace, update a route, change a WAF rule) without updating the IaC. These manual changes accumulate over time, causing the IaC to no longer reflect the actual running infrastructure. The next terraform apply overwrites the manual changes. There is no alerting on infrastructure drift, no record of out-of-band changes, and no reconciliation workflow.

Required Fix

Enable Terraform drift detection via a scheduled CI job: run terraform plan -refresh-only daily and alert (Slack / PagerDuty) if the plan shows any differences between IaC state and actual CF resources. Additionally: enable CF Audit Logs (available on all plans) and stream them to the SIEM. Alert on any API call that creates, modifies, or deletes a CF resource outside of the expected CI/CD service account: alert.rule = 'actor not in [ci-service-account] AND resource_type in [kv_namespace, r2_bucket, zone_ruleset]'. Create a standard process for emergency manual changes: apply the change, immediately create a PR to reflect it in IaC, with a post-incident review within 24 hours.

G-AL42 CRITICAL Database Scaling — DO SQLite Limits

DO SQLite 10GB Limit Has No Approaching-Limit Warning or Automated Migration

The Gap

Cloudflare Durable Objects SQLite storage has a 10GB hard limit per DO. SpacesDO stores all conversation history, agent definitions, knowledge documents, and workflow state for an entire builder product in a single DO. High-volume Spaces (popular products with millions of messages) will approach this limit over time. The spec acknowledges the limit but documents no mechanism for: detecting approach (threshold alert), warning the builder, or automatically migrating to Turso when the limit approaches.

Required Fix

Add a storage monitoring alarm to every SpaceDO: the hourly alarm handler checks current SQLite storage usage via a SELECT page_count * page_size AS size_bytes FROM pragma_page_count(), pragma_page_size(). If usage exceeds 7GB (70% of limit): send a builder notification and emit an alert. If usage exceeds 9GB (90%): trigger automatic migration initiation to Turso. The migration pipeline: (1) Provision a Turso database for this Space. (2) Export all SQLite tables to Turso via streaming INSERT. (3) Verify row counts match. (4) Switch the Space to Turso read/write mode. (5) Compact the DO SQLite (VACUUM) and retain only the last 30 days of data. Test the migration pipeline monthly with a high-volume test Space.

G-AL43 HIGH Database Scaling — Read Scaling

Hot-Spot SpaceDO Serializes All Reads — No Horizontal Read Scale Pattern

The Gap

CF Durable Objects are single-instance: all requests (reads and writes) for a given Space are serialized through one DO. For read-heavy Spaces (a popular product where thousands of users are simultaneously fetching agent definitions, conversation history, and knowledge articles), all reads queue behind each other. There is no read replica pattern, no edge cache for frequently-read DO data, and no documentation of what happens when DO request queue depth grows large.

Required Fix

Implement a tiered read pattern for high-read-rate data: (1) Agent definitions, Space config, and knowledge article metadata are read-only after creation (or version-stamped). Cache these in KV with a 60-second TTL: kv.put(`space:${id}:agents`, JSON.stringify(agents), {expirationTtl: 60}). All Workers read from KV cache first; only on cache miss do they fall through to SpaceDO. (2) For rapidly-changing data (conversation messages, live usage counts): continue routing through SpaceDO but add a request coalescing layer: multiple concurrent requests for the same data are deduplicated to a single DO call. (3) For analytics data: route to Analytics Engine (already done in spec) rather than SpaceDO SQL. Measure DO request queue depth via Analytics Engine; alert if queue depth > 100.

G-AL44 HIGH Database Scaling — SQLite Configuration

WAL Mode Status in DO SQLite Is Undocumented — Concurrent Behavior Is Unknown

The Gap

The spec references 'WAL-based recovery' but never explicitly states whether Cloudflare DO SQLite enables WAL (Write-Ahead Logging) mode. WAL mode allows concurrent readers with a single writer — without it, SQLite uses DELETE journal mode which blocks all readers during a write. Given that SpaceDO handles both writes (new messages) and reads (load agent config) in overlapping requests, the concurrency behavior depends critically on whether WAL is enabled. Without knowing, the team cannot reason about DO performance under concurrent load.

Required Fix

Explicitly enable WAL mode in SpaceDO's initialization: add PRAGMA journal_mode=WAL; as the first SQL executed on DO startup. Verify CF's DO SQLite actually supports WAL mode (test in a staging DO by reading PRAGMA journal_mode after setting it). If WAL is supported: document the confirmed behavior in the architecture guide. Also set PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL (not FULL) for better write throughput in WAL mode while maintaining crash safety. Set PRAGMA wal_autocheckpoint=1000 to prevent WAL file from growing unboundedly. If CF does not support WAL mode, document the single-writer contention implications and implement a write-coalescing queue in the DO to batch writes.

G-AL45 MEDIUM Database Scaling — Query Patterns

N+1 Query Pattern in Agent List and Thread List Endpoints

The Gap

The agent list endpoint fetches all agents in a Space (SELECT * FROM agents WHERE space_id = ?), then for each agent, makes a separate SQL call to fetch its tools, its last-run stats, and its config. For a Space with 50 agents, this is 50×3 = 150 additional SQL queries per list request. SQLite executes these synchronously in the DO single-thread, adding significant latency. Similar N+1 patterns exist in the thread list (fetch threads, then fetch last message per thread) and knowledge base list.

Required Fix

Replace N+1 query patterns with JOIN-based or CTE-based queries: for the agent list endpoint, use a single query that JOINs agents with their associated tools using a LEFT JOIN and aggregates tool data via GROUP_CONCAT. For thread list: JOIN threads with the last message per thread using a correlated subquery or ROW_NUMBER() window function (supported in SQLite 3.25+). For knowledge base list: include document count and last-updated-at in the main list query via a GROUP BY subquery. Add a query latency assertion to the test suite: agent list for a Space with 50 agents must complete in < 10ms in the test DO.

G-AL46 HIGH Database Scaling — SQLite Indexes

LIKE Full Table Scan on Knowledge Keyword Search and Missing Indexes on High-Frequency Tables

The Gap

Knowledge keyword search uses LIKE '%term%' — a leading-wildcard pattern that cannot use a B-tree index and forces a full table scan of the knowledge documents table. For Spaces with thousands of documents, this scan adds seconds of latency per search. Additionally, the token_buffer table cleanup and the threads/runs tables lack indexes on columns that are used in WHERE clauses of frequent queries (created_at, status, space_id combinations).

Required Fix

Fix keyword search: replace LIKE '%term%' with SQLite FTS5 full-text search. Create a virtual FTS5 table: CREATE VIRTUAL TABLE knowledge_fts USING fts5(content, content_id, tokenize='unicode61'). Keep it synchronized with the knowledge_documents table via INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE triggers. FTS5 supports: exact phrase search, prefix search (term*), AND/OR/NOT operators, and snippet highlighting. Fix missing indexes: add composite indexes for all high-frequency query patterns: CREATE INDEX idx_threads_space_created ON threads(space_id, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_runs_space_status ON agent_runs(space_id, status, created_at DESC). Run EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN on all DO SQL queries in the test suite and assert that none show 'SCAN TABLE' (full table scan).

G-AL47 HIGH Database Scaling — Migration

Turso Migration Threshold Undefined — No Automated Trigger for DO-to-Turso Promotion

The Gap

The spec mentions Turso as the solution for Spaces that outgrow DO SQLite's 10GB limit, but never documents: the storage size threshold that triggers migration, whether migration is automatic or manual, the migration procedure step-by-step, how to handle in-flight requests during migration, or the Turso plan required (and its connection limits). Without this, large Spaces will hit the 10GB wall with no recovery path.

Required Fix

Define and automate the DO-to-Turso migration pipeline: trigger at 70% DO storage usage (7GB). Migration steps: (1) SpaceDO.startMigration(): set a migration_in_progress flag in SQLite, reject new writes with 503. (2) Stream all SQLite tables to Turso via the Turso HTTP API (libsql transactions, 1000 rows/batch). (3) Verify integrity: row counts, checksum of random sample rows. (4) Atomically update the Space's db_backend field in SpaceRegistryDO from 'do-sqlite' to 'turso'. (5) Clear the migration flag; resume accepting writes (now to Turso). (6) Keep DO SQLite as a read replica for 7 days, then VACUUM to reclaim space. Test migration monthly with a canary Space. Publish migration status in the builder dashboard.

G-AL48 HIGH Database Scaling — Cross-DO Queries

No Cross-DO Federated Query Pattern — HybridQueryDO Is a Stub With No Implementation

The Gap

The spec references a HybridQueryDO that 'federates reads across shards' for large Spaces that have been sharded across multiple DOs. However, this component has zero implementation details: no query semantics, no consistency model, no handling of partial results from a shard that is slow or unavailable, and no documented API. Builders who shard their Space across multiple DOs have no supported pattern for querying across them.

Required Fix

Implement HybridQueryDO as a coordinator pattern: (1) It maintains a shard registry: {shard_id, do_stub, row_ranges}. (2) For a given query, it determines which shards are relevant (range partitioning by created_at or space_id hash). (3) It dispatches the query to each relevant shard DO in parallel via Service Binding RPC. (4) It aggregates results: UNION for row results, SUM/MAX for aggregations. (5) It handles partial failures: if a shard is unavailable, return partial results with a shard_unavailable warning in the response headers. Consistency model: eventual (shard results are from the shard's current committed state). Document the limitations and use cases in the architecture guide.

G-AL49 HIGH Database Scaling — Transaction Safety

Multi-Step DO Alarm Handlers Not Wrapped in SQLite Transactions — Partial State on Failure

The Gap

DO alarm handlers execute multi-step sequences: billing aggregation writes credits, then updates subscription status, then marks the alarm as complete. If the DO crashes or times out after the first write but before the last, the DO is left in inconsistent partial state. The next alarm re-runs and may double-charge or skip processing. The spec declares rollbackSql for migrations but alarm handler jobs are not transactionally safe.

Required Fix

Wrap all multi-step alarm handler SQL in explicit SQLite transactions: const tx = this.ctx.storage.sql; tx.exec('BEGIN IMMEDIATE'); try { /* all alarm handler SQL */ tx.exec('COMMIT'); } catch (e) { tx.exec('ROLLBACK'); throw e; }. For alarm handlers with both SQL and side effects (HTTP calls to Stripe, queue messages): structure the handler as: (1) Write to a pending_operations SQLite table within a transaction. (2) Execute side effects (HTTP calls). (3) On success, delete the pending_operations row within a transaction. On failure: the pending_operations row remains; the next alarm run retries. This two-phase pattern ensures at-least-once execution with idempotency keys on side effects.

G-AL50 HIGH Database Scaling — Index Coverage

SpaceDO SQLite Lacks Composite Indexes for Multi-Column Queries — Slow at Scale

The Gap

The SpaceDO SQLite schema has indexes on individual columns (space_id, created_at, status) but lacks composite indexes for the actual query patterns that combine multiple WHERE clauses. A query like SELECT * FROM agent_runs WHERE space_id = ? AND status = 'running' AND created_at > ? cannot use any single-column index efficiently — SQLite uses the most selective single-column index and then filters remaining rows. For Spaces with millions of agent runs, this causes multi-second query latency.

Required Fix

Audit all frequent query patterns in SpaceDO and create composite indexes matching their WHERE + ORDER BY patterns: CREATE INDEX idx_runs_space_status_created ON agent_runs(space_id, status, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_messages_thread_created ON messages(thread_id, created_at DESC); CREATE INDEX idx_knowledge_space_type ON knowledge_documents(space_id, doc_type, created_at DESC). Run ANALYZE after creating indexes so SQLite's query planner uses them. Add a query performance test suite: populate a test SpaceDO with 1M rows per table and assert that each query template runs in < 50ms using EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN verification. Run this test as a weekly performance regression check.
